title: After 7 months, Glasswing overwelms maintainers with underwhelming findings
body_text: After 7-months, Glasswing Overwelms Maintainers with Underwhelming Findings | Blog | VulnCheck Products Government Resources Community Company Partners Sign In / Join Sign In Go back November 9, 2026 After 7-months, Glasswing Overwelms Maintainers with Underwhelming Findings Patrick Garrity in/patrickmgarrity/ ai cve kev VulnCheck Community gives you free access to VulnCheck KEV, NVD++, Initial Access Community, and VulnCheck XDB Join Now Key Takeaways: Seven months into Project Glasswing, VulnCheck has tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic, roughly 0.5% of all CVEs published this year, with only two identified as exploited in the wild. Of Anthropicâs 37,966 reported findings, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public and just 217 have been marked fixed. Since September, Anthropic has added nearly 12,000 findings while recording just 15 additional fixes, widening the gap between discovery and remediation. Roughly 1,654 findings (4.4%) have been marked as duplicates, nearly eight times the number fixed, and another 419 have been withdrawn. Anthropicâs claimed true positive rate has risen from 90.8% to 94.2%, raising questions about how it accounts for duplicates and withdrawn findings. Anthropicâs OSS Scanner shifts validation work to maintainers, with curl rejecting 19 of 34 published reports as vulnerabilities, confirming six as low severity and leaving nine awaiting assessment. Also putting Anthropic's true positive rates into question. We're seven months into Anthropic's flagship Project Glasswing, and it's time for another update on the results. I've been tracking the project to see whether its claims are overhyped or grounded in reality. As we all recall, Anthropic launched Project Glasswing on April 7th, claiming, "We have identified thousands of additional high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we are working on responsibly disclosing to open source maintainers." What surprised me was how little evidence the project offered, which made me wonder whether this was more of an overhyped marketing campaign. That said, we shouldn't overlook that AI is an effective tool for finding vulnerabilities. But that story goes well beyond any single frontier model's capabilities. If you're just catching up, this builds on my earlier posts: Tracking CVEs Attributed to Anthropic Researchers and Project Glasswing - April 15 Observations on Anthropic's Vulnerability Disclosure Ledger - June 9 1H-2026 State of Exploitation Report - July 28 The Anthropic Glasswing Receipts Are Starting to Trickle In - September 8 So let's look at the resultsâ¦ Tracking Anthropic-Discovered Vulnerabilities I started tracking Anthropic's discovered vulnerabilities on April 17th, shortly after launch, in an open source repo called Anthropic Credited CVEs . The goal was to see whether Anthropic's claims lived up to the hype. This was before Anthropic launched its own disclosure ledger , which is only updated in infrequent bulk batches. My repo tracks every vulnerability attributable to Anthropic using CVE records, GHSAs, Linux kernel commits, and Anthropic's own ledger. I also manually audit advisories to catch CVEs that might otherwise get overlooked. After seven months, I've tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic. That's an average of just 63 per month. Out of the 93,450 CVEs published this year, that's only about 0.5% of all CVEs. For comparison, Anthropic's own public ledger lists just 217 fixed vulnerabilities, so I've tracked more than twice as many as Anthropic has disclosed itself. The Danger Narrative Isn't Adding Up You may recall that Glasswing launched with the message that we'd entered the Mythos era of vulnerability discovery. But are these vulnerabilities actually useful to attackers? To find out, I've been tracking Anthropic-discovered CVEs against VulnCheck KEV. So far, only 2 of the 442 have been exploited in the wild, just 0.45%. (CVE-2026-61500 and CVE-2026-26980) Anthropic's Ledger Continues to Underwhelm When Anthropic first launched its ledger in May, it reported 23,019 findings and a 90.8% true positive rate. As of its most recent update on November 2nd, there are 37,966 findings and just 217 fixes. That looks like a staggering failure to me, but let's take a closer look. Of the 37,966 findings Anthropic reports, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public. Just 217 of those have been marked fixed. The more glaring number is that 4.4% (1,654) of the project's findings have already been marked as duplicates, 7.5x more duplicates than fixes. On top of that, 419 findings have been withdrawn. It seems odd that the ledger now claims a 94.2% true positive rate, up from 90.8% at launch, when more findings have been withdrawn or marked as duplicates than fixed, likely a feedback loop missing to the triage rates listed as âTrue Positivesâ. The trend since my September update is even more telling: September 8 November 2 Change Total findings 26,153 37,966 +11,813 Made public 2,736 (10.5%) 7,349 (19.4%) +4,613 Fixed 202 217 +15 Withdrawn 245 419 +174 Duplicates 2 1,670 +1,668 Claimed true positive rate 91.4% 94.2% +2.8 pts In two months, Anthropic added nearly 12,000 findings and fixed just 15 more. Duplicates went from two to thousands, which is exactly what I warned about in September: the longer findings sit, the more likely someone else finds and fixes them first. I don't know how anyone can read these numbers as anything but damning. You may also notice a correction in my visual. There appears to be a bug on Anthropic's ledger that inflates the number of findings marked as disclosed. Check for yourself using the "disclosed" filter. Anthropic's Pivot to OSS Scanner Having humans triage every finding clearly didn't scale, and Anthropic has said as much. In its OSS Scanner launch post on October 8th, Anthropic said it had found more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities but had manually reviewed only about 6,000, and that it remains "bottlenecked on our human capacity to validate these findings." It had also already sent nearly 5,000 unverified reports to maintainers who asked for everything in bulk. So with the Glasswing open source initiative hitting a wall, launching a self-service OSS Scanner that projects can opt into makes sense. Maintainers can now request a scan and triage the findings themselves. Anthropic is upfront that these reports are "fully model-generated, without human review or triage" and that "it is possible reports will be incorrect or invalid." In other words, the triage bottleneck didn't go away. It moved to the maintainers. If the true positive rate is really as high as Anthropic claims, that shouldn't be a problem. curl Gives Anthropic's OSS Scanner a Reality Check Three days ago, Daniel Stenberg , who maintains curl, announced that the project had received a batch of 45 vulnerability reports from Anthropic. Anthropic rated only one as medium severity and the rest as low. Daniel is moving them over to GitHub at a deliberate pace "to soften the impact for the team," with plans to have them all published by the end of the week. This gives us a rare look at what Anthropic's findings look like once a maintainer actually validates them. Of the 34 reports published so far, 19 have been marked as not a vulnerability, 6 have been confirmed as low severity, and 9 are still awaiting assessment. That puts the false positive rate at 55.9% so far, and only 17.6% of findings have been confirmed, all of them low severity. That's a lot of work dumped on open source maintainers for a small handful of low-impact bugs, and when a maintainer has to pace reports just to protect his team, that says plenty about the burden. This also isn't new for curl. Back in May, Daniel wrote that five Mythos findings boiled down to a single confirmed vulnerability. It's a far cry from the 94.2% true positive rate Anthropic currently claims on its ledger. It also undercuts the "high- and critical-severity" framing Glasswing launched with. In September, I found that Claude rated 91.5% of ledger findings as critical or high, while maintainers rated only 51.3% that way. I'm curious whether other open source projects are seeing the same thing. curl took a bold move by deciding to publish low and medium vulnerabilities findings publicly as issues for full transparency and we encourage other open source maintainers to follow their lead. Takeaways After Seven Months AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities, and I'm not discounting that. But seven months in, the evidence still doesn't match the launch narrative. The CVEs are a sliver of this year's total, almost none are being exploited, fixes have stalled while duplicates and withdrawals pile up, and the triage burden is shifting onto the open source maintainers Glasswing promised to help. The receipts keep coming in. They still don't reconcile. body_text: Neil Fraser: News: .name Grandfathered Neil's News   2026   .name Grandfathered   Request for Reconsideration   .name Termination   Blockly AGC   2025   2024   2023   2022   2021   2020   2019   2018   2017   2016   2015   2014   2013   2012   2011   2010   2009   2008   2007   2006   2005   2004   2003   2002 .name Grandfathered 10 November 2026 We won! After a long and expensive battle, news just dropped that Verisign is retracting its plan to terminate 22,000 domain names and email redirects. Although they will be closing new registrations for 3rd-level .name domains, all existing domains (including this website) and email redirects will remain indefinitely. This was a team effort. It was inspiring how many talented people joined this fight. From Doytchin who kicked everything off, to Jim who flew to Bali to make the case to ICANN in person, to Patrik, Troy, Huyen, Keith, Judy, Erik, and Ryan who wrote formal reconsideration requests, to my lawyers Jan, Flip and Diégo who threw the book at ICANN, to Beverly, Stefan, Vaughan, Irv, Pablo, Larry, Lionel, Daniel, Ori, Markus, Kirk, Ed, Jeremy, Stephan, Matija, Jan, Simon, Mark, and Evan who filed letters of support. I'd also like to sincerely thank selected individuals within ICANN who had the courage to stand up against the bureaucracy. Without exception, everyone I spoke with was a remarkable person. < Previous | Next >   Legal yada yada: My views do not necessarily represent those of my employer or my goldfish. title: Scion is back and is going to sell a kei truck in America
body_text: Scion Is Back! And It's Going To Sell A Freaking Kei Truck In America - The Autopian Skip to content Youtube Facebook-f Twitter Instagram Rss Sign in Register Sign out Account Sign in Register Sign out Account Night Panel Disable Night Panel News Reviews Merch Toys Tips Glovebox Become a Member Menu News Reviews Merch Toys Tips Glovebox Become a Member Home » Scion Is Back! And It’s Going To Sell A Freaking Kei Truck In America Scion Is Back! And It’s Going To Sell A Freaking Kei Truck In America By Leslie Hanna November 10, 2026 11:07 am 91 Comments When Toyota first introduced the Scion marque in 2003, it had one primary goal – sell cars to the younger generation. Its cars were cheaper and available in fun colors with fun names like “High Voltage Yellow” and “xPRESSO.” When I was a kid in the early 2000s, I often dreamed of one day owning a tC in Black Cherry Pearl and enjoyed lovingly calling xBs “toaster cars.” Over half of new Scions sold were to people under 35, and the tC boasted the youngest average buyer age in the entire industry at a sprightly 29. Their sales numbers peaked in 2006, but dropped nearly 75% by 2010. After sustained financial struggle, Toyota retired the marque in 2016. But now, a decade later, everyone’s favorite toaster brand is seemingly back. Today, Toyota announced the official revival of Scion, but instead of being a quirky and budget-conscious line, they are becoming Toyota’s cornerstone of curiosity. Now called “Scion by Toyota,” it is being launched as a “freedom lab” where drivers can, and are encouraged to challenge conventional ways of thinking about mobility through design, vehicle concepts, and features. “Okei,” let’s go. Toyota Their first production vehicle is the KEI-01, an ultra-compact utility truck, otherwise known as a kei truck. Toyota will be using its existing manufacturing infrastructure in Indiana to “produce” them for sale in the American market. “Produce” is in quotation marks because the KEI-01 is quite literally a rebadged Toyota Pixis, which is a rebadged Daihatsu Hijet Jumbo Cab. Based on its initial imagery it is seemingly also still right-hand drive, and there’s no word on if a LHD variant will be available in the future. With its friendly little 660cc engine and CVT transmission, the KEI-01 was certified to meet American low-speed vehicle safety standards, meaning it has a limited top speed of less than 25mph and is only legal on roads with a posted speed limit of less than 35mph. This makes it not really usable as a daily driver, but keeps it in this beautiful sweet spot where it has a shocking number of commercial and agricultural uses. Toyota The KEI-01 has a 600-pound payload (which means cargo and passengers) and a three-way fold-down cargo bed, making it a well-equipped workhorse for use on farms and in warehouses. It’s only about 5 feet wide and 11 feet long, which makes it great for use as a delivery or work vehicle in dense, urban areas like New York City. Believe it or not, it also has 4WD, which means it can traverse uneven terrain in more rural areas with ease. And don’t worry if it’s hot outside, because heat and air conditioning are standard. Toyota It’s worth noting that, while Kei trucks are currently sold new in the U.S. as “mini trucks” through independent distributors, this one is sold directly by Toyota. Before you rush to your local Toyota dealer to place a deposit, I’m going to have to burst your bubble a bit. Initially, the KEI 01 is only going to be available in a low-volume, niche pilot program entirely focused on fleet usage beginning in late 2027. Depending on performance and owner feedback, availability of the KEI-01 may eventually be expanded, but no further information is available from Toyota at the time.   View this post on Instagram   A post shared by The Autopian (@theautopian) The Hybrid Side-By-Side Toyota Two other mobility concepts accompany the KEI-01 in the Scion by Toyota lineup, the SxS Concept and the BXE Concept. The SxS Concept was unveiled at the 2025 SEMA Show as a purpose-built side-by-side all-terrain vehicle ( click here for our coverage). Developed by Toyota North America, the off-road concept is outfitted with a turbocharged four-cylinder from the Tacoma making in the realm of 300hp. You won’t have to worry about your turbo spool scaring away local fauna, as it is equipped with a “Silent Mode,” which allows the driver to switch from the boisterous internal combustion system to a much more civilised fully electric driving mode. Unlike the KEI-01, the SxS Concept is still just that – a concept, with no current plans to have a version available to the public. Toyota Last, but not least, is the BKE Concept. The BKE concept is entirely focused on personal mobility in the outdoors, filling the gap between the utility of the KEI-01 and the pure performance of the SxS Concept. Its small form factor and rugged tires make it an ideal off-roader for traversing narrow paths while being portable enough to stow away when not in use or easily tote around in the back of a car. Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth Pushmeet Kohli and Swarat Chaudhuri Read the technical paper Share Copied How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signalâs cryptographic protocol â long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, weâre sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verificationâmathematically proving code runs correctly without flawsâis the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. How we verified Signal AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signalâs security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human â just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them. But most protocol verification stops at the design level. Our agents went further, proving that the compiled code fulfills the key security properties â such as keeping messages protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised â down to the exact code running on devices. Because real-world vulnerabilities often hide in the gap between design and implementation, bridging this gap makes these proofs vastly more complex. Even at this complexity, our verification process took just four weeks â a task that historically takes expert teams years â proving that Signal's core cryptographic code delivers the security protections our experts specified. To confirm that AlphaProof Code can tell correct code from buggy code, we reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated version of Signal's code. In both cases, the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure. In AlphaProof Code, AI agents help users write a specification, then autonomously prove that the implementation meets it. Every proof is checked by Lean to verify the agents' work. While prior formal verification focused on smaller portions of the code, Google DeepMind's approach enables significant expansion,â said Ehren Kret, Chief Technology Officer of Signal. âUsing AI agents to translate live code into valid Lean theorems is a major breakthrough. As AI-driven security threats grow, rigorously verifying the Signal protocol implementation gives us even greater confidence in our code's privacy guarantees. Ehren Kret Chief Technology Officer of Signal While prior formal verification work has necessarily focused on smaller scopes, this new approach enables a significant expansion. Traditionally, verifying that production code strictly matches its cryptographic design required extensive manual effort, making the use of AI agents to automatically translate live code into valid Lean theorems a great breakthrough. As AI-driven security threats grow, having the core Signal protocol rigorously verified with automated theorem proving gives us even greater confidence that our code delivers on its privacy guarantees. The future of security Achieving this long-standing challenge demonstrates how AI can bring elite security assurance to businesses, governments, and critical infrastructure, helping defend against agent-driven cyber threats. Verifying Signal's core cryptography lays the groundwork to secure other vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software. Scaling these techniques requires continued research. Paired with automated defense agents like CodeMender , formal verification can help counter the speed and scale of modern cyber threats to create software with mathematical proof that its protections work. We are open-sourcing our formal verification artifacts for community use. Read the technical paper below. Read the technical paper Acknowledgements This research was developed by Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli. We thank Eric Wieser for help with open-sourcing our code, Owen Jones for program management support, and MartÃ­n Abadi, Christopher Henson, Katerina Hristova, Henryk Michalewski, Jonathan Protzenko and George Tsoukalas for helpful discussions. We thank Signal's Rolfe Schmidt, Michael Rosenberg, and Ehren Kret for their feedback on our methodology. title: Smart home devices should work without the internet
body_text: Smart home devices should work without the internet — Do Code That Matters Do Code That Matters Blog About Do Code That Matters Blog About Smart home devices should work without the internet Oct 2026 · 4112 words · 21 min read · Spencer Kittleson Your browser does not support the audio element. Download audio Scissors cutting an ethernet cable under the words No Internet, No Problem. AI;DR: I wrote the first draft, AI helped me edit and rewrite it, and I made the final pass. The rules, setups, and talks are my own. TLDR; Nothing core in my house depends on a vendor’s server. If the internet goes down, the house keeps running. That’s been rule one for about ten years, and my other rules came out of it. This post has the rules, then both talks I’ve given on home automation, slide by slide. Why local My Nest integration worked until Google broke the API. That’s the failure I plan around now. The talks have a few more: a Samsung fridge showing a TLS certificate error on its own screen, and a Camp Chef grill controller that needs Wi-Fi to show you the temperature. Everything that matters runs on hardware I own. That’s Tasmota on ESP boards, an MQTT broker, and Node-RED on a Raspberry Pi. I do use some cloud services, mostly Alexa and a few AWS ones. Alexa is just another way to flip a switch. If it’s down, the wall switches and the wall dashboard still work. The rules From the first talk, restated in the second: No internet, no problem. Core stuff has to work with the internet unplugged. Alexa can be a way in, but never the only way. Don’t remove the old way while adding the new one. If someone tapes a wall switch on so a smart bulb keeps power, I skipped this rule. Be agile. Rooms get used differently and people move in and out, so it all has to be cheap to change. Check your automations. I once had four scheduled triggers hitting the same garden pump. Exceptions must be exceptional. I can break a rule, but only for a reason I’d still agree with six months later. Added after year five, once more people lived in the house: A cloud device needs an API with logs or it doesn’t get installed. I don’t want a black box in the house. Config lives in one place instead of five vendor apps. More than one way in: an app, Alexa, a QR code, or an NFC tag. If I keep doing the same steps, they become a routine. Devices talk pub/sub over MQTT instead of point to point. No batteries unless they last a year or more between changes. Nobody wants to swap a door sensor battery at 2am. The build I get asked about most is the Tasmota sprinkler controller . It’s in both talks, and so is the garage door setup, which has been running about as long. Talk One: Home Automation Nobody needs any of this. I like building things that just work in the background, and each automation is a small puzzle. Everything talks to a cloud now: phones, laptops, thermostats, locks. Those clouds may or may not be up when you need them, so know what you’re signing up for before you plug something in. Most people start here: a thermostat, a plug, a lock. Each has its own app and account. Every device lands somewhere on this triangle. A cloud camera is cheap and easy, and it costs you privacy. A switch I flash myself takes longer to set up, but I can hook it into anything. I figure out where a device lands before I buy it. Someone (often me) automates a light, then has to tape the wall switch on so the smart bulb keeps power. If a switch in a room ever did nothing, this is why. The better fix is an in-wall Wi-Fi switch. The switch still works like a normal switch and I can still automate it. It’s more work to install than a smart plug, but nobody has to change their habits. Rule one: if the internet goes down, my lights still turn on. It’s never done. Rooms get used differently, people move in and out, new devices show up. Whatever you build has to be cheap to change. The garage cooling flow starts from a manual trigger and checks if the door is closed. Then it opens the door, waits, and turns on the fan. If cooling is already running, it just sends a notification. Small flow, but it has kept the garage from baking more than once. The door sensor and reed switch both report into a transform step that sets a global garage-closed flag and logs to Grafana. Below that is the chart from a few real days: 21 opens, with spikes showing when each one happened. It’s easy to skip reporting/alerting. This can alert me if the garage was left open, which is useful when I accidentally leave it open. Four scheduled triggers all hit the same pump. It’s easy to end up with automations fighting over one device, so every so often I check whether they still make sense together. I’ve broken all of these plenty of times, so they’re more like guidelines. Three ways to do “event in, action out.” Node-RED is my main tool. Alexa routines and IFTTT-style applets cover the stuff I don’t want to build myself. MQTT keeps things decoupled. The temperature sensor publishes and doesn’t care who’s listening, so a phone and a backend can both subscribe without the sensor doing anything extra. The sprinkler controller in the Tasmota post works the same way. A Sonoff Mini fits inside the fireplace wiring, and the dashboard or Alexa can flip it. A fake fire you can turn on by voice is a good party trick. The whole sprinkler build: the relay and ESP module in the enclosure, the 3D board render, the Tasmota UI with BME280 sensor readings, the Node-RED schedule feeding the pump, and the finished PCB layout. The sprinkler post has the full writeup, including why I picked Tasmota over custom firmware. It’s a bit hacky but I love it :D The whole talk in five lines. The one I break most is the first, don’t introduce a new way while removing the old one, and I regret it every time. The last one stops me from breaking the others for no good reason. “I was in a hurry” doesn’t count. That was talk one. Most of the “memorable automations” later broke in some new way or got replaced, so there’s a sequel. Talk Two: Home Automation, The Sequel Enough time passed between the talks that I had a new list of problems. More devices means more decisions made without me. It’s a little unsettling but mostly harmless. Same slide as before, with more icons. Everyone else is dealing with this too: a fridge showing a TLS certificate error, a grill controller that needs Wi-Fi to show the temperature, and a note taped to a pole about an internet-connected printer someone forgot to log out of. The same rules from talk one, worded a bit tighter, since part of the audience hadn’t seen the first talk. The rules stayed the same, but what they had to survive got harder. My setup assumed one person lived in the house. When that changed, I had to patch a single-user system into a multi-user one. The next few slides are how that went. More people meant more foot traffic and more keys, and longer trips away meant things could fail with nobody around to notice. A water flooding scare finally got me to take leak and presence detection seriously. Same joke, new rules. The first set came after year one, these after year five. These are rules 6 to 11 at the top of the post, written after the house went from one person to several. Now the builds, my favorite part. A motor and PVC pipe rig for outdoor lighting, a UV grow light clipped to a houseplant, and a UV strip under the cabinets for sanitizing. Same sprinkler slide as talk one. It’s one of the few builds that never needed a rewrite. A sensor that sits on a credenza, a robot vacuum that runs on its own, and an AirGradient kit I put together from a CO2 sensor, a particulate sensor and a microcontroller, with its own dashboard. The air quality kit gives me the most peace of mind of anything here. This dashboard replaced more apps than anything else: garage door, side door unlock, front lock, all lights on or off, brightness, a coffee bar color picker, and warm-to-cool for the living room. It’s one cheap tablet next to the thermostat, so nobody digs through five apps. The lights behind the TV run through the same system instead of their own remote. The smart locks came out of the more-people-more-keys problem. The newer one takes a password, the app, a keycard or a regular key, so everyone uses what they’re comfortable with. The parts bin, for anyone who wants to build this. The ESP32 D1 mini handles anything custom. The smart plug is the off-the-shelf shortcut when I don’t need custom. The Pi 4 runs Node-RED and Grafana. LED strips for ambient lighting, power transistors for higher-current loads, and small relay modules so a microcontroller can switch mains voltage safely. The rest of the bin: a resistor assortment, color-coded wire so I can trace a circuit later, and a capacitor kit for smoothing and timing. Node-RED for the logic, Grafana to see what’s happening, Tasmota on anything I flash, Telegram for notifications, and Python or JavaScript for glue code that doesn’t fit in a flow. The garage flow today. The door sensor and reed switch feed Grafana and a global closed state. Toggle nodes publish straight to Tasmota command topics. Notifications go to Telegram and an audio chime, and a light-on counter resets at midnight. The tabs across the top (Lights, Sensors, Garage, Sprinkler, NFC Tags, Door Lock Security) show how much it has grown since the single garage cooling flow in talk one. This is the “is everything okay” dashboard: humidity, temperature, dew point, pressure and gas on one side, and energy use, door opens and on-status history on the other. I built it because I got tired of guessing. Dashboards and Grafana panels work for me. Everyone else in the house just wants the light on. The “more than one way in” rule in hardware: the wall tablet for whoever is standing there, NFC tags and a QR code to tap, and an Echo Dot for anyone who would rather talk to the house. The tools I build and debug all of this with. A soldering iron for permanent connections, a 3D printer for enclosures and brackets you can’t buy, a multimeter for when something isn’t working, and a precision screwdriver kit for devices the manufacturer didn’t want opened. That’s both talks, five years apart. The rules barely changed between them, but the list of problems kept growing. A third talk is coming, built around agentic use cases. The same rules should hold when an AI agent is the one flipping the switches, and I expect to add a few. What readers told me I shared the “no internet, no problem” rule on LinkedIn and asked for the most pointless internet dependency people had found in a device. Dozens of people answered. A Hacker News thread added more. Here’s what came back. Everyone has one Most examples were basic functions locked behind an app, an account, or a server: A fridge whose temperature can’t be changed because of a bug in the manufacturer’s phone app. A TV that can’t even switch inputs when the internet is down, and another that has to be signed in before it works as a plain HDMI monitor. One reader’s older smart TV has dead apps but still works as a regular TV, which is how a device should fail. A heating system whose app doesn’t work from the local network. A kitchen vent and a dishwasher that need the internet even when you control them from Home Assistant. A smart plug that can’t be set up on an isolated network. Noise-cancelling headphones that search for a Bluetooth device forever, so you can’t just turn on the noise cancelling. Synthesizers and MIDI keyboards that need a cloud login for first use or firmware updates. A meat thermometer that only worked through its app and stopped working when the company went out of business. The meat thermometer bothers me most. The hardware outlived the company, and it stopped working anyway. Rules readers added Offline first, with the internet for extras. A device should do its main job on its own. Treat every third-party dependency as a risk. APIs change, so plan a local fallback or a clear degraded mode. One mobile developer works the same way: the core action works offline or from cache, and only the extras wait for a connection. Decide what must work offline. My answer is turning things on and off, temperature and safety controls, and anything a guest has to use without learning an app. As one reader said, if a visitor can’t turn something on or adjust the temperature without an app account, the design has failed. A stricter version of my first two rules: everything core works with the Wi-Fi or the automation server shut down, and smart features never take away the dumb ones. The wall switch should control the light directly and let automation flip it. A switch that only sends a request to the automation fails. That reader says my sprinkler controller fails this bar too. The only sprinkler controller they’d found with a local API and full control on the device itself was RainMachine, which is gone. Clean up when you throw things away. Remove a connected printer from your account first. An abandoned connected device can be an easy way in for an attacker. Practical tips Use local protocols. One reader recommends Zigbee and Z-Wave over Wi-Fi, because a switch that doesn’t need the cloud tends to behave the same year after year. Another uses Zigbee for the smart plugs that can’t be set up without internet. Let an LLM find the firmware. One reader buys the cheapest hardware that does the job, ignores reviews that complain about the app, and asks an LLM for local-first custom firmware once it arrives. That has worked for their switches, a thermostat, an air quality monitor, a thermometer, and a window fan. They’d have paid about 2.5x for hardware that was local out of the box. Old Nest thermostats have a way out. No Longer Evil is open source firmware for Nest Gen 1 and Gen 2 thermostats. Smart TVs can be tamed. Reset the TV and never connect it to the network, and the input problem goes away. Remote access is the cost of staying local. I use Tailscale on the router and keep the individual devices off the tailnet. One reader ran OpenVPN on OpenWrt, which worked but felt clunky, and is now trying Tailscale. There’s a gap to fill. One reader would happily pay for a pre-built, open “works with everything” Raspberry Pi image with MQTT. DietPi and OpenWrt come close and have a small footprint, but you need some understanding to get going. Another wanted a hub that ships with the house, like a water heater or a router. Home Assistant sells hub hardware that’s close to that. Right to repair is the bigger fight. Readers pointed to the right-to-repair movement and groups like the FULU Foundation , which work to keep companies from locking you out of what you bought. Counterpoints Connectivity has real uses. A connected meat thermometer lets you watch the game while the steak cooks. The same reader also had an oven decide to update its software in the middle of cooking. One reader pointed out the business model behind all of this: companies would rather sell you a service than a product. Another expects the shift away from internet-connected devices to come from resilience worries rather than consumer complaints, since enough connected homes make a target. And one skips connected appliances entirely, keeping only computers and phones online. Devices I’ve used (This section has Amazon affiliate links. If you buy through them, I may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.) These are the parts from my home automation builds, grouped by project. Sprinkler controller Gear Purpose Buy HiLetgo ESP8266 NodeMCU board (3 pack) Wi-Fi microcontroller that runs Tasmota Amazon SSD1306 OLED screen Status display for the sprinkler state Amazon Inkbird SSR-40DA solid state relay Switches the 24 VAC sprinkler valve Amazon BME280 sensor Temperature, humidity and pressure Amazon 24 VAC power supply Powers the sprinkler valve Amazon Lights, switches and plugs Gear Purpose Buy Martin Jerry smart dimmer switch (Tasmota pre-flashed) Wall light switch that runs Tasmota out of the box Amazon Martin Jerry humidity fan switch Runs the bathroom fan when humidity gets too high Amazon Sonoff S31 smart plug Power watchdog for the cable modem Amazon Serial-to-USB adapter Connects an ESP8266 to your PC for flashing Tasmota Amazon Garage door Gear Purpose Buy Raspberry Pi 3 Runs Docker and the web API Amazon SunFounder 2-channel 5V relay module Simulates the button press to toggle the door Amazon LiftMaster wired control panel (78LM, replaces the 41A5273-1) Bypasses the anti-tamper wiring Amazon Around the house Gear Purpose Buy GL.iNet Flint 2 router (GL-MT6000) Runs OpenWrt and an MQTT broker locally Amazon Cheap tablet Mounted on the wall as the dashboard Amazon Lefant robot vacuum Cleans the floors Amazon See something inaccurate or need more detail? title: Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers
body_text: Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers [LWN.net] LWN .net News from the source Content Weekly Edition Archives Search Kernel Security Events calendar Unread comments LWN FAQ Write for us User: Password: | | Log in / Subscribe / Register Synaptics patent claims stop work on DisplayLink drivers [LWN subscriber-only content] Welcome to LWN.net The following subscription-only content has been made available to you by an LWN subscriber. Thousands of subscribers depend on LWN for the best news from the Linux and free software communities. If you enjoy this article, please consider subscribing to LWN . Thank you for visiting LWN.net! By Joe Brockmeier November 10, 2026 Mike Lothian owns a docking station (or dock) that uses a DisplayLink chipset that had, at least in his opinion, subpar performance on Linux. He decided to try improving the Linux driver, with LLM assistance, but ran into one problem that he could not solve—so he asked for help, hoping that Synaptics's developers would lend a hand. (DisplayLink was acquired by Synaptics in 2022.) Rather than help him in improving the driver, however, the Synaptics legal team responded with patent infringement claims, a demand that he cease unauthorized implementation of DisplayLink technology, and threats of expensive legal penalties. For now, it appears that Linux users of the company's docks will have to continue to live without feature parity with other platforms. Synaptics and Displaylink The dock that he was trying to support is a Dell device that connects to a system via USB 3 and allows users to connect multiple monitors and other devices to their computer. It provides its DisplayLink Manager (DLM) software for Linux for the devices via an APT repository for Ubuntu. The company only provides DLM software in binary form, and only for x86-based platforms. The software is proprietary, but the company does maintain an open-source, out-of-tree kernel module that is included with DLM, the Extensible Virtual Display Interface (EVDI) project. It provides a driver that's compatible with Linux DRM and allows users to manage their docked displays with standard tools used for display settings, such as xrandr or GNOME and KDE Plasma's utilities. A short article explains why the company has not released source code for DLM: the software uses a proprietary graphics technology called DL3 to create a compressed stream of the various channels (e.g., USB, DisplayLink video, audio) over a communication channel (USB 3 in this case) and decode it again for output to the user's devices. Unfortunately, the vendor-supplied software did not work well for Lothian. I spoke and chatted with him via Signal while writing this article; he said that the driver kept crashing under Linux, so he decided to use his Claude subscription to try to develop a new driver and support software. Vino He posted the first patch series for Vino—his Rust-based DRM/KMS driver—to the kernel's dri-devel list as an RFC on June 17. Lothian noted that it was in an incomplete state, and asked for help with a blocker that he had run into trying to communicate with the dock's control plane. " If you have knowledge of the DisplayLink DL3 control-plane engagement sequence, or ideas for isolating a whole-bus timing/ordering property a per-channel diff cannot see, help would be very welcome. " He received feedback from a few developers, including guidance from Danilo Krummrich to rework the driver to use the Rust KMS bindings , but no advice specific to the problem he was trying to solve. Lothian also opened an issue on the EVDI GitHub repository on June 17. It explained the work he'd done so far, outlined the approach in trying to reverse-engineer the DL3 protocol, provided links to his GitHub repository with the Vino code, and asked for clarification on a few issues. There was no reply to his issue. He also reached out to Łukasz Spintzyk of Synaptics directly by email; his correspondence with the company between July 5 and October 7 is available in this PDF compiled by Lothian . He noted that he had found a few bugs in EVDI and opened a pull request (that went unreviewed for several months), and also asked for assistance where he was blocked on Vino. On July 20, he received a reply, not from Spintzyk, but from Michal Lukaszek of Synaptics: The reason I'm writing is that DisplayLink is not an open standard. The protocol, codec, and other technologies used by DisplayLink devices are proprietary to Synaptics and are protected by a substantial portfolio of patents in a number of jurisdictions, including the UK. From what you've published, it appears that the VINO project is progressing beyond interoperability work and toward implementing technology that we believe is covered by those patents. While many developers understandably focus on avoiding copyrighted source code, patent law is different. An independently written or clean-room implementation does not necessarily avoid patent infringement if it implements patented inventions. Lukaszek said it was entirely possible that Lothian was unaware of the " intellectual property landscape surrounding DisplayLink ", so he wanted to make him aware now rather than " have the situation become more formal later ". Lothian lives in Scotland and has a ".co.uk" email address, which explains why the email made reference to the UK. Cease and desist On August 17, Andrew Bateman, an assistant general council of intellectual property for Synaptics, sent a cease-and-desist notice . The letter stated that Lothian had not " substantially responded " to Lukaszek's communication, and had continued with " public statements and further development activities ". It included an appendix with a list of 125 patents that " cover fundamental aspects of DisplayLink's architecture and operation ", but did not specify which patents might be infringed by the work. Synaptics included a list of eight demands it expected immediate compliance with, including ceasing development of " any software or other implementation that infringes any Synaptics patent ", withdrawing submissions of materials " made to Linux kernel maintainers, mailing lists, code-hosting platforms, package maintainers, distributions, or any other person or organization ", and to identify in writing every location " in which the relevant materials have been published, submitted, stored, or distributed ". It also demanded that he provide Synaptics with a signed confirmation, by August 28, that he had complied with its demands. Lothian, instead, posted version three of his Vino work for the DisplayLink docks to the dri-devel list on August 26. He said that the previous two versions had " never lit a panel ", but the new work could control three generations of DL3 docks without any vendor software. There were no substantive reviews of the patch set posted to the list, though there were some automated reviews from Sashiko. On August 27, Lothian responded to Bateman and asked him to elaborate on the patents that Synaptics thought were being infringed. " A claim chart mapping the relevant claims to the relevant code would make it much easier for me to understand and properly respond to your concerns. " He also expressed confusion about Synaptics's position that his work was being treated as patent infringement. Synaptics is a member of the Open Invention Network (OIN), which was created to help open-source developers and vendors deal with the threats of expensive patent litigation. It holds a large, cross-licensed portfolio that serves to provide patent protection to individuals, open-source projects, and large vendors alike. Lothian said that he was now an OIN licensee as well, and he thought that it was supposed to " reduce exactly this sort of patent problem around Linux and open source software ". He asked Bateman to explain how Synaptics claims " interact with our respective OIN commitments ", and expressed a desire to sort things out with Synaptics constructively. " I don't think a public dispute between Synaptics and an individual open source developer would be particularly helpful for either of us, especially within the Linux and open source communities ". Lothian did not think he could " reasonably provide the signed undertaking " Synaptics had demanded by August 28 without understanding which patent claims it was alleging. He asked for an extension to the deadline. There was no response from Bateman, so Lothian sent a follow-up email on September 18. He said he was concerned there was no acknowledgment to his last email, and wondered it was safe to assume he could continue his work. He had been running the Vino driver himself for quite a while, and was eager to move it upstream without having patent threats hanging over the work. Bateman responded the next day and said that he should be concerned: As you previously requested, we have been documenting your ongoing patent infringement by mapping your Vino driver to specific claims of our DisplayLink patents. I will provide this claim mapping documentation to you within the next two weeks. I will also be sending to you our demand for substantial monetary compensation to recoup the cost and effort required to create such documentation of your infringing acts. I previously gave you the opportunity to stop your infringement, but you decided to push back and not heed my warnings, and so now we are escalating as we deem appropriate. The letter continued to claim that Lothian would be " single-handedly eviscerating DisplayLink's competitive advantage in this crowded market by educating our competitors and other third parties as to how we implement our proprietary technology ". He said that DisplayLink is not a member of OIN, and none of its technology is licensable through OIN or any other organization. Bateman sent a follow-up letter , dated October 5, that included two claim charts for UK patents: GB2484736B ("Display control device") and GB2485613B ("Image generation"), both filed in 2010 and published in 2012. He reiterated Synaptics's demands from its previous letter, and said that the deadline was now October 11; failure to comply would result in the company seeking " monetary compensation from you in the amount of US$25,000 to recoup the costs and effort required to create the attached documentation of your infringing acts ". That amount would be increased by $25,000 each week until the company's demands were complied with. Lothian responded the next day, by email, to say that he was on vacation, and would not be back home until October 13. He asked for an extension of the deadline to return home and go through the claim charts " ideally with someone qualified to help me read them ". Bateman replied that Synaptics would agree to extend the deadline to October 18, though no further extensions would be granted. He reiterated that " DisplayLink is not a member of OIN " and none of its technology was licensable through OIN. OIN to the rescue? Synaptics is a member of OIN, and is listed in the community directory . In addition to joining OIN, Lothian had reached out to the organization to try to solicit its help and has been in communication with some of the staff there. OIN indicated that it would look into the matter and see if he had any protection as an OIN member. That process took longer than Lothian hoped, though OIN did eventually provide its conclusion. OIN's portfolio covers a wide range of software that matches its Linux System Definition , but it does not cover everything that might be implemented for a Linux system. In particular, its definition specifies that codecs (" a component of a program capable of performing transformations of a video, still image or audio data stream or signal ") are not covered unless specifically mentioned in this list of components. I spoke briefly to OIN CEO Keith Bergelt on October 23, shortly after OIN staff informed Lothian of the result of their research. Bergelt said that OIN's conclusion was that, since codecs are explicitly not covered by OIN's Linux System Definition, its protections did not extend to Lothian's attempted kernel contributions. OIN had recommended that Lothian reach out to a lawyer in the UK, and provided a recommendation. Status Unfortunately, that referral did not pan out, Lothian said. He has not given up entirely, but he has taken down the GitHub repository to comply with Synaptics's demands. For now, he may continue working on some of components that are not affected by the patent claims, but the work on Vino will not be submitted to the kernel. " Vino itself has to remain local until this is sorted out, I just can't afford to defend myself against Synaptics. " Perhaps amusingly, Lothian told me that someone from Synaptics finally replied to the pull request on October 7. Lothian told me he does not intend to follow up on the comments: " You can't threaten to sue me and then say 'can you update your pull request?' " For the time being, Synaptics has succeeded in shutting down an effort to improve the way DisplayLink docks work with Linux. It is an unpleasant reminder that, while much of the current conversations in open-source communities are concerned with LLM-driven development, software patents still pose problems for free-software developers and users. to post comments Surely there is plenty of very old prior art on these? Posted Nov 10, 2026 16:15 UTC (Tue) by paulj (subscriber, #341) [ Link ] GB2485613B seems ludicrous. Its claim appear to be no more than using image compression (in general!) to display to a screen over a general purpose data transport, such as USB, Ethernet, etc., wherein the compressed data is received, demuxed from whatever containing headers, stored, decompressed and displayed. Come on Synaptics... Nonsense. And GB2484736B seems to be about using a Haar wavelet/transform to compress and decompress an image, by way of encoding/decoding sub-groups of the image. I don't know enough about image compression and Haar's transform to know if there is anything novel about, but knowledge of using Haar's transform for image compression goes back to at least the 1970s - e.g., see US4224678A from 1976. The idea of applying compression to an image in sub-groups of the image is surely also long described (??). Anybody want a Foldable Triple Monitor? Posted Nov 10, 2026 16:29 UTC (Tue) by smurf (subscriber, #17840) [ Link ] I bought $SUBJECT last month, expecting it to run well enough on my Linux laptop. No such luck. Obviously, Synaptics wants to be on our boycott lists. Now I only need to find a Windows or Mac user to sell the thing to … … or found/join an underground network for stealth driver development. Kernel driver development on Radicle? LLM prompts Posted Nov 10, 2026 16:42 UTC (Tue) by ianmcc (subscriber, #88379) [ Link ] (5 responses) I wonder, it might be easier to supply some hints on what LLM prompts to use for users to recreate their own driver at home... LLM prompts Posted Nov 10, 2026 16:54 UTC (Tue) by ccchips (subscriber, #3222) [ Link ] (1 responses) Aha! Something I could present to people who whine about AI. Reverse-engineer something for personal use, and keep it to yourself. What are these legal beagles going to do about that? ...and Trump calls it Super Intelligence... I use AI for lots of things, because it saves a lot of time, which is becoming short for me... LLM prompts Posted Nov 10, 2026 21:38 UTC (Tue) by gspr (subscriber, #91542) [ Link ] Here's something us whiners might still whine about: This approach 1) is without sharing. Sharing knowledge and code and understanding is core to the hacker and FOSS ethos. How can you so gleefully ditch that? 2) very often relies on an opaque, non-free third party that can censor or cut you off at any moment. I can't think of anything more antithetical to the hacker and FOSS ethos. LLM prompts Posted Nov 10, 2026 18:46 UTC (Tue) by nhippi (subscriber, #34640) [ Link ] (2 responses) Just let the LLM reverse engineer and write a highly detailed document on how the hardware works. Documentation can't infringe patents. LLM prompts Posted Nov 10, 2026 21:24 UTC (Tue) by roc (subscriber, #30627) [ Link ] (1 responses) Yeah, this is a very interesting workaround for software patents. There's ample precedent that reverse-engineering a system and writing a detailed spec can be done without infringing patents or copyrights. Writing a good test suite should be fine too. Then each user can use an LLM to generate an implementation. I guess those users each individually infringe the patents, but they're impossible to target. LLM prompts Posted Nov 10, 2026 21:50 UTC (Tue) by gspr (subscriber, #91542) [ Link ] This sounds awfully lot like "individual users can probably just use leaked proprietary source code, as long as they do it in secret". What is happening to the FOSS community? Since when did we find that a satisfactory approach? I think LLM assistance in reverse engineering is one of the few good LLM usecases, to be clear. But the proposed approach after that is pure capitulation! synaptics doesnt understand what patents are Posted Nov 10, 2026 18:03 UTC (Tue) by mebrown (subscriber, #7960) [ Link ] (4 responses) The ENTIRE point of patents is to publish in the open the methods used in sufficient detail as to teach others how to use the invention. Their claim that this code does this is just ludicrous when their actual patent does that already. (quite aside from the separate discussion on if they have a valid patent at all). They have a patent on hardware. Even if all this code is published, they still have that hardware patent and can prevent anybody else from producing such hardware. Acting this way to prevent a real driver from being developed is incredibly short sighted of them as it does nothing to affect the actual underlying hardware. As somebody who holds over 50 patents myself and sits on my company patent committee, this is a total face-palm for me. Just misunderstanding and stupidity all around. synaptics doesnt understand what patents are Posted Nov 10, 2026 20:30 UTC (Tue) by IanKelling (subscriber, #89418) [ Link ] (3 responses) > Their claim that this code does this is just ludicrous when their actual patent does that already. I don't really see where you are coming from. The patent gives knowledge but restricts the use of that knowledge in various ways. This is the general premise of patents that you seem to be calling it ludicrous, and I don't follow. synaptics doesnt understand what patents are Posted Nov 10, 2026 21:21 UTC (Tue) by roc (subscriber, #30627) [ Link ] (2 responses) Maybe it's clearer to point out that the following sentence is incompatible with the patent-based legal argument: > By open sourcing our DisplayLink technology for whatever personal reasons you may have as a "hobbyist," you will be single-handedly eviscerating DisplayLink's competitive advantage in this crowded market by educating our competitors and other third parties as to how we implement our proprietary technology, which we have gone to great lengths and great expense to prevent. This sentence seems to be claiming that "DisplayLink's competitive advantage" is a *trade secret*. Patents don't protect trade secrets; in fact it's the opposite --- a patent is supposed to reveal your methods while giving you a monopoly over implementations of them. You could claim that some parts of your technology are patented and others are trade secrets, but you'd have to carefully lay out which parts are which, and the lawyer didn't do that here. synaptics doesnt understand what patents are Posted Nov 10, 2026 21:46 UTC (Tue) by Cyberax ( ✭ supporter ✭ , #52523) [ Link ] Moreover, this is actually a ground for getting the patent revoked: "lack of enablement". synaptics doesnt understand what patents are Posted Nov 10, 2026 21:59 UTC (Tue) by wahern (subscriber, #37304) [ Link ] And any aspects that are trade secrets are fair-game for independent reverse engineering, anyhow. The lawyer is just saber rattling. Crap on every platform Posted Nov 10, 2026 18:17 UTC (Tue) by jbills (subscriber, #161176) [ Link ] If these are the same docks I use at work, then they really aren't much better on Windows. I have constant issues with them, including Low power delivery Long time from connection to display activation Displays sometimes fail to activate on the lock screen Pass through of keyboard and mouse sometimes fails The computer sometimes slows down dramatically until a reboot when connecting to these docks. Previously, I have had issues where the screens would randomly fail to activate at all, requiring disconnecting and reconnecting 3-8 times before activating If somebody wants to come around and knock these guys out of the market with a better product and open source software, that would be amazing and very welcome. Kick Synaptics out of OIN Posted Nov 10, 2026 18:59 UTC (Tue) by bluca (subscriber, #118303) [ Link ] (4 responses) > I spoke briefly to OIN CEO Keith Bergelt on October 23, shortly after OIN staff informed Lothian of the result of their research. Bergelt said that OIN's conclusion was that, since codecs are explicitly not covered by OIN's Linux System Definition, its protections did not extend to Lothian's attempted kernel contributions. This is a ridiculous conclusion? The entire point of OIN was deterrence via mutually assured destruction. Why would it matter if the specific aspect is covered or not? A member of OIN is threatened with patent litigation for open source work on Linux, the appropriate response is to kick Synaptic out of OIN, and aim the patent-cannon at them for everything they have. In theory, yes. In practice, afaik OIN has never ever done this. So I suspect this was done to reduce the pressure to get rid of software patents and has no other real world impact. They will have zero credibility left. I also don't think this is the first time one of these 'wait OIN doesn't protect us???' events has occurred but getting patent clarifications take so long that we forget. title: Val Town is winding down
body_text: Val Town is winding down | Val Town Blog val.town blog.val.town Elsewhere Elsewhere RSS Email Twitter Bluesky Discord YouTube GitHub LinkedIn OSS Pledge Code and prose written on val.town Val Town is winding down Steve Krouse Nov 10, 2026 Dear Val Town community, We’ve made the difficult decision to wind down Val Town. You took a big leap of faith to build on us. We thank you for your trust, and we’re sorry we can’t continue to serve you. The bad news about our business – that we couldn’t compete in the cloud computing space – is good news for you migrating off: there are many wonderful hosting providers you can migrate to, and today’s LLMs are great at these types of migrations. We have guides for migrating to Cloudflare, Vercel, Netlify, and Render. Please reach out if you need help at support@val.town or on Discord. We are pausing billing today, and will continue servicing existing subscriptions for free. If you pre-paid for our annual plan, we will issue you a partial refund. Here’s the timeline on our wind-down: Service End of life date New signups and plan upgrades Nov 10, 2026 (today) Read-only mode (not including sqlite and blob storage) Dec 10, 2026 All other services Jan 10, 2027 Open-sourcing Val Town Feb 1, 2027 Thank you, the members of the Val Town team, for giving it your all over the past four years. Thank you Tom, Jackson, Charlie, Pete, Potluck, Charmaine, Max, Andre, Sophie, Wolf, Justin, Rodrigo and JP. It was an honor. Thank you, Dan Levine, for being the best investor I could’ve asked for. Thank you, my other investors, for your trust, support, and capital. Thank you, our customers and users, for building on us with passion and creativity. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform. Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community. Documentation · Eval Dashboard · Source Code · Report an Issue Quickstart npx modern-web-guidance@latest install This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See Alternative Installation Methods below. Try it out (without installing) # Search for relevant guides npx modern-web-guidance@latest search " animate a dialog modal backdrop " # Retrieve a guide by ID npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve " animate-to-from-top-layer " # Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan . Why? Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions. Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code. Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap. Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on: Modern Browser APIs : Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse. Performance & Accessibility : Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances. Responsible Fallbacks : Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries. What's Included? We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are designed to be token-efficient ; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know. Core Disciplines 🎨 User Experience Smooth visual states (View Transitions, entry/exit animations, parallax scroll, CSS scrollbar-color ). 📐 CSS Layout Modern layout systems (container queries, subgrid , modern color spaces like oklch , text-wrap tuning, and line-height trimming). ⚡ Performance Speed optimizations (instant preloading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) diagnostics, and scheduling tasks via scheduler.yield ). 📝 Forms & UI Native components (Anchor Positioning for tooltips, Popover API, dialogs, :user-invalid validation, and auto-sizing fields). ♿ Accessibility Important considerations (screen reader and keyboard operability, content navigation and discoverability). 🤖 Built-in AI Local client models (native translation, summarization, and language detection APIs).
