canvases, or large data grids—across both directions (whether diagonally or changing direction mid-gesture) without the gesture locking to a single horizontal or vertical axis. anchor-positioning-tab-underline : Transition an element seamlessly between two target element positions. For example, moving a selected tab underline between the previously selected tab and the currently selected tab. animate-element-entry-exit : Smoothly hide/show elements as they are added/removed from the DOM or as their display values are toggled. animate-to-from-top-layer : Animate elements such as dialogs, popovers, and tooltips as they're entering/exiting the top layer. carousel-snap-highlights : Visually highlight the currently snapped non-interactive item in scroll-snapping carousels, galleries, or full-page swipe experiences. For example, expanding a card when snapped, or revealing hidden content. consistent-cross-document-transitions : Ensure critical page state is loaded and stable before initiating a cross-document view transition. This means critical CSS styles are loaded and applied, critical JavaScript is loaded and run, and the HTML visible for the user's initial view of the page has been parsed before the transition runs. cross-document-transitions : Create smooth, seamless transitions between full page navigations, such as cross-fades, custom reveal effects, or morphing of content from one page to the next. custom-button-actions : Declaratively connect a button to any element to trigger custom, application-specific actions using declarative button commands, invoker commands, button commands, custom commands, or declarative toggle actions. declarative-dialog-popover-control : Toggle the visibility of a dialog or popover from a button without writing JavaScript. directional-navigation-transitions : Animate visual state changes to reflect the direction of a user's navigational flow, such as sliding new content in from the right when advancing forward or from the left when returning to a previous screen. drag : Support dragging to move a floating element around the page. drag-and-drop : Support dragging to rearrange the children of a container along one axis (horizontal or vertical) while preserving their state and accessible order. dynamic-sibling-animations : Stagger animation or transition timing across sibling elements so each one starts after a computed delay based on its position in the sibling list. dynamic-sort : Best practices for handling dynamic user-triggered reordering of a container's children (e.g. list items, table rows, or a card grid), with optional animated reordering that respects user preferences, good screen reader UX, and optimal performance for large lists. group-element-transitions : Smoothly rearrange and animate list items, cards, or grid elements into their new positions simultaneously when adding, removing, shuffling, or reordering—such as removing a product from a shopping cart. highlight-text-ranges : Highlight arbitrary text ranges on a page such as search results, spelling errors, or collaborative editing cursors. interactive-content-reveal : Create interactive reveal effects, such as a spotlight that follows the user's pointer to uncover details within an image or UI section. interest-triggered-action-previews : Show a live preview of a button's effect when a user signals interest (e.g. hovering, focusing, or long-pressing) but before they commit to clicking. interest-triggered-tooltips : Show a tooltip or supplemental information when a user hovers over, focuses on, or long-presses an interactive element, without requiring a click. light-dismiss-a-dialog : Create a modal dialog that can be closed via light dismiss (i.e. clicking or tapping outside of the dialog) motion : Animate UI with CSS transitions, animations, scroll-driven animations, and view transitions while keeping motion on the compositor and respecting reduced-motion preferences. move-dom-element-without-losing-state : Move or reparent a DOM element without losing important element state, such as interactivity states (:focus/:active), &lt;iframe&gt; loading state, animation/transition state, etc parallax-scroll-effects : Create scroll-based effects (such as parallax) where foreground and background layers move at different rates, creating a sense of depth as the user scrolls. persistent-top-layer-ui : Keep a modal dialog, fullscreen element, or native popover visibly open and functionally active when its underlying DOM node is moved or reparented in the DOM. physics-based-easing : Create custom, physics-based animation and transition effects, like bounce and spring, that feel more natural and engaging than traditional easing curves. platform-controls-dismiss-dialog : Create a modal dialog that can be closed via standard platform-specific user actions, such as pressing the Esc key on desktop platforms, or a "back" or "dismiss" gesture on mobile platforms prevent-page-scroll-under-modal-dialog : Prevent the underlying page from scrolling while a modal dialog is open. same-document-transitions : Visually connect persisting elements across different page states or navigations in a Single Page Application (SPA) (e.g. expanding a product thumbnail into a full-bleed hero image) by smoothly morphing their size, position, or other styling properties. scoped-component-transitions : Animate state changes inside a single component (a card, list, panel, or other subtree) while the rest of the page remains interactive, and other transitions run concurrently. scroll-completion-effects : Trigger visual effects, animations, or focus changes on a target element only after a smooth programmatic scroll to that element has finished. scroll-entry-exit-effects : Create fade-in, scale-up, or other complex reveal-type effects on elements as they enter and exit the scrollport (or viewport) while the user is scrolling. scroll-snap-realtime-feedback : Provide real-time visual feedback in linked UI elements while a user scrolls through snap-aligned content, before the scroll gesture completes. scroll-snap-state-sync : Synchronize navigation indicators, linked content panels, and analytics tracking with the actively snapped item in a scrollable container. scroll-target-on-load : Build a scrollable list of elements (e.g. a carousel of images or a chat conversation thread) that can be displayed with a particular element scrolled into view on the initial render. scrollytelling : Animate visual properties on a target element — such as fading a backdrop, shifting a background color, or to create scrollytelling experiences — driven entirely by the scrollport position of a completely different element. search-hidden-content : Hide content from view using patterns such as accordions, tabs, and "Read more" sections, while ensuring the hidden text reveals itself during native "Find in page" searches, allows search engine indexing, supports URL fragment deep links, and maintains ARIA accessibility. sortable-table : Progressively enhance a data table with behaviors that allow users to sort rows by clicking on column headers. spatial-navigation : Implement accessible spatial navigation using arrow keys that works correctly in different layout modes (grid etc) swipe-to-remove : Let users act on items in a list (remove, archive, mark as read, etc.) with a horizontal swipe gesture, so they can process entries quickly without tapping a separate control. swipe-to-reveal : Let users swipe horizontally on a list item or content pane to reveal contextual action buttons or a side menu without automatically triggering an action. ui-components accordion : Build an accordion component with animation, optional exclusive (one-open-at-a-time) behavior, and brand-consistent styling. app-menus : Build an application menu bar where several top-level menus (such as File, Edit, and View) act as a single keyboard stop and switch between each other on hover or arrow keys. breadcrumbs : Build a breadcrumb trail that shows the user's location within a site hierarchy and lets them navigate to ancestor pages. card : Build a card component that adapts its presentation to its own available space and contents. carousel : Build a carousel component that displays a set of items in a horizontal or vertical layout. checkbox : Style checkboxes, including custom icons, layout, colors, check/uncheck animations, while preserving native functionality and accessibility. copy-button : Build a copy button that copies text from arbitrary elements to the clipboard. dark-mode-toggle : Build a dark mode toggle component that allows users to override their system color scheme preference for the current site. dialog : Build a modal or non-modal dialog component that is accessible, manages focus appropriately, and can be dismissed the way users expect on each platform. hovercard : Build a hovercard component that displays an interactive structured preview of the page a certain type of link (e.g. a user profile) will navigate to when hovered over. menu : Build a menu component that displays a list of options or actions, with support for nested submenus. navbar : Build a site navigation bar that adapts across screen sizes and indicates the current page. navigation-drawer : Create a navigation drawer component that, when triggered from a menu button, slides in from the side overlaid on top of existing page content, and slides out when dismissed (by swiping away, tapping outside, or pressing escape). persistent-app-tours : Create persistent onboarding walkthroughs using tethered native overlays that stay open during user interaction. persistent-toast-notifications : Create non-intrusive toast and overlay notifications for persistent, stackable messaging and state communication. progress : Build a styled progress bar that communicates completion of a task or process, in both determinate and indeterminate states. progress-ring : Build a progress ring component that visually represents the completion status of a task or process, with support for content in the center and brand-consistent styling. scrollspy : Highlight the currently visible section of a page in a navigation menu spinner : Build a loading spinner that communicates busy state to all users, respects reduced-motion preferences, and animates efficiently. stack-drill-down : Build full-screen hierarchical navigation that lets users drill down into nested views and swipe or navigate back to return, with browser history kept in sync. tabs : Build a responsive tabbed interface with good UX when not all tabs fit on screen. toolbar : Build a toolbar component that displays a set of controls for performing actions. user-experience content-first-noise-reduction : Maximize content and reduce noise by removing blocking popups, keeping persistent navigation compact, and moving secondary content behind on-demand disclosure. form-factor-adaptation : Adapt layouts, controls, and text to any device or container so touch targets stay usable, content fits its space, and nothing collides with system UI. natural-interactions : Implement natural interactions with clear hover, focus, and press feedback, motion that opens from its trigger, swipeable content, and keyboard-reachable actions. visual-design adapt-scrollbar-to-contrast-preferences : Enhance scrollbar visibility for users who prefer high-contrast interfaces apply-webgl-shaders : Apply custom visual effects with WebGL shaders to HTML content. browser-ui-theming : Theme browser-generated UI such as text selection, scrollbars, form controls, and pickers with CSS instead of re-creating it with custom elements. color : Color guidance for the web, including contrast requirements, light and dark color schemes, Forced Colors Mode, and generating tints and shades from a base color. complex-shapes : Clip elements and their content to any free-form shape, like a symbol, brush stroke, or organic texture for more expressive designs. contrast-color : Select a readable text color with sufficient contrast on a dynamic background color. custom-text-decorations : Add text decorations such as underlines, overlines, strikethroughs, or entirely custom shapes, with reveal animations, custom offsets and end insets, and flexible ink skipping. customize-scrollbar-color-and-thickness : Customize the color or thickness of a scrollbar dark-mode : Implement dark mode support in a way that respects the user's light/dark theme preference and adapts browser UI (e.g. scrollbars, form controls, etc) equal-width-text-lines : Make every line of a multi-line heading or lockup span the same width, as in poster-style or stacked-headline typography. Unlike justified text, the text itself is sized to the width rather than the spacing stretched export-html-media-from-canvas : Capture and export dynamic HTML content as images or video frames from within canvas. expose-canvas-content-to-browser-features : Expose content rendered in a canvas to browser features like assistive technologies, translation, or reading mode. improve-text-layout-and-legibility : Improve the layout and legibility of short standalone text content, such as headings no longer than a few lines, by enabling the browser to apply evenly balanced line breaks when wrapping text. interactive-content-in-3d-scenes : Integrate interactive HTML elements into a 3D scene. precise-text-alignment : Achieve precise vertical alignment with text of any font. For example, exactly equal visual padding above and below text, or aligning text perfectly flush with adjacent icons or images. shaped-cutouts : Combine multiple shapes to create complex cutouts or 'knockout' effects in elements, such as adding a notch to an element. soft-edge-content-fade : Apply a transparency gradient to content edges to indicate further scrollable areas or to obscure payment-walled text. typography : Typography best practices for the web, including font sizing units, line height, text wrapping and balancing, and fluid type that scales with the viewport. visual-effects : Visual effects with CSS such as layered shadows, blend modes, gradients with predictable color interpolation, and patterns like stripes, checkerboards, dots, and pie charts built from gradients alone. visually-stable-font-fallbacks : Define font styles such that text remains readable and visually consistent in the event that there's a swap between the preferred font and one of the fallbacks (or vice versa). visually-stable-mixed-fonts : Define font styles such that text remains readable and visually consistent in situations where multiple fonts are used to render a single block of text. visually-texture-content : Apply realistic weathering and texture patterns to elements to give them an organic, aged, or physical material appearance. wasm cpp-on-the-web : Compile C/C++ to WebAssembly using Emscripten webmcp agentic-forms : Expose client-side functionality as tools to AI agents by annotating standard HTML forms with WebMCP attributes. agentic-javascript-tools : Programmatically register client-side JavaScript functions as tools for AI agents using the WebMCP Imperative API. webmcp : Use this guide to implement WebMCP in browser applications, exposing client-side functionality as tools to AI agents via declarative or imperative APIs. Safe Adoption of Modern Features Progressive Enhancement & Nuanced Fallbacks : We distinguish between purely additive enhancements (like speculative preloading) which are safe to let older browsers silently ignore, and critical behaviors (like dialog controls or network beacons) where we write highly considered, low-overhead fallbacks. Responsible Fallbacks : We prioritize lightweight, case-specific custom fallbacks (<50 LOC) or conditionally-loaded polyfills instead of heavy third-party bundles. Gotchas & Quirks : We document hidden platform limitations, such as the 64KB payload quota for fetchLater() or macOS-specific scrollbar behaviors. Baseline-Aware Integration : We leverage real-time compatibility data from the Baseline project so agents dynamically adapt to current browser support. Origin Trial & Volatile Feature Gates : Guides covering experimental Origin Trial APIs or volatile features (single-engine features shipped within the last 3 months or still stabilizing) remain discoverable via search , but are gated on retrieve so agents do not adopt unstable APIs without explicit developer consent. Project Configuration ( .mwgrc ) Configure Origin Trial and volatile feature opt-ins for a repository with an optional .mwgrc JSON file in your project root (or ~/.mwgrc as a user-level fallback), which you can commit to share across your team: CLI Command .mwgrc Key Effect npx modern-web-guidance@latest set-allow-origin-trials "allowOriginTrials": true Unlocks guides for experimental Origin Trial APIs. npx modern-web-guidance@latest set-allow-volatile-features "allowVolatileFeatures": true Unlocks guides for volatile single-engine features. How It Works Activation : The coding agent activates the modern-web-guidance skill because of a relevant task. The agent is instructed to use the modern-web-guidance CLI for web platform queries. Local Semantic Search : The agent runs modern-web-guidance search "<query>" . The tool matches the query to the best guide using an offline, zero-dependency embedding model and BM25 search engine (no network calls, no API keys). Guide Fetch : The agent retrieves the guide via modern-web-guidance retrieve <guide-id> , inserting targeted code patterns, gotchas, and fallbacks directly into its context window. Tip Note: We use npx to ensure the content doesn't go stale, but the CLI works offline, completely private and local. The npm package is self-contained, with no extra dependencies to ensure both low-latency and supply-chain security. Alternative Installation Methods Vercel Skills CLI (aka npx skills ) npx skills add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance GitHub CLI gh skill install GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance Google Antigravity agy plugin install https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance GitHub Copilot CLI /plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance /plugin install modern-web-guidance@googlechrome Claude Code Plugin /plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance /plugin install modern-web-guidance@googlechrome /plugin # Select GoogleChrome marketplace, press enter, enable AutoUpdate /reload-plugins Grok Build CLI grok plugin install https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance --trust Kimi Code /plugins install https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance OpenAI Codex codex plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance codex plugin add modern-web-guidance@googlechrome Updating If you installed the skill using npx modern-web-guidance@latest install , you can update with: npx modern-web-guidance@latest update . Otherwise, consult your agent's documentation for updating plugins and skills. Evals to prove this works well We developed a robust eval harness to ensure that the content is empirically proven and continuously calibrated so AI agents write better code. We run automated evaluations using a closed-loop validation pipeline: [ Expert-authored guidance and demo ] │ ▼ [ Target generation ] ──> Tasks on real webapps, Golden solutions, Playwright graders │ ▼ [ Calibration loop ] ───> Runs Grader on Golden Solutions (Must Pass 100%) │ Runs Grader on Unmodified Base App (Must Fail 100%) ▼ [ E2E agent evals ] ────> Runs coding agents in guided vs. unguided modes Compares pass rates and accessibility w/ and w/o the skill Simulated Developer Tasks : We define realistic developer prompts against full base applications ( daily-grind , devtools-times ) that mimic real-world requests (e.g., "make my images load faster"). Prompts avoid naming APIs or features, testing whether the agent can naturally discover and apply the right guides. Static & Browser-Based Assertions : Playwright graders verify that each implementation requirement was followed—checking source patterns, computed styles, runtime DOM behaviors, and accessibility states. Self-Healing Calibration : Graders are calibrated against multi-agent (Claude/Codex/AGY) golden solutions (100% pass target) and an unmodified baseline application (0% pass target). E2E Testing : We measure coding agent performance on real tasks with and without guidance. The opportunity (100% - unguided pass rate) and uplift (guided - unguided pass rate) are key: if models already succeed without guidance, we prune redundant advice; where agents struggle, we refine guides to maximize uplift. Recent eval results snapshot Explore full per-agent and per-guide breakdowns on the Eval Dashboard . Date Agent + Model Tasks / Assertions Unguided → Guided (Uplift) Nov 8 antigravity_cli (gemini-4-argon) 214 / 1673 58% → 94% ( +36pp ) Nov 8 codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) 215 / 1795 54% → 82% ( +28pp ) Nov 8 claude_code (opus-5-5) 215 / 1801 57% → 88% ( +31pp ) Nov 6 codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) 212 / 1773 53% → 86% ( +33pp ) Nov 6 claude_code (opus-5-5) 212 / 1773 56% → 90% ( +34pp ) Nov 6 antigravity_cli (gemini-4-argon) 212 / 1722 60% → 96% ( +36pp ) Nov 4 codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) 209 / 1743 52% → 85% ( +33pp ) Nov 4 claude_code (opus-5-5) 209 / 1743 57% → 90% ( +33pp ) Nov 4 antigravity_cli (gemini-4-argon) 207 / 1722 60% → 96% ( +36pp ) Nov 2 codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) 205 / 1729 55% → 82% ( +27pp ) Available Skill Packs You can customize which skill packs are installed using the --choose flag: npx modern-web-guidance@latest install --choose modern-web-guidance (~205 tokens): Comprehensive guidance on modern browser APIs, layouts, and performance. chrome-extensions (~175 tokens): Guidance on Manifest V3, background workers, extension APIs, and Chrome Web Store publishing. Telemetry & Privacy Google collects anonymous usage information to improve the tool's reliability, relevance, and performance. Collected information includes installation counts, the calling agent name, guide retrieval IDs, and CLI tool search queries generated by the agent (e.g. "dark mode scrollbar color-scheme"). Raw user prompts are not collected. You can inspect what is collected in modern-web.ts . Tip To Opt-Out: set the DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 env variable in your shell profile (e.g., .bashrc or .zshrc ): export DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 Google handles this data in accordance with the Google Privacy Policy . Shop now Step Sequencer , ARA 2 , Drum Synth , Capture Automation , Contextual Browsing , Rack Updates , Looplet , Transient Shaper , Clipper , Envelope Clips , New Rack Types , Device Slots , Core Library Updates , Softube Effects New in Live 13 What’s new 1. Keep ideas moving with Step Sequencer ARA 2 Drum Synth Capture Automation Contextual Browsing Step Sequencer Create beats, melodies and polyrhythms in Live’s new step sequencer clips. Play Step Sequencer video Expand ARA 2 Work with ARA 2 plug-ins in Live for faster, more advanced audio editing. Play ARA 2 video Expand Drum Synth Design your own percussion at the source with a choice of over 20 drum engines. Play Drum Synth video Expand Capture Automation Tweak controls as you explore, then press Capture to turn gestures into automation. Play Capture Automation video Expand Contextual Browsing Load devices or swap presets from the device chain or mixer as you build a sound. Play Contextual Browsing video Expand 00:00 2. Follow sounds further with Rack Updates Looplet Transient Shaper Clipper Envelope Clips Rack Updates Expand your favorite Racks with up to 32 Macros, custom mapping curves and much more.   Play Rack Updates video Expand Looplet Layer and loop different parts of a single sample with four playheads. Play Looplet video Expand Transient Shaper Shape attack and sustain separately for punchier hits, louder tails or choppy loops. Play Transient Shaper video Expand Clipper Tame peaks transparently or drive into soft clipping for deliberate harmonic distortion. Play Clipper video Expand Envelope Clips Add automation or modulation to effects and mixer settings on Return tracks. Play Envelope Clips video Expand 00:00 3. Bring the mix into focus with New Rack Types Device Slots Core Library Updates Softube Effects New Rack Types Shape tone and stereo width with new Multiband and Mid-Side Racks.   Play New Rack Types video Expand Device Slots Get a clear overview of the devices on each track, directly in the mixer. Play Device Slots video Expand Core Library Updates Production-ready effect presets and Racks for vocals, guitars, mixing and mastering. Play Core Library Updates video Expand Softube Effects Shape dynamics and tone with five Softube effects modeled on sought-after studio hardware. Play Softube Effects video Expand 00:00 FAQs What’s new in Ableton Live 13? Ableton Live 13 adds new audio and MIDI workflows, sound design tools and mixing effects. Highlights include: A built-in Step Sequencer, ARA 2 support for compatible audio-editing plug-ins, Capture Automation, and Contextual Browsing for adding devices and swapping presets directly from the device chain. Drum Synth, new Multiband and Mid-Side Racks, expanded Rack controls, and Envelope Clips for automating and modulating effects on return tracks. Device Slots in the mixer, and new Core Library Drum Racks, instrument presets, Audio Effect Racks, samples, and MIDI clips. Arrangement Sync for Ableton Link, support for exporting tempo automation and time signature changes, and more precise event timing in exported MIDI files. Mixer improvements including Send sliders, a persistent Mixer Configuration menu for choosing which sections are visible, smoother mixer resizing, and an Unsolo button on the Main track, plus an updated Phaser-Flanger interface. Live 13 Suite also includes Melodyne essential, Looplet, Clipper, Transient Shaper and the Classic Dynamics & EQ Pack by Softube. See the full Release Notes for every change. What’s new for Push? Push 3 gains Custom Layouts, a new Step Sequencer layout, a new Performance Mixer, and Device Mode upgrades. Custom Layouts combine Session View, note areas, XYZ and mixer controls on a single page. The Step Sequencer brings the step editing experience from Live to the hardware. Device Mode adds jog wheel navigation and up to 32 Rack Macros. Push 2 supports the new Step Sequencer and most Device Mode improvements (except jog wheel navigation), but not Custom Layouts, Performance Mixer or Expressive Step Editing. See the full Release Notes for every change. What’s the difference between Ableton Live 12 and Live 13? Live 13 is the next major version of Ableton Live, following Live 12. It adds audio and MIDI workflows including ARA 2 support, Step Sequencer and Capture Automation, plus instruments and effects, expanded Rack controls, updated Core Library content, and more. Everything you can do in Live 12 you can still do in Live 13. What’s the difference between Live 13 Intro, Standard and Suite? Ableton Live 13 comes in three editions: Intro, Standard and Suite. They share the same core workflow but differ in their features and included instruments, effects and sounds. Live Intro is limited to 16 tracks and Scenes. Standard allows unlimited tracks and Scenes, and adds many more built-in instruments, effects and sounds.  Suite includes everything in Standard plus Max for Live, the complete instrument and effect collection, and Live’s full Core Library. Suite also comes with Melodyne essential for ARA 2 editing, plus the Classic Dynamics & EQ Pack by Softube and Looplet as free downloads at release. Compare editions in detail . When is Ableton Live 13 released? Ableton Live 13 will be released in early 2027. Subscribe to our Newsletter to be notified at release Can I pre-order Live 13? Yes, in two ways: If you already own Live 12 – pre-order Live 13 at 20% off. If you don’t own Live 12 yet – buy or upgrade to Live 12 at 20% off during the announcement offer and get the corresponding Live 13 edition free when it’s released. How do I upgrade to Live 13? Log in to your User Account and visit the Ableton shop to see the upgrade options for your license. From now until the release of Live 13, you can buy or upgrade to Live 12 and get the corresponding Live 13 edition for free on release day.  What happens to my Live 12 Rent-to-own license when I upgrade? You can extend your existing plan to cover the cost of upgrading to Live 13 Suite and start using it as soon as it’s released. Visit the Ableton shop to see your upgrade options. How do I get access to the Live 13 beta? Limited places for the Live 13 public beta are available to Live Standard and Suite owners. Learn more about the  Ableton Live beta program . Which ARA plug-ins work with Live 13? Most ARA 2 plug-ins work with Live 13, including Melodyne. Live 13 Suite comes with Melodyne essential. A small number have known compatibility issues. See the full Release Notes for more information. One ARA plug-in can be used at a time, across multiple clips and tracks. Read the Release Notes Save 20% on Live 12 now, upgrade to Live 13 for free. title: AI usage generates a fragile codebase
body_text: AI usage generates a fragile codebase Evan X. Merz Programmer / Master Gardener / Doctor of Music / Curious Person AI usage generates a fragile codebase 2026-11-07,  Evan X. Merz programming , artificial intelligence , ai , llm , web programming I can only speculate as to the reasons why I was laid off from Meta in May, but I suspect that one of the reasons is that I was a little bit more resistant to adopting AI/LLMs as coding tools than some of my peers. Don't get me wrong, I generated at least 90% of my code using AI in my last few months there, which was the minimum for a decent rating. But AI didn't 10X the amount of code I was writing. It didn't even 2X it. I was focused on code quality. I saw the code being pushed by some of my peers who were heavily reliant on AI, and I saw that it was brittle code. There were many subtle issues that would lead to tech debt in the long term, and even some glaring issues were ignored by very good programmers. For instance, I saw one of the best programmers on my team try to merge code that used javascript events for mouseover CSS effects rather than using the :hover selector, which is a totally unscalable way of writing mouseovers. Now I'm employed at another large tech company and I've fully made the switch to generating 100% of my code using AI because that's the expectation today. Still, I can see lots of people becoming aware that this isn't a sustainable way to continue development of a large scale SaaS product. AI tends to solve the problems that can fit within its context window very well, but it's totally oblivious to the long term issues that can't be understood in that relatively small frame. In this post I'm going to list four ways that AI usage results in a fragile codebase that isn't resilient to the demands of highly available and highly scalable SaaS applications. By the way, every word of this article was written by a human. Even though the following image was generated by AI, this article isn't AI slop. Four ways AI makes codebases fragile Here are the four most common ways that I have seen AI generating a fragile codebase. 1. AI writes shallow tests One of the most obvious failures of modern LLMs is that they tend to write simplistic automated test cases that don't cover the things that matter to humans. Frequently I see AI agents writing lots of tests of get/set methods which are trivial and don't typically require much testing. When AI writes e2e tests, they tend to only cover the cases which are already covered in the codebase. In other words, the AI writes tests only covering one type of user, or only covering surface level interactions. This creates massive gaps in the test coverage that are invisible to developers because they aren't captured by the line level coverage metric. 2. AI writes overly complex ccode AI also tends to write overly complex code. It frequently uses two or three helper methods when a single one would suffice. It tries to follow coding guidelines, such as DRY, to a fault, without realizing that the added complexity of that rigidity makes the code more difficult for human developers to debug or understand. 3. Reliance on AI decreases human understanding And that's the third issue with AI codebases: Humans don't understand them. The longer a company relies on AI agents to generate the code, the fewer developers are going to understand the codebase. This means that developers can't do the things that are necessary to build a resilient codebase. They don't understand the data structures and algorithms well enough to see when a pull request contains a new abstraction that doesn't work with the pre-existing structures. 4. AI moves too quickly to maintain a high quality bar AI moves too quickly for human developers to maintain a high quality bar. Each pull request comes faster than the prior one and has to be reviewed in even less time. This leads to developers skimming the code and missing crucial details that result in long term tech debt. Small quality issues like testing gaps and poorly named variables accrue in the codebase until it becomes a morass of spaghetti code. Four signs that you have a fragile codebase If you're unsure whether coding agents are harming your codebase or not, then you might look for the following symptoms of a fragile, AI-generated codebase. 1. AI generated codebases have more incidents When you switched the department over to agentic coding did the number of incidents slowly start rising? At first when we were all using agents to generate massive amounts of code, it didn't seem that different from traditional coding. The PRs came and were merged and everything seemed alright. But oh, there was that one p0 that came in at the end of the month, then there were two SEVs the following month. Then even more the next month. Now, after a year or two of agentic coding, it seems like there's an incident every weekend. AI coding agents are the reason why there are more incidents impacting customers. 2. Recovery from incidents takes longer in AI codebases Not only are there more incidents, but the incidents take longer to be mitigated. The fact is that the human developers on your team now have a more shallow understanding of the codebase. If your coding agent can't find the issue that your customers are facing, then humans are going to have to dig through a codebase that is highly complex and poorly tested. They will essentially be entering unfamiliar territory, so it takes longer for them to figure out what is going wrong. Hence, companies lose more and more money to incidents that take longer to resolve. 3. AI generated codebases create errors that are only visible to users When humans don't spend time in the code, they fail to see all of the use cases. They fail to understand how actual humans are using the code because they aren't ensuring that the AI is instrumenting analytics and catching all the errors properly. Hence, invisible errors start appearing in the codebase. Errors are uncaught and only visible to real world users, as opposed to the types of users that are being tested in automated tests or in developer manual testing. 4. AI results in a poor user experience And that leads to the ultimate problem with AI codebases: they weren't made for humans. AI codebases are software made by AI for AI. They aren't being tailored to the way that human users use the product, and they aren't being tailored for the way human developers need to maintain the product. The experience degrades on both the user and the developer side, leading to a vicious cycle of enshittification. Products made for humans require a human touch The fact of the matter is that for a product to satisfy human customers, it has to be informed by a human perspective. Nobody likes ordering from machines at a restaurant. Shopping for clothes from a website always results in worse fits than shopping in person. The same is true of SaaS products. Any time you leave your SaaS product in the hands of a machine, you are losing the human touch that is valuable to your users and your developers. This may work for the cheapest products that only compete on price, but high quality software products will continue to have a human touch. The best, most expensive products will be tailored for human users by human developers. They will be charming and enjoyable to use. They won't be fragile because they won't be primarily developed by AI. About me Buy my art

title: Blender 5.3 released with Gaussian Splat support
body_text: 5.3 — Blender Toggle navigation Roadmap Download Support Get Involved About Jobs Store Donate Download LTS Release Notes Previous Versions Requirements Daily Builds Demo Files Benchmark Extensions Release Notes 5.3 5.2 LTS 5.1 5.0 4.5 LTS 4.4 4.3 4.2 LTS 4.1 4.0 3.6 LTS 3.5 3.4 3.3 LTS 3.2 3.1 3.0 Roadmap Download Support Get Involved About Jobs Store Donate Download LTS Release Notes Previous Versions Requirements Daily Builds Demo Files Benchmark Extensions Release Notes 5.3 5.2 LTS 5.1 5.0 4.5 LTS 4.4 4.3 4.2 LTS 4.1 4.0 3.6 LTS 3.5 3.4 3.3 LTS 3.2 3.1 3.0 Good Things Come in 5.3s Gaussian splats, DLSS denoising, light dispersion, EEVEE fisheye, Outliner sorting, ripple video editing, and so much more. Download Blender 5.3 Watch Recap Video Watch the Recap Video New features overview by Jonathan Lampel and Wayne Dixon from CGCookie . Make a Splat Welcome native 3D Gaussian Splats support to Blender 5.3! Import them as point clouds, experiment with Geometry Nodes, preview them in Workbench, and render them natively with EEVEE or Cycles. Gaussian Magic 3D Gaussian Splats are commonly used to reconstruct 3D scenes from photos or videos. They consist of many small, soft, transparent blobs that combine to represent complex geometry and shading. Blender can now import Gaussian Splats from PLY , SPZ , and glTF files, store them as point clouds, process them with Geometry Nodes, and render them in EEVEE, Cycles, and Workbench (solid mode). PLY file imported as gaussian splats, featuring DOGWALK by Blender Studio. Point of View Gaussian splats are represented as point clouds, using a new type to tell them apart and with special attributes: scale : A vector represneting the size of the splat. rotation : A quaternion to control the rotation of the splat. radiance:base : 4D Vector as base (DC) radiance of the splats, followed by opacity. radiance:sh_{index} : Coefficients of the spherical harmonics bands >= 1. The order is <L=1 M=-1> , <L=1 M=0> , <L=1 M=1> , <L=2 M=-2> … where L is the band index and M is the basis function. Read Manual Radiant Future By default, a 3D Gaussian Splat is rendered using an emissive shader. The radiance attribute provides access to the resolved radiance of the splat at the current shading point. There is rudimentary support for making the splat relightable by replacing the Emission node with a hard surface BSDF such as Diffuse BSDF. Performance is still being optimized. Rendering may produce inaccuracies due to differences between the sRGB space used by most Gaussian Splat authoring tools and Blender’s linear color space, particularly in areas with low opacity and high radiance. Simple example of relit Gaussian Splat. More About Shading Added support for seven Geometry Nodes Improved color management interoperability See all rendering changes CYCLES Divide and Shine The Principled BSDF now supports Dispersion ! Turn ordinary glass and diamonds into beautiful little rainbows by splitting white light into its colorful components. Cycles Dispersion overview on YouTube by Chris Tyler Butterflies specter shader by Cartesian Caramel CYCLES A diamond in the Rough With Dispersion in the Transmission panel, the Principled BSDF can now reproduce the characteristic rainbow effect seen in glass and gemstones. This corresponds to OpenPBR v1.1.1. Roughness anisotropy is also now supported by the Glass BSDF and the transmission component of the Principled BSDF. It behaves just like anisotropy for specular reflections. Read Manual CYCLES Gone with Denoise Blender 5.3 integrates DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction as a new denoiser, delivering cleaner images faster by upscaling and reusing samples from previous frames. Think Cycles looks with EEVEE responsiveness. NVIDIA DLSS brings near-final render quality to the viewport, making lighting and look development faster and more responsive while virtually eliminating flickering between frames during animation playback. Find it in the Denoise panel under Render properties, Sampling. DLSS denoising requires NVIDIA driver version 620 or newer. Learn More Ready to Spark Blender 5.3 brings native support for NVIDIA RTX Spark devices running Windows 11, including memory optimizations. Learn More EEVEE Lights Meet Material Nodes Material Lighting nodes allow authoring how the Material reacts to Lights. This can, for example, be used for toon and stylized shading, but also for complex physical effects like iridescence. All the nodes you need to adjust lighting to your liking. Lighting to Your Liking Per-light data, evaluation, and shadow information are now available in the Shader Editor, giving you more control over how materials respond to individual scene lights. Four new nodes and two that received a “Light” mode/space: Light Accumulation : Evaluates its inputs for each light in the scene and accumulates the results. Light Info : Exposes light data properties (Color, Power, and Position). Light Evaluation : Evaluates position-dependent light properties (Diffuse/Specular Term, Attenuation Mask, Direction, and Distance). Shadow Raycast : Outputs a shadow mask value for the light being shaded. Attribute (Light Mode) : Queries custom properties from the Light Object or Light Data being evaluated. Vector Transform (Light Space) : Transforms coordinates to and from the local space of the light being evaluated. A Wider Perspective EEVEE can now render panoramic cameras, supporting all types of projections, from equirectangular and cubemap formats to various fisheye models and mirror ball. EEVEE fisheye matching Cycles 1:1 The current implementation has a few limitations: depth of field, raytracing, and volumetric temporal reprojection in the viewport are not yet supported. Learn More More in EEVEE & Viewport Sky Texture now shows Sun Disc Vulkan is now default Raytraced Shadows in Workbench See all EEVEE & Viewport changes Give back to Blender. Releases are possible thanks to donations by the community. COMPOSITOR Side Effects You can now stack Effects on your scene just like you would modifiers or constraints. Applying compositing effects has never been easier. Scene Effects stack featuring Storm by Blender Studio New Compositor & Effects tab in the Properties editor. One-click, Bloom ! Choose from built-in effects such as Bloom , Chromatic Aberration , Film Grain , and Vignette , as well as effects from online asset libraries or your own custom compositor node groups. Internally, each effect is its own node group, with its output passed on to the next effect. You can further customize effects at any time in the Compositor editor. Read Manual COMPOSITOR Bundle Up 17 Geometry Nodes are now supported in the Compositor, bringing a range of new capabilities across bundles , math and logic, and utility operations. This includes bundle support with Get Bundle Item , Store Bundle Item , Combine Bundle , Typed Bundle , and Separate Bundle . Math and logic nodes such as Boolean Math , Compare , Float to Integer , Integer Math , Matrix SVD , Combine Transform , and Separate Transform . Plus utility nodes including Hash Value , Random Value , Is Viewport , Import Text , and Bone Info . See All Compositing Nodes Play Fast Playback is now up to 2x faster on GPU, particularly when playing back EXR sequences. The interactive compositor now supports playback caching . It can be enabled from the sidebar, Options panel. Anisotropic Kuwahara is now up to 10x faster on Apple GPUs, 2x faster on NVIDIA GPUs, and 25-30% on CPU. Blender 5.2 Blender 5.3 CPU NVIDIA GPU Apple GPU Relative time to process Anisotropic Kuwahara filter. Lower is better. More in Compositor Blend name as default file output name Text Info overlay Gizmos support for transform nodes See all Compositing changes Study the artwork Blender splash artwork source files are available for you to play with! Download Blend File (337 MB) More Splash Blend Files OVERGROWN, by Blender Studio The new File → Project menu, to create, open and access projects. CORE Blender, meet projects . Until now, Blender’s preferences (such as asset libraries) were shared across all projects, and it was up to users to keep related files and resources organized. Blender now supports projects, giving you a way to group related files, share resources, and manage settings across an entire project, whether you’re working alone or as part of a team. Everything Everywhere All In a Project Projects support custom variables that can be used throughout a project, such as a character’s name or a frequently used file path. Per-project asset libraries and color management configurations are also supported. You can even set up a custom splash screen for your project, providing quick access to its files and other recent projects. Add-ons and other extensions per-project will follow in future Blender versions. Projects are entirely optional, most of the time you’ll probably work without one. Learn More Project-specific splash and color management configuration. ASSETS Asset Libraries ♥ Extensions Asset libraries can now be shared as extensions! Just like add-ons or themes. Browse hundreds of public domain assets available on the Extensions platform via the Get Extensions tab and install them directly from within Blender. Create and share your own asset library extension. Optionally, access can be controlled via authentication tokens . Browse Asset Libraries Read Manual A selection of public domain assets by the popular library Poly Haven is now available from within Blender. No add-ons required. See All Changes to Assets GREASE PENCIL Drawn to Select Draw Mode now has its own selection tools: Tweak , Lasso , Box , and Circle . Select strokes and adjust them right where you draw. Move, rotate, scale, duplicate, copy, paste, and delete strokes using the usual shortcuts, or access all these actions from the new Stroke menu. Read Manual Carve Diem Meet the new Carver tool in Draw Mode. It cuts shapes using proper Boolean subtraction, creating clean cuts in strokes and fills based on a lasso selection. Holes are created automatically when needed. When a shape has both a stroke and a fill, carving a hole into it also creates a stroke around the hole. Fills that are split apart become separate shapes, making them easy to sculpt further. Read Manual The new Carver tool uses booleans to cut through strokes and fills. Fill with color multiple regions at once using the new Fill tool in Blender 5.3. One Tool to Fill Them All The Fill tool can now fill multiple regions at once. Simply draw a path across multiple regions to fill them all as a single shape, with no gaps or borders in between. Read Manual Ramp It Up Gradient fills now use a ColorRamp input instead of being limited to just two colors. Read Manual Assign Flip View a shortcut or add it to Quick Favorites for easy access. Flip Out Mirror the camera view horizontally with the new Flip View operator to evaluate the composition from a different perspective and spot asymmetry or visual imbalances. This only affects the viewport display. It does not change the camera object’s transform or the final render, which remains unchanged. Use the operator again to restore the original orientation. Flip View has no shortcut assigned by default, but you can assign your own through the right-click menu or add it to Quick Favorites (Q) for easy access. Read Manual See all Grease Pencil changes I/O USD Collection Importer Collections can now be associated to importers . Similar to the Collection Exporters introduced in Blender 4.2 LTS, Collection Importers make it easy to re-import data with a single click, without having to navigate menus or adjust settings repeatedly. Configure them through the Importers panel under Collection Properties. Settings are stored in .blend files, making them easy to share and preserving them across Blender sessions. Only the USD importer is supported in Blender 5.3. Read Manual Learn More See all USD , Alembic , glTF , OpenEXR , and other I/O changes. VIDEO SEQUENCER Cut to the chase The Video Sequencer gets a full ripple editing framework, a rewritten blade tool, and a long list of editing, interface, and performance improvements, including initial OpenTimelineIO support. Ripple, Shuffle, Overwrite Welcome Ripple editing to Blender 5.3! This new overlap mode automatically moves strips forward or backward as edits are made, maintaining timeline continuity without the need to manually close gaps. Ripple , Shuffle , and Overwrite modes are now consistently used across editing operations. Switch between them while moving strips using R , S , and V . Making Waves Complete the ripple workflow with these handy operators: Ripple Add : Hold Shift while dragging and dropping strips to insert them using ripple behavior, automatically making room in the timeline. Ripple Trim : Trim selected strips at the playhead and automatically close the resulting gaps. Use Shift+Q or Shift+W to trim from either side. Ripple Delete : Delete selected strips and move subsequent content back to close the gaps. Use Shift+X . Cutting Edge: Blade 2.0 Splits are now visualized as a line when using Blade and as a region when using Box Blade . Tooltips display frame values at the split location, while a real-time preview shows the frame beneath the cursor. Press and hold C in the timeline to temporarily activate the Blade tool. Release it to switch back to the previously active tool. Read Manual But wait, there’s more: Hardware decoding , thumbnail support for Scene and other strips, OpenTimelineIO import and export, and much more. See all Video Sequencer changes USER INTERFACE Search. Sort. Scribble. Blender 5.3 gets more than a layer of polish. Long-awaited quality of life features and improvements that make this release take a leap in usability. Sorted Out Arrange your objects freely with custom sorting in the Outliner. Finally. Switch back to alphabetical order from the header popover. Plus improvements to filtering, drag-and-drop behavior, and hierarchy management. See all Outliner changes Place objects anywhere you want in the Outliner. Press Ctrl/Cmd + F to find anything in the sidebar. Side Quest Sidebars in all editors now support search , making it possible to find any property or operator, even inside tabs created by add-ons. Press Ctrl/Cmd + F while hovering the sidebar and start typing right away, or through the context menu of the tabs and panels. To clear the search, press Alt/Option + F . Mark it Down The Blender UI now supports rendering basic Markdown formatting. In node editors, write markdown directly in the new Comment node, or in regular layouts for scripts/add-ons through the label_markdown widget. Another handy widget for long strings is label_multiline , it behaves just like labels but allows text to wrap. Read Manual New Comment node to annotate node trees, with Markdown support. Rendered node on the left, Edit mode on the right. But wait: IME support , improved tooltips , box-select gesture, browsable node editor context paths , better Attribute Viewer overlay, Curve widget selection, and more! See all User Interface changes What’s Next ? Blender on tablets, texture layers, animation layers? Show your support for upcoming development projects and help shape the future of Blender. See Blender’s Roadmap BUT WAIT, THERE’S MORE Geometry Nodes Volume Grids nodes Construct Curves NURBS input nodes See all Geometry Nodes changes. Modeling Loop Tools New primitive: Quad Sphere Snap to Origin See all modeling changes. Sculpt, Paint, Texture Multires now supports texture display in Sculpt mode . Automasking in Vertex & Weight Paint. Improved Weight Paint default. See all Sculpt, Paint, Texture changes. Core Improved Undo . Linking & Appending improvements. See all Core changes. Animation Copy Paste World Space Convert Rotation Mode Improved Playback . Pose changes. Rigify B-Bone segments. Batch rename Timeline Markers . See all Animation & Rigging changes. Python API Access to all and selected markers . OpenEXR and OpenTimelineIO modules. Better color space interoperability . See all Python API changes. Plus hundreds of bug fixes, code cleanups and refactors. See the full list of changes . CREDITS Blender is a community project. Learn more on how you can contribute to Blender . List of developers who contributed to Blender 5.3 and all-time contributors. Splash artwork: OVERGROWN, by Blender Studio Cycles diamonds render by Chris Tyler . Butterflies specter shader by Cartesian Caramel . Grease Pencil drawings by Vivien Lulkowski from Blender Studio, Cowboi and Storm by Blender Studio . Huge thanks to everyone involved! 🧡 The Blender team. title: What's new in the .NET 11 runtime

What's new in the .NET 11 runtime Feedback Summarize this article for me In this article This article describes new features in the .NET runtime for .NET 11. It was last updated for release candidate 2 (RC 2). Updated minimum hardware requirements The minimum hardware requirements for .NET 11 have been updated to require more modern instruction sets on both x86/x64 and Arm64 architectures. Additionally, the ReadyToRun (R2R) compilation targets have been updated to take advantage of newer hardware capabilities. Arm64 requirements For Apple, there's no change to the minimum hardware or the ReadyToRun target. The Apple M1 chips are approximately equivalent to armv8.5-a and provide support for at least the AdvSimd (NEON), CRC , DOTPROD , LSE , RCPC , RCPC2 , and RDMA instruction sets. For Linux, there's no change to the minimum hardware. .NET continues to support devices such as Raspberry Pi that might only provide support for the AdvSimd instruction set. The ReadyToRun target has been updated to include the LSE instruction set, which might result in additional jitting overhead if you launch an application. For Windows, the baseline is updated to require the LSE instruction set. This is required by Windows 11 and by all Arm64 CPUs officially supported by Windows 10 . Additionally, it's inline with the Arm SBSA (Server Base System Architecture) requirements. The ReadyToRun target has been updated to be armv8.2-a + RCPC , which provides support for at least AdvSimd , CRC , LSE , RCPC , and RDMA , and covers the majority of hardware officially supported. OS Previous JIT/AOT minimum New JIT/AOT minimum Previous R2R target New R2R target Apple Apple M1 (No change) Apple M1 (No change) Linux armv8.0-a (No change) armv8.0-a armv8.0-a + LSE Windows armv8.0-a armv8.0-a + LSE armv8.0-a armv8.2-a + RCPC x86/x64 requirements For all three operating systems (Apple, Linux, and Windows), the baseline is updated from x86-64-v1 to x86-64-v2 . This changes the hardware from only guaranteeing CMOV , CX8 , SSE , and SSE2 to also guaranteeing CX16 , POPCNT , SSE3 , SSSE3 , SSE4.1 , and SSE4.2 . This guarantee is required by Windows 11 and by all x86/x64 CPUs officially supported on Windows 10. It includes all chips still officially supported by Intel and AMD, with the last older chips having gone out of support around 2013. The ReadyToRun target has been updated to x86-64-v3 for Windows and Linux, which additionally includes the AVX , AVX2 , BMI1 , BMI2 , F16C , FMA , LZCNT , and MOVBE instruction sets. The ReadyToRun target for Apple remains unchanged. OS Previous JIT/AOT minimum New JIT/AOT minimum Previous R2R target New R2R target Apple x86-64-v1 x86-64-v2 x86-64-v2 (No change) Linux x86-64-v1 x86-64-v2 x86-64-v2 x86-64-v3 Windows x86-64-v1 x86-64-v2 x86-64-v2 x86-64-v3 Impact Starting with .NET 11, .NET fails to run on older hardware and might print a message similar to the following: The current CPU is missing one or more of the baseline instruction sets. For ReadyToRun -capable assemblies, there might be additional startup overhead on some supported hardware that doesn't meet the expected support for a typical device. Reason for change .NET supports a broad range of hardware, often above and beyond the minimum hardware requirements put in place by the underlying operating system. This support adds significant complexity to the codebase, particularly for much older hardware that's unlikely to still be in use. Additionally, it defines a "lowest common denominator" that AOT targets must default to, which can, in some scenarios, lead to reduced performance. The update to the minimum baseline was made to reduce the maintenance complexity of the codebase and to better align with the documented (and often enforced) hardware requirements of the underlying operating system. For more information, see Minimum hardware requirements updated . Runtime Async .NET 11 introduces runtime-native async (Runtime Async V2), a significant step toward replacing compiler-generated async state machines with runtime-managed suspension and resumption. Instead of the compiler emitting state-machine classes, the runtime itself tracks async execution, producing cleaner stack traces, better debuggability, and lower overhead. Runtime Async is a preview feature. To opt in, add the following property to your project file: <PropertyGroup> <Features>runtime-async=on</Features> </PropertyGroup> A net11.0 project no longer requires <EnablePreviewFeatures>true</EnablePreviewFeatures> to use Runtime Async. The .NET runtime libraries themselves are compiled with runtime-async=on . The runtime libraries no longer contain compiler-generated state machines and rely entirely on runtime-provided async. This makes it possible to migrate an entire app (with only library dependencies) to the new model, and it provides broad functional and performance validation of the feature. The product team welcomes any reportsâpositive or negativeâabout throughput and library size changes you observe. .NET 11 also includes two additional improvements: Covariant Task â Task<T> overrides: When a derived class returns Task<T> for a base method that returns Task , the runtime now generates a void-returning thunk that bridges the calling convention difference, so virtual dispatch works for both flavors. The same fix applies to NativeAOT. Inlining in crossgen2: Restrictions that prevented runtime-async methods from being inlined during ReadyToRun (R2R) compilation have been removed. All async tests pass with both crossgen2 and composite R2R, and inlining of await-less async calls (the synchronous fast path) is confirmed end-to-end. Note The DOTNET_RuntimeAsync and UNSUPPORTED_RuntimeAsync environment variables that previously controlled runtime-async behavior have been removed. To opt out of runtime-async per project, set <UseRuntimeAsync>false</UseRuntimeAsync> in your project file instead of relying on the environment variable. Cleaner live stack traces The most visible improvement is in live stack traces âwhat profilers, debuggers, and new StackTrace() see during execution. With compiler-generated async, each async method produces multiple frames from state-machine infrastructure. With Runtime Async, the actual methods appear directly on the call stack. // To enable runtime async, add the following to your .csproj: // <Features>runtime-async=on</Features> await OuterAsync(); static async Task OuterAsync() { await Task.CompletedTask; await MiddleAsync(); } static async Task MiddleAsync() { await Task.CompletedTask; await InnerAsync(); } static async Task InnerAsync() { await Task.CompletedTask; Console.WriteLine(new StackTrace(fNeedFileInfo: true)); } Without runtime-async â13 frames, state-machine infrastructure visible: at Program.<<Main>$>g__InnerAsync|0_2() in Program.cs:line 24 at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.AsyncMethodBuilderCore.Start[TStateMachine](...) at Program.<<Main>$>g__InnerAsync|0_2() at Program.<<Main>$>g__MiddleAsync|0_1() in Program.cs:line 14 at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.AsyncMethodBuilderCore.Start[TStateMachine](...) at Program.<<Main>$>g__MiddleAsync|0_1() at Program.<<Main>$>g__OuterAsync|0_0() in Program.cs:line 8 at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.AsyncMethodBuilderCore.Start[TStateMachine](...) at Program.<<Main>$>g__OuterAsync|0_0() at Program.<Main>$(String[] args) in Program.cs:line 3 at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.AsyncMethodBuilderCore.Start[TStateMachine](...) at Program.<Main>$(String[] args) at Program.<Main>(String[] args) With runtime-async â5 frames, the real call chain: at Program.<<Main>$>g__InnerAsync|0_2() in Program.cs:line 24 at Program.<<Main>$>g__MiddleAsync|0_1() in Program.cs:line 14 at Program.<<Main>$>g__OuterAsync|0_0() in Program.cs:line 8 at Program.<Main>$(String[] args) in Program.cs:line 3 at Program.<Main>(String[] args) Note Exception stack traces (from catch (Exception ex) ) already look the same with or without Runtime Async, because existing ExceptionDispatchInfo cleanup in compiler-generated code handles that case. The improvement is in what you see during live execution. This improvement benefits anything that inspects the live execution stack, including profiling tools, diagnostic logging, and the debugger call stack window. NativeAOT and ReadyToRun support Runtime Async supports NativeAOT and ReadyToRun compilation. This extends the feature beyond JIT-compiled code to ahead-of-time compiled scenarios. The runtime also reuses continuation objects more aggressively and avoids saving unchanged locals, reducing allocation pressure in async-heavy code. Debugging improvements Breakpoints now bind correctly inside runtime-async methods, and the debugger can step through await boundaries without jumping into compiler-generated infrastructure. Runtime Async performance improvements Runtime Async includes several performance improvements: JIT async support: The JIT compiles a dedicated runtime-async version of a synchronous, task-returning method rather than delegating through a thunk. The JIT turns the method's tail calls into runtime-async calls and awaits the task that would otherwise be returned, eliminating an extra layer of indirection. Tail-merged suspension points: The JIT tail-merges async suspension points so generated code is smaller. Cached continuations: Continuations used for runtime-async callable task thunks are cached and reused. Pooled methods opt out: Methods that are already pooled opt out of runtime-async, avoiding redundant work. Tiered async compilation: Async versions now flow through tiered compilation, so hot async methods get tier 1 optimizations after warm-up. Task and ValueTask factory intrinsics: The JIT recognizes common factories, such as Task.FromResult , Task.CompletedTask , and ValueTask.FromResult , and folds them into faster async paths. Tail-await optimizations: Implicit tailcalls from async methods are enabled again when the method directly returns another async result, and await Task.Yield() avoids extra allocations in runtime-async paths. Async continuations without ExecutionContext Async continuations can now opt out of ExecutionContext capture and restore. ExecutionContext carries ambient stateâsuch as AsyncLocal<T> valuesâacross await points. Every Task continuation previously captured a snapshot of the context and restored it before running, even when no AsyncLocal<T> state was in use and the restore was a no-op. The runtime now detects when a continuation has nothing to restore and skips the capture/restore cycle entirely. Task , Task<T> , ValueTask , and ValueTask<T> all benefit from this change, as does the runtime-async implementation path. Applications that use ConfigureAwait(false) and AsyncLocal<T> sparingly see reduced overhead in high-throughput async code paths. JIT improvements Bounds check elimination: The just-in-time (JIT) compiler now eliminates bounds checks for the common pattern where an index plus a constant is compared against a length, such as i + cns < len . It also eliminates more redundant bounds checks for index-from-end access (for example, values[^1] ). These improvements reduce redundant checks in tight loops and improve throughput for array and span operations. Redundant checked context removal: The JIT can now prove and remove redundant checked arithmetic contextsâfor example, when a value is already known to be in range. This optimization eliminates unnecessary overflow checks in generated code. Switch expression folding: Multi-target switch expressions now fold into simpler branchless checks when the targets are a small set of constants, for example x is 0 or 1 or 2 or 3 or 4 . Faster uint-to-float/double casts: Casting uint to float or double is faster on pre-AVX-512 x86 hardware. SVE2 intrinsics: New Arm SVE2 (Scalable Vector Extension 2) intrinsics are available: ShiftRightLogicalNarrowingSaturate(Even|Odd) . These expand the set of vectorized operations available on Arm hardware that supports SVE2. Math.BigMul on x64: Math.BigMul(long, long, out long) is now significantly faster on x64. The JIT generates a single MUL r/m64 instruction when both operands are 64-bit values and the caller requests the high half of the result, eliminating the previous helper call. Single-IG prolog restriction removed: The JIT no longer requires the function prolog to fit in a single instruction group (IG). Complex prologues with many saved registers, large stack allocations, or runtime-async state setup no longer trigger fallback paths. SELECT(cond, cns, cns) folding: The JIT now folds conditional selects whose two branches both produce the same constant into just that constantâfor example, condition ? 42 : 42 becomes 42 . This fold eliminates unnecessary comparisons that can appear after earlier optimizations unify branches. AVX-VNNI-512 intrinsics: System.Runtime.Intrinsics.X86.AvxVnni.V512 exposes 512-bit forms of the AVX-VNNI multiply-add intrinsics on CPUs with AVX512-VNNI support. Saturating floating-point conversions: Unchecked float and double conversions to small integer types now saturate to type bounds instead of wrapping through intermediate truncation. ARM64 Vector<T> by reference for SVE: When the runtime is compiled with ARM SVE support, Vector<T> values are passed by reference rather than by value, aligning with the ARM calling convention for scalable types and enabling better code generation for SVE-intensive code. For better performance and code quality, .NET 11 adds several more JIT optimizations: Constant-folding SequenceEqual The JIT can now fold a string.Equals or ReadOnlySpan<T>.SequenceEqual call whose operands are both compile-time constants, replacing the byte-by-byte comparison with the constant true or false result. This matters most after inlining, when a caller passes another literal to a helper that compares against a known string. When IsAdmin is inlined into a caller that passes "Guest" , the JIT sees "Guest" == "Admin" and folds it to false : static bool IsAdmin(string role) => role == "Admin"; The optimization applies to string literals, const string fields, and UTF-8 literals (for example, "PNG"u8 ). Devirtualization improvements The JIT can now devirtualize generic virtual methods, including non-shared generic virtual methods and shared generic virtual methods that don't require a runtime lookup. Default interface methods declared on generic interfaces can now be devirtualized as well. In addition, the result of Activator.CreateInstance<T>() is now treated as having an exact type, allowing the JIT to devirtualize subsequent calls made on the returned object. These improvements unlock further downstream optimizations such as inlining and constant folding, reducing runtime dispatch overhead and improving performance. For example: IfaceGeneric<string> caller = new Caller<string>(); Iface obj = Activator.CreateInstance<Impl>(); caller.DefaultImpl(obj, "test"); // Can be optimized down to Console.WriteLine("test") interface Iface { void GenericMethod<T>(T value); } interface IfaceGeneric<T> { void DefaultImpl(Iface obj, T value) => obj.GenericMethod(value); } class Impl : Iface { public void GenericMethod<T>(T value) => Console.WriteLine(value); } class Caller<T> : IfaceGeneric<T> { } Here the JIT can determine the exact implementation behind both interface calls, devirtualize them, inline through the call chain, and ultimately fold the code down to the equivalent of Console.WriteLine("test") . Eliminating bounds checks after an empty-span guard The JIT now picks up the length != 0 assertion from an empty-span check and uses it to prove the bounds check on the first element succeeds: if (!span.IsEmpty && span[0] == value) { // The bounds check on span[0] is now eliminated. } Redundant branch and test elimination When an outer predicate is already implied by an inner branch, the JIT now removes the redundant outer check. Similarly, when code assigns a value in a conditional and then immediately tests it, the second test is eliminated: if (x > 0) { if (x > 1) S(); // The outer x > 0 check is folded away. } int y = condition ? 1 : 2; if (y == 1) A(); else B(); // The y == 1 test is eliminated; // each branch of the ternary goes directly to A() or B(). These optimizations are most visible after inlining, where guards from different methods land in the same compiled body. Hardware intrinsics and code generation .NET 11 includes several new hardware intrinsics and code generation improvements: Hardware FP16 instructions for Half arithmetic and conversions: The JIT uses hardware FP16 instructions for Half arithmetic and conversions when the processor supports them. On x64, arithmetic uses AVX10.1, while conversions between Half and float can use F16C (available on most AVX2-capable hardware). On Arm64, arithmetic uses the optional FP16 instruction set, while conversions between Half and float or double use baseline Arm64 instructions. The optimization requires no application changes and preserves the existing ABI representation of Half . Better cost modeling for x86/x64 SIMD: The JIT's floating-point execution and size costs previously reflected x87-era assumptions. Updated costs that reflect modern SSE/AVX hardware let the JIT make better decisions about hoisting and common subexpression elimination (CSE) around SIMD code. Faster DotProduct on AVX: Lowering for Vector128.Dot -style operations now emits a mul + permute + add sequence instead of vdpps / vdppd when AVX is available, which is consistently faster. Faster IndexOfAnyAsciiSearcher on Arm64: Arm64 versions of Vector*.Count , IndexOf , and LastIndexOf no longer route through ExtractMostSignificantBits , yielding a 5â50% improvement in workloads that use these APIs in their core loop. Arm64 ToScalar for 64-bit integers: ToScalar on Vector*<long> and Vector*<ulong> now uses fmov instead of umov , which is shorter and faster on most cores. SVE CreateWhile API expansion: CreateWhile gains signed, double , and single variants alongside the existing unsigned ones, completing the predicate-generation surface for SVE loops. New SVE2 and Arm64 instruction-set detection: The runtime now reports SVE_AES , SVE_SHA3 , SVE_SM4 , SHA3 , and SM4 as separate instruction sets, allowing Sve2*.IsSupported queries for those features on capable hardware. AVX10 detection fix: The CPUID-bit cache for AVX10 was being overwritten by a later query, which could cause AVX10 to be misreported on capable hardware. This is now fixed. ReadyToRun improvements Comparer<T>.Default and EqualityComparer<T>.Default are now specialized in ReadyToRun (R2R) images. Previously, the default comparers used reflection that R2R couldn't see ahead of time, causing callers to fall back to the JIT. R2R now generates a specialized helper in the imageâmirroring the NativeAOT approachâand benchmarks show up to a 20Ã improvement for collections operations that rely on the default comparer. VM improvements Cached interface dispatch on non-JIT platforms: On platforms that lack JIT support, such as iOS, interface dispatch was falling back to an expensive generic fixup path. Cached dispatch yields up to 200x improvements in interface-heavy code on these targets. Guid.NewGuid() on Linux: Guid.NewGuid() on Linux now uses the getrandom() syscall with batch caching instead of reading from /dev/urandom , yielding approximately 12% throughput improvement for GUID generation. WebAssembly improvements Browser and WebAssembly support has several improvements: WebCIL payload loading: The runtime can now load WebCIL payloads directly, improving compatibility with browser-based deployment scenarios. Better debugging symbols: Symbol and stack trace quality for WebAssembly debugging has improved, making it easier to diagnose issues in browser-hosted .NET apps. float[] , Span<float> , and ArraySegment<float> marshaling: float[] , Span<float> , and ArraySegment<float> are now marshaled more directly across JavaScript boundaries, reducing overhead for interop-heavy code. .NET includes improvements to CoreCLR-on-WebAssembly: WebCIL V1 is the default for CoreCLR WASM builds: The shared WebCIL header gains a TableBase field (28 â 32 bytes). Both Mono and CoreCLR readers accept V0 and V1. Crossgen2's WasmObjectWriter produces V1 directly, and CoreCLR-flavored WASM SDK builds default WasmWebcilVersion to V1 . Native re-link works for CoreCLR WASM apps: A full Emscripten-based pipeline replaces the previous stub targets. Re-linking dotnet.native.wasm from the runtime pack and including custom native code via NativeFileReference now works. JavaScript minification in Release builds: Browser CoreCLR Release builds ship minified JavaScript. NativeAOT publish for WASM no longer drops package satellites: Satellite assemblies from NuGet packages are now passed to ILC and pruned from the publish output, fixing localization for AOT-published apps that depend on packages such as System.CommandLine . CoreCLR on WebAssembly now runs the libraries test suite end to end. Platform support for more than 1024 CPUs The .NET runtime can now initialize on machines with more than 1024 logical processors. Previously, sched_getaffinity was called with the default cpu_set_t (capped at 1024), causing initialization to fail on high-core-count servers. The runtime now allocates the CPU set dynamically. The GC retains its 1024-heap limit, but the CPU count limit is removed. In-process crash report logging A new in-process crash reporting mechanism captures diagnostic information from within the crashing process before it terminates. Previously, crash diagnostics were collected by an out-of-process monitor. While the out-of-process approach is safe, it can miss information that's only available inside the dying process. The new in-process path logs the managed stack trace, module list, and key runtime state to a well-known path before the process exits. This capability originated on mobile platforms and is now also available on Linux and macOS. When DOTNET_DbgEnableMiniDump isn't enabled, set DOTNET_EnableCrashReport=1 or DOTNET_EnableCrashReportOnly=1 to select the in-process reporter. Existing createdump behavior remains in place when minidumps are enabled. NativeAOT: faster interface dispatch NativeAOT now uses a dispatch helper for interface method calls. Instead of a direct fat-pointer call sequence, the runtime routes interface dispatch through a shared helper that can be patched to the correct implementation after the call site warms up. This reduces the binary size of interface call sites and improves throughput on workloads with many interface method calls. Generic virtual method dispatch also uses the shared dispatch-cell infrastructure, which improves both monomorphic and polymorphic call performance. In addition, Assembly.GetCallingAssembly() now works on NativeAOT when stack trace data is available. SIMD lane construction and composition System.Runtime.Intrinsics now includes lane construction and composition APIs for hardware vector types. The new APIs let you construct a vector from individually specified lanes and extract or reorder lanes between vectors. This enables precise, portable control over SIMD vector element placement without falling back to platform-specific intrinsics. The new methods fall into a few families: Patterned construction: CreateGeometricSequence , CreateAlternatingSequence , and CreateHarmonicSequence build a vector from a starting value and a rule. Interleave and de-interleave: Zip , ZipLower / ZipUpper , Unzip , UnzipEven / UnzipOdd . Rearrange: The Concat family ( ConcatLowerLower , ConcatLowerUpper , ConcatUpperLower , ConcatUpperUpper ) and Reverse . using System.Runtime.Intrinsics; // {1, 2, 4, 8} â each lane is the previous lane times two Vector128<int> powers = Vector128.CreateGeometricSequence(1, 2); // Interleave two vectors lane-by-lane (Vector128<int> lower, Vector128<int> upper) = Vector128.Zip(Vector128.Create(1), Vector128.Create(2)); These APIs are available on Vector128<T> , Vector256<T> , Vector512<T> , Vector64<T> , and Vector<T> . They're building blocks for image processing, audio digital signal processing (DSP), and other SIMD-intensive workloads that need fine-grained control over vector element layout. File locking on iOS and tvOS On iOS and tvOS, including simulators, CoreCLR now disables advisory file locking by default. A FileStream that acquired an advisory lock could cause the operating system to terminate an app when the app entered the background while it held the lock. As a result, FileShare restrictions are no longer enforced by those locks on iOS and tvOS, including between handles in the same process. Mac Catalyst and other platforms keep their existing defaults. If your app relies on FileShare enforcement and you accept the risk of suspension-related termination, restore file locking by using either of the following settings: Set the DOTNET_SYSTEM_IO_DISABLEFILELOCKING environment variable to 0 . Set the System.IO.DisableFileLocking runtime configuration property to false . For example, in the runtimeconfig.json file: { "configProperties": { "System.IO.DisableFileLocking": false } } Reliability fixes The runtime includes fixes for the following issues: On Linux, the SDK no longer crashes on Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8 on Arm64, and the runtime correctly traverses cgroup v2 memory limits at the root of the hierarchy. Generic virtual method dispatch no longer hangs after repeated AssemblyLoadContext unloads. TryDequeue no longer spuriously reports an empty queue while a segment freezes during growth. TryPeek has the same reliability fix. On Windows, garbage collection works correctly on machines with multiple CPU groups. Runtime diagnostics The async profiler now instruments both runtime-async methods and compiler-generated async state-machine methods, so tools receive one consistent event model regardless of async implementation style. The runtime also adds improved interpreter perf-map logging support, and fixes parsing of CORECLR_NOTIFICATION_PROFILERS lists that don't end with a semicolon.
