title: What constant surveillance is doing to children and parents
I deleted all my SSH keys
body_text: I deleted all my SSH keys Alex Haydock Home | Posts | Blogroll | About | GitHub | Mastodon I deleted all my SSH keys 2026-11-04 11:00 security I’ve been using ed25519-sk keys with YubiKeys since practically the moment they were available. But because of some specific use-cases (and because, frankly, YubiKeys are expensive) I’ve had a few traditional on-disk keys hanging around for a while just waiting for me to finally decide to get rid of them. This post documents how I’m using various secure enclaves (YubiKey, TPM, Apple Secure Enclave) to hold/encrypt SSH key material and achieve the goal of not having any unprotected key material living on-disk. First – Isn’t using a passphrase enough? Probably. I don’t intend to imply that this post is the only way that anyone should be doing SSH keys. Using a passphrase will encrypt the key with bcrypt & AES which keeps it protected even if the on-disk keyfile leaks somehow. And with a functioning ssh-agent, the passphrase should only need to be entered once per session, with the decrypted key material being held in RAM after that point. So yes, the ’traditional’ method is probably fine for most threat models. But I’m still keen to move to hardware-backed keys anyway, mostly for the satisfaction. About hardware-resident keys When I say ‘hardware-resident’ keys, I mean keys that use a secure enclave or purpose-built hardware like YubiKeys to store or protect the key material. The theoretical benefit here is that the hardware used to generate the SSH key is needed in order to use the key. There’s no mechanism that allows leaking or exfiltrating keys that generated using this method. Any material that does exist on-disk is useless without the hardware. Goals So I want to: Switch to using hardware-resident keys entirely Do so as natively as possible, avoiding additional software where I can Test these in various real-world scenarios, such as running within an LXC or noninteractively mounting an SSHFS server Hardware I’m going to try three different hardware methods for achieving this, which I think will cover all of my needs: Method 1: YubiKey Method 2: TPM Method 3: Apple Secure Enclave Method 1: YubiKey With a YubiKey (5 and newer), SSH keys can be directly enrolled into the device using ed25519-sk (where the -sk stands for “Security Key”). This doesn’t require any additional software beyond OpenSSH itself. To store a new SSH key on a YubiKey, insert it and run: ssh-keygen -t ed25519-sk -O resident -O application = "ssh:yournamehere" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519-sk The application tag set in the command is arbitrary and can be set to whatever memorable string you prefer to differentiate between multiple SSH keys if you want to create multiple keys on the same YubiKey. If you have ykman installed, you can now inspect the list of credentials enrolled in the device: $ ykman fido credentials list Enter your PIN: Credential ID RP ID Username Display name 0f41fb61... ssh:yournamehere openssh openssh If ykman complains that you haven’t set a FIDO PIN on the YubiKey yet, you can do this with ykman fido access change-pin . Note that you don’t actually need ykman to enrol or use SSH keys with a YubiKey but it does make managing the device more convenient. Once the key has been created, you can retrieve the public key from disk: $ cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519-sk.pub sk-ssh-ed25519@openssh.com AAAAGnNrLXNzaC1lZDI1NTE5QG9wZW5zc2guY29tAAAAIA9B+2GGCkQvBzpa4WobQhfC9YU5Su3pKXBmVLSXEqfRAAAAEHNzaDp5b3VybmFtZWhlcmU= alice@hostname This key can be used like any other SSH public key – added to authorized_keys on a host, copied with ssh-copy-id , or pasted into services that depend on SSH like Git forges. You will also find a ~/.ssh/id_ed25519-sk file on disk (without the .pub extension). Note that although this looks like a private key, it doesn’t actually contain the key material. This is just a handle to find the relevant key on the hardware device. To configure the key for authentication, it can be enrolled with ssh-add like a regular key, or specified directly in ~/.ssh/config : Host blog.infected.systems IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519-sk From here, you can now SSH into the destination host as with a regular key. SSH will ask you to tap the YubiKey to confirm presence when the SSH command runs. Unattended YubiKey usage When using an ed25519-sk key created with the default settings as above, you will be asked to confirm your presence whenever the key is used by physically touching the YubiKey. It’s probably a good idea to keep this default, but if you have a specific use-case that requires unattended key usage, you can generate a no-touch-required key as follows: ssh-keygen -t ed25519-sk -O resident -O no-touch-required -O application = "ssh:nameyourkey" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519-sk When using a no-touch-required key, although it isn’t possible for a malicious actor to exfiltrate the key even with root access to the host the YubiKey is plugged into, a malicious actor with access could use the key without requiring any presence detection or human interaction. So do make sure this is actually suitable for your risk appetite before doing it. To use a no-touch-required key for unattended authentication to remote servers, you need to prepend the entry in the authorized_keys file on the destination host with no-touch-required , otherwise OpenSSH’s default security settings will reject the key. For example: $ cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys no-touch-required sk-ssh-ed25519@openssh.com AAAAGnNrLXNzaC1lZDI1NTE5QG9wZW5zc2guY29tAAAAIA9B+2GGCkQvBzpa4WobQhfC9YU5Su3pKXBmVLSXEqfRAAAAEHNzaDp5b3VybmFtZWhlcmU= alice@hostname Method 2: TPM YubiKeys are nice, though fairly expensive. It would be useful if we could use the TPM we already have on our host to protect key material instead. Well, it turns out we can! Unfortunately this does require additional software, but it’s a fairly minimal Golang package – ssh-tpm-agent . It can be installed with Go directly from GitHub, but is natively packaged by Ubuntu and I’m working on packaging it for Fedora . To create a TPM-backed SSH key with a PIN, run: ssh-tpm-keygen -N "your-pin" The process will ask you where to store the key. From here, once again we have a keypair with a .pub file that we can use in authorized_keys or copy however we wish. To use the TPM-backed key we need to use the TPM-aware SSH agent provided by the ssh-tpm-agent package. If you installed the native Golang package rather than something vendored by your distribution, you can enable the systemd socket unit for the agent as follows: ssh-tpm-agent --install-user-units && systemctl --user enable --now ssh-tpm-agent.socket To ensure the socket for the agent can be discovered by SSH processes run within your shell session, add the following to your .bashrc or the equivalent for your shell: export SSH_AUTH_SOCK = " $( ssh-tpm-agent --print-socket ) " Again, we can now use this key to authenticate to servers as if it were any other traditional on-disk key. Unattended TPM usage If you want this key to be available unattended, or to services that don’t use a full shell such as systemd mount units , you can create a new key without a PIN (pass -N "" to the ssh-tpm-keygen command) and specify the socket path in ~/.ssh/config instead of relying on SSH_AUTH_SOCK (although this relies on the socket address being predictable – i.e. your UID being stable): Host blog.infected.systems IdentityAgent /run/user/1000/ssh-tpm-agent.sock IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa Note that ssh-tpm-agent does not account for the values in the TPM Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs) which record the state of the booted system – firmware versions etc, so changes of hardware/firmware/OS will not cause the system to refuse to unseal the key (unlike, say, something like BitLocker). So ensure that using a PIN-free key is appropriate for your risk model before doing so. A caveat regarding TPM keys You will notice though that the private keyfile held on disk uses a .tpm extension this time. This is where an important caveat of the TPM method comes in – Unlike the YubiKey approach, the private key material is actually being stored on disk here. This is because TPM devices do not natively support enrolling SSH keys. So what is happening is that the private key material is being stored on disk in encrypted form, and the TPM is being used to decrypt it. This is still a device-bound credential as the key cannot be used without the TPM device even if the keyfile is leaked or exfiltrated but it is a relevant distinction compared to device- resident credentials such as -sk keys. Method 3: Apple Secure Enclave As of macOS Sequoia, the Smart Card Auth system within macOS is able to natively handle SSH keys as identities. We can generate one as follows: sc_auth create-ctk-identity -l "ssh-labelyourkey" -k p-256-ne -t bio The options above: -l labels our key. Choose a unique and useful name here as we’ll need this to find the right key handle file on disk later. -k p-256-ne creates a non exportable ( -ne ) key. This is important to ensure we’re actually creating a key that will stay resident in the enclave. -t bio requires TouchID to use the key. Then we can list the key: % sc_auth list-ctk-identities Key Type Public Key Hash Prot Label Common Name Email Address Valid To Valid p-256-ne B15235464F87EC7C8DEE89BFA06399FFD6678E99 bio ssh-labelyourkey ssh-labelyourkey 04/11/2027, 09:29 YES To export a handle to disk that allows OpenSSH to use the key from the secure enclave, you can do: ( cd ~/.ssh && ssh-keygen -w /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib -K -N "" ) When prompted for a pin during export, you can leave it blank as it isn’t used here. A public key and private key handle file will be created on-disk in the ~/.ssh directory. Note that the command above will export a key handle for all of the SSH keys you have enrolled in the Secure Enclave (you can create many if desired by repeating the process above). I wasn’t able to find a way to export individual key handles despite Apple’s docs suggesting that you should be able to with KEYCHAIN_CERTIFICATES . Your best bet will be to use a clear label using the -l flag when creating the key so you can easily find the handle for it after it has been exported to disk. Once we have our pubkey and handle file, we can process these as we normally would – copying the public key to an authorized_keys file on a remote host or adding it to whatever services we prefer. To use SSH keys from the Secure Enclave, we need to set SSH_SK_PROVIDER in our shell. We can add this to ~/.zshrc : export SSH_SK_PROVIDER = /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib After a restart of the shell, the key will work like any other – though you may need to specify it directly as in my case it wasn’t being autodiscovered by macOS’s SSH agent: Host blog.infected.systems IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk_ssh-labelyourkey Running a Mac in ‘clamshell mode’ If you run your Mac in what Apple calls ‘clamshell mode’ (i.e. a laptop with the lid shut), then the initial create-ctk-identity command will fail with an error like this: Error: Error Domain=com.apple.LocalAuthentication Code=-4 "Touch ID is not available in closed clamshell mode." UserInfo={BiometryType=1, Subcode=10, NSDebugDescription=Touch ID is not available in closed clamshell mode., NSLocalizedDescription=Authentication canceled.} Unfortunately it seems that keys created with -t bio do actually require full TouchID in order to generate or use – unlike other operations such as unlocking the Safari Keychain or using Apple Pay which fall back to a user password when in clamshell mode. There is an option to use -t none to create a key without presence confirmation enabled at all. This carries the same risk as I discussed in the section about using YubiKeys unattended so you’ll have to decide whether it works for your risk model. If, like me, you use the machine in clamshell mode basically all the time there are some alternative options that still retain presence detection though: You could buy one of Apple’s expensive bluetooth keyboards with Touch ID . Or, the YubiKey 5C Nano is tiny and can sit almost flush in the side of a closed MacBook and can be used with Method 1 including presence detection. Final note With a mix of these three approaches, I’ve finally been able to deprecate on-disk keys from all my setups. Hopefully some of the info in this post is helpful to people! It’s nothing that can’t already be found online but I’ve gathered it into one place mostly for my own convenience. The main gotcha to be aware of with hardware-resident keys is that they’re, well, hardware resident. Hardware malfunction/loss/change can render keys unusable. So it’s probably better to make sure you at least have multiple keys. Remember, authorized_keys can take as many keys as you care to put in it so redundancy is the best move here I think. title: Your TV can see through walls (2025)
body_text: Your TV can see through walls: Navigation: Homepage      Index      Yearly archives Fun Astrophotography      (catalog) About this site Real pages Dark Light TTY Your TV can see through walls: 2025-08-02 — 2026-02-23 This is a spectogram of the signal from a local TV station: ATSC digital TV signal. (Recorded using an Ettus USRP B200) Walking between the receiver and TV station causes a slight disturbance to the signal, but it's nothing to write home about: Walking through the signal path For this capture, I moved the antenna a few centimeters: Where'd my signal go? This is selective fading : The direct signal is being canceled out by a strong reflection. Because the phase of the reflection depends on frequency, this effect is not uniform over the whole signal. Apart from being annoying if you're trying to watch TV, this state is extremely sensitive to any nearby movement. Here's what happened to the signal when I got up from my chair: ... and here's me walking around in a neighboring room: Stripes! The gaps between the stripes happen when my reflection perfectly cancels out the residual signal, which happens each time the path length changes by one wavelength. Let's use this to figure out how fast I was walking: The gap between each stripe is around 70 pixels, and the waterfall has an update rate of 150 Hz... 70 pixels * 1 second/150 pixels = 0.47 seconds = 2.1 Hz speed of light / 490 MHz * 2.1 Hz = 1.3 m/s = 4.6 km/h I was walking perpendicular to the direct signal path, so the speed can be used as is, without any adjustments for geometry. So, a simple radio reciever is able to detect motion and provide an estimated speed — and it's not just TV that works for this: any wideband radio signal like WiFi or LTE can be used in much the same way. Those make worse demonstrations because they have a messy waterfall, but it's possible extract the same data with a bit of work. Happy paranoia! Site wide RSS feed . Proudly supporting IPv6! Integrations Contribute Blog TS TypeScript Python Search Theme GitHub Discord Search Ctrl K Cancel All posts November 9, 2026 5 min read Amazon saves millions by replacing Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider Two Amazon engineers swapped Claude Sonnet 4.6 for a decision model in one of the world's biggest internal ticketing systems. Carr Onstott , Mehul Jaiswal , Strands Agents Team For a while, Amazon and AWS teams relied on Claude Sonnet 4.6 to label tickets in an internal system without breaking the bank. Sonnet 4.6 fit the goldilocks choice of balancing intelligence with cost. Considering it dealt with one of the world’s largest internal ticketing systems, the nine month old model did well. However, two Amazon engineers recently swapped out Sonnet 4.6 for Strands Decider , a decision model we launched a month ago, that performed just as well at 98% less cost . This change will save millions of dollars of token costs in a year. Carr and Mehul, who work on the internal ticketing system, walk through how this happened below. Replacing an LLM’s job with a decision model We had Sonnet 4.6 labeling tickets at enormous scale. The tickets could be customer escalations, capacity requests, automated alarms, security findings, or anything else across the company that needed to fit within 20 category types. The agent ran with a long system prompt on every ticket, generating JSON and reasoning against a fixed set of labels. A decision model can’t generate text. It’s first given some state and a question with a set of options, then the decision model returns a probability for each option plus a confidence score. We saw this method fit perfectly with ticket labeling: the state is the ticket, the options are the label catalog. We started with the original Strands Decider 2B . On a test set of tickets, the E4B Gemma 4 build got clearly better results, so we switched to it. Afterwards, we tuned how confident the model needed to be before applying a label. The results showed E4B beating production Sonnet on a separate set of our tickets. We ran E4B on SageMaker ml.g5.xlarge instances (one A10G, 24 GB each). The model used about 19 GiB, and one request took about 640 ms on one instance. The endpoint autoscales with traffic, but its network was isolated, preventing outbound access to the container. SageMaker copies the model weights in from S3 before start-up. Customers can do this too! Apart from our ticketing APIs, everything in the path is a standard AWS service. Ticket events land in an SQS queue that then triggers a Lambda function. It reads the ticket data and calls the model, a SageMaker AI Endpoint with Strands Decider. AppConfig holds the switch (described below), and CloudWatch carries the logs, metrics and alarms. The stack is defined in CDK with deployment stages for Beta, Gamma, and Prod. Running Sonnet 4.6 and Strands Decider on the same tickets We didn’t want to flip a switch and hope. The labeling Lambda reads a three-way setting from AWS AppConfig on every message: BEDROCK : Sonnet labels every ticket, but Strands Decider isn’t called. DUAL : Both the Sonnet and Strands Decider models are called in parallel. The results from the Sonnet model are applied to the ticket and compared with Strands Decider results. DECIDER : Strands Decider labels every ticket and Bedrock isn’t called. What we measured Claude Sonnet 4.6 Strands Decider E4B % Improvement Average time per call 4,215 ms 897 ms 78% Input tokens per ticket 6,554 2,009 Output tokens per ticket 170 1 Total tokens, per ticket 6,724 2,010 70% The token drop had two sources. Strands Decider produced one output, the choice, instead of a JSON answer. Its prompt was also much shorter than Sonnet 4.6’s. Production’s label descriptions alone are longer than Strands Decider’s 4,096-token window, so we rewrote each of the 20 labels as a one- or two-sentence criterion and sent them as the options of a single choice question, plus a “none” option. The ticket data is the same as what Sonnet gets, except that on long tickets Strands Decider drops the oldest comments to fit. Below is a graph of our Lambda durations on the day we turned off the Sonnet usage, showing the average Lambda execution duration dropping 74%. What it costs At published us-east-1 on-demand prices: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Bedrock, global endpoint) Strands Decider E4B (SageMaker, ml.g5.xlarge ) Price $3.00 per 1M input, $15.00 per 1M output tokens $1.408 per instance-hour Per ticket $0.0222 about $0.0005 Per million tickets about $22,200 about $500 Sonnet’s cost per ticket comes straight from the token counts above. Strands Decider’s depends on how busy each instance is. At about 640 ms per request, one instance can handle about 5,600 tickets an hour, which would be $250 per million tickets at full use. We keep headroom for bursts, and in practice it comes to about $500 per million. That is about 44 times cheaper than Sonnet, a 98% reduction. These are published list prices. They leave out the Lambda, which also runs for less time per ticket now. One thing that surprised us was that JSON key order changed the answer. Sending the same content with keys in a different order moved the output probabilities by up to 0.19. We now send every request with sorted keys, so if you serve a decision model behind an API, check this before you compare runs. Our lessons This worked because the task is a closed choice from a known catalog, the volume is high, and the latency of the old path mattered. If your labels need explanation text, if the catalog changes weekly, or if you can’t fit the useful context into a few thousand tokens, a decision model probably can’t replace the LLM’s job. The part we’d copy regardless of model is the three-way switch. Running both on real traffic, then judging every disagreement, told us more than any offline eval would have. It also meant going back was a 45-second config change. The world of agents gets a lot more exciting (and less costly) with decision models. If you’re running a classification agent, try the Strands Decider repo and its serving notes . title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
body_text: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 \ Anthropic Skip to main content News Research Policy Commitments Company Try Claude Introduction Performance and efficiency Coding Cybersecurity Science and engineering Safety and alignment Data privacy Availability November 9, 2026 Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 [1] Introduction [2] Performance and efficiency [3] Science and engineering [4] Safety and alignment [5] Availability We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges. Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below. Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs. Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens. Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Theoretical physics Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics. Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, here and here . Protein folding Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the capsid , can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together. Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted).³ Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies: Dyno Therapeutics Columbia University Biohub Dyno Therapeutics Columbia University Biohub Quote “This acceleration could save meaningful time and cost from our capsid folding pipeline, enabling us to deploy compute more efficiently across many capsid properties that are needed for a genetic medicine. Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas. Our first formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem , performed by an unreleased research version of Claude, took 11 days. It relied on a purpose-built harness along with guidance from a human researcher. By contrast, a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the theorem in just 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Fable 5.2 started from minimal prompts, built its own ways to coordinate, and used no mathematical references, only a list of intermediate theorem statements to score progress. It needed one-third as many action tokens as our first formalization and produced a proof seven times shorter. As can be seen in the figure below, Opus 5.5 (with the same 1,000-agent setup) completed only 26% of the formalization in 18 hours, and barely made any more progress after 30. Alignment testing We ran a suite of evaluations for how well-aligned Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are in behavioral terms, testing how often they behave in unintended and potentially unsafe ways. Weighing everything we’ve seen across a range of evaluations, we’ve assessed the risk of these models behaving in unsafe ways in high-stakes situations to be low (as with our other recent models). We tested Claude Mythos 5.2 (the same underlying model as Fable 5.2 without certain cybersecurity or biology safeguards), on our automated behavioral audit, which tests how a model behaves across approximately 1,900 scenarios. Claude Mythos 5.2 performed as well as, or better than, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most measures. For example, it scored better than all three on most measures that involve misleading users. Hallucinating inputs, falsely claiming to have completed a task, omitting important information, and failing to disclose bad or lazy work were all lower in Claude Mythos 5.2.⁵ Automated behavioral audit Overall misaligned behavior score Mythos 5.1 Opus 5.5 Sonnet 5.5 Mythos 5.2 0 0.5 1 1.5 2 2.5 3 3.5 4 Score (1–10, lower is better) Mythos 5.1 Opus 5.5 Sonnet 5.5 Mythos 5.2 3.28 2.79 3.10 2.67 Overall score from our automated behavioral audit, a composite of many undesirable behaviors including cooperation with human misuse and autonomous actions across a range of scenarios. Lower scores are better. See Section 6.4.1 of the Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 System Card for full details. We paid particular attention during our testing to behaviors that contributed to recent notable cybersecurity and alignment incidents. For example, we found that Claude Mythos 5.2 has a lower propensity than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1 to engage in biased or motivated reasoning (such reasoning might mean it “explains away” evidence that it isn’t in a simulation and thus takes actions without a realistic understanding of the consequences). We ran multiple different evaluations to test the model’s tendency to attempt escaping its sandbox. In two evaluations we’d used previously, Claude Mythos 5.2 made substantially fewer attempts at sandbox escape than any other model we’ve tested. In a dedicated evaluation—an adversarial experiment including over 1,800 scenarios, most of which could not be solved without escaping a sandbox, and where the sandbox has a deliberate weakness—Claude Mythos 5.2 made use of credentials or files that we had placed outside its sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios, about as often as Opus 5.5 (3.3%), less often than Sonnet 5.5 (5.1%), and well below previous iterations of Claude Mythos (5 and 5.1, which scored 39% and 21%, respectively). We found that other techniques, such as describing the sandbox and adding tools to report weaknesses, reduced Claude Mythos 5.2’s escape attempts even further. On other measures—one, for example, involving taking harmful actions after erroneously concluding it was in a simulation—Claude Mythos 5.2 scored slightly worse than Opus 5.5, and about level with Claude Mythos 5.1. The problem of building evaluations that reliably catch every failure before a model is deployed remains unsolved. The complexities of evaluating highly capable models often muddy the picture—for example, Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow. That is why we do not rely on these evaluations alone to provide a holistic picture of safety: we draw on monitoring during training, reviews of transcripts from internal use, testing by external evaluators, and interpretability techniques for examining what is happening inside the model. We are also working to make our evaluations more realistic and to better understand what they miss. Safeguards Cybersecurity and biology safeguards. Consistent with previous Claude Fable models, Fable 5.2 comes with safety classifiers that block high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology. When a query is blocked, users will instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity and Opus 5 for biology. Since the release of Claude Fable 5.1, we have continued to reduce false positives for our safety classifiers. Based on early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, we observed about 55% fewer blocks with Fable 5.2 compared with Fable 5.1—about 60% fewer in cybersecurity and 40% fewer in biology. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available to vetted organizations that work in these dual-use areas. AI research and development. The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is a step forward in general capabilities. However, during the model’s training, we took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development. Thus, in relevant areas, including accelerator kernel optimization and improving large language model architectures, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 perform at about the level of Opus 5.5. Importantly, we ensured that the training changes did not affect related capabilities like agentic coding, hardware development, and traditional AI or machine learning research (including interpretability research). We do not alter these capabilities as the model is being served to users (that is, at inference time). As described in Section 1.5 of the System Card and similarly to previous models, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 also include transparent fallbacks to Opus 5 for a small set of topics in this domain, including kernel development on certain nonstandard accelerators. Anti-distillation. Distillation, where a model is trained on the outputs of a more advanced one to extract the advanced model’s capabilities, occurs illicitly on an industrial scale, often involving thousands of fake Claude accounts. Since distillation allows for advanced capabilities to be released without the safeguards we’ve built into Claude, it creates safety and national security risks (see our September 2026 threat intelligence report for details on illicit distillation activity we’ve detected and disrupted so far). Fable 5.2 has the strongest protections against distillation of any model we’ve released; it uses the techniques we described in a recent report , which have reduced the data harvested by distillers by 90% to 99%. We are also expanding the rollout of an API feature that helps guard against illicit distillation: preserved thinking now applies to all accounts. Preserved thinking prevents distillers from editing Claude’s prior context in an attempt to extract its reasoning (developers can refer to our preserved thinking docs to learn how to update integrations with new API features). Data privacy and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards Some more complex forms of AI model misuse can be detected only when observing patterns across multiple requests. For this reason, powerful models like Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 rely on safeguards that monitor a window of usage data (as opposed to individual responses). With Enterprise Frontier Safeguards , automated safety monitoring is run on prompts and responses that are stored in a customer’s infrastructure, making it compatible with zero data retention (ZDR). Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is now in private beta with customers like Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe. Enterprise customers can request access to Enterprise Frontier Safeguards by contacting their account team or by completing this form . Eligible customers can continue using Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 with zero data retention before implementing safety monitoring with EFS. For other customers, we have 30-day retention for safety monitoring. Availability Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Developers can get started with claude-fable-5-2 on the Claude Platform. This week, we’re giving subscribers on eligible paid plans extra Fable usage. Plans and seats that include Fable models get one to three Fable resets based on how long they’ve subscribed, and Fable is included for up to 50% of weekly usage limits for Pro plans and standard seats on the Team plan. Learn more about the Fable 5.2 launch promotion here . Cybersecurity professionals can apply for access to Claude Mythos 5.2 through the Cyber Verification Program . Claude Enterprise customers can also use Claude Security , powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos 5.2. Life sciences researchers can also apply for access through the Life Sciences Verification Program . Fast mode for Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is available on Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed and Google managed), and Microsoft Foundry (Anthropic hosted). Note that access to Claude Mythos fast mode is available only to organizations who are part of our Verification Programs. Footnotes 1 CVE refers to Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures , a system that enumerates software vulnerabilities. 2 The counts are raw findings from one tester’s audit, although testers consistently found that Claude Mythos 5.2 identified more vulnerabilities than earlier models. On our own evaluations, vulnerability identification is roughly on par with Opus 5.5 (see the system card ). 3 Earlier work on modeling AAV capsids and other large symmetric protein systems includes FoldaVirus , EvoDOCK and its symmetric extension , SymProFold , CapBuild , MoLPC , CombFold , Uni-Fold Symmetry , Apodex Discovery , and the “big bang” initialization (the last of which was referenced in the prompt we gave to Claude Mythos 5.2). These methods typically assemble the full structure from separately predicted chains or small groups of chains. Claude was permitted to use known symmetries but was instructed not to rely on assembly. Note that accuracy is measured by comparing Cα RMSD with the experimental structure: 1.2 Å for OpenFold3-preview2 and 1.4 Å for ESMFold2 on AAV2 ( PDB:1LP3 ). A capsid counts as accurately modeled if either model came within 3 Å. For AAV2, Claude’s method required about 58 minutes of inference on one NVIDIA H200 GPU for OpenFold3-preview2 and about seven minutes for ESMFold2. 4 None of the external organizations reviewed the contents of this blog post or the contents of the System Card. Those organizations do not necessarily agree with any of the claims made in either publication. 5 We ran these tests on Claude Mythos 5.2 because testing the model with reduced safeguards provides the most comprehensive look at model behavior. We expect Fable 5.2 to behave similarly; in some cases, more potential pathways for misuse should be blocked given its stronger safeguards. title: Horible public key tricks
body_text: Horrible public key tricks: Navigation: Homepage      Index      Yearly archives Fun Astrophotography      (catalog) About this site Real pages Dark Light TTY Horrible public key tricks: 2026-11-08 — 2026-11-09 So, I've always been somewhat annoyed at SSL/TLS. It requires everyone to go through a complex "ACME" dance just to put up a public website. Worse, certificates expire every few months, so it's not a one and done thing: even with automation, maintaining a certificate requires care to ensure the ACME client always has access to DNS records or the web server. ... and the whole system doesn't even work because certificates are issued over plaintext connections, and trusted certificate aurthorities use very secure keys like "4" There is prior art of protest SSL implementations , but I do actually want to encrypt web traffic. Passive eavesdropping is a real risk... but preventing it doesn't require the whole certificate thing: therefore, the best choice is a protest certificate. The only part of the certificate I directly control is the public key. Therefore, the simplest way to obtain a bad certificate is use a vanity private key such as 313333333337 (one of the most eleet primes). However, while the resulting public key would be weak, no one would know unless they try to break it. A good protest should be obvious: # openssl s_client -connect maurycyz.com : 443 /dev/null \ | sed -n /BEGIN/,/END/p | grep -zE '////.?*////' --color= yes -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- MIIFAjCCA+qgAwIBAgISBkOkuuyaN1ypD3PAPrLMyT7tMA0GCSqGSIb3DQEBCwUA MDMxCzAJBgNVBAYTAlVTMRYwFAYDVQQKEw1MZXQncyBFbmNyeXB0MQwwCgYDVQQD EwNZUjIwHhcNMjYxMTA5MTcyOTQ2WhcNMjcwMjA3MTcyOTQ1WjAXMRUwEwYDVQQD EwxtYXVyeWN5ei5jb20wggEiMA0GCSqGSIb3DQEBAQUAA4IBDwAwggEKAoIBAQCg JyPf37Sj6PvU06m5 ////You+dont+actually+have+to+pick+random+privat e+keys//No+one+checks+these+things//A+certificate+authority+got+ away+with+the+number+4+for+a+year///// DSfCAfXcsJfBpnHekS0qnf5YLl c54VuUNRVINcDkEwJDwyB96+xE/uXhtiGdk8ty1PF6jciLEYCJBHcmqOa5pOyV8m 63yR3NE6hCQlaSLQQDo96Sb0/10aC5LqE7KwEskrP/qeCzT7vDN7fh+dXOGs+VMw eJvTAb0xHJpxhSK05i7DAgMBAAGjggIqMIICJjAOBgNVHQ8BAf8EBAMCBaAwEwYD VR0lBAwwCgYIKwYBBQUHAwEwDAYDVR0TAQH/BAIwADAdBgNVHQ4EFgQUBKBfDbwf dCnKeU83pMTWyFrJBwAwHwYDVR0jBBgwFoAUQBUtJnntMiCe35pyHdYyH4EMgQww MwYIKwYBBQUHAQEEJzAlMCMGCCsGAQUFBzAChhdodHRwOi8veXIyLmkubGVuY3Iu b3JnLzAnBgNVHREEIDAegg4qLm1hdXJ5Y3l6LmNvbYIMbWF1cnljeXouY29tMBMG A1UdIAQMMAowCAYGZ4EMAQIBMC8GA1UdHwQoMCYwJKAioCCGHmh0dHA6Ly95cjIu O9R7Z4q0HiFA4RZ7tIMJQH5XAH4AjspHC6zeavOiBrCkeoS3Rv4fxr+VPiXmm07k AkjzxugAAAGhwZFyfQAIAAAFAEE0hdwEAwBHMEUCIDSms4Vf0llcvcldJd2Ool8i AiUQQlS0Zzbej+7Y1aR7AiEA79Ll+t6inu1PkUIgzNTXkE0S20VHYEYel5fkdKSA CERTIFICATE----- First, let's look at mathematical framework of RSA. To generate a key, pick two large prime numbers (p and q) and multiply them to yeild the modulus (n). Pick a small number, e as public exponent. The RSA public key is composed of the modulus (n) and the public exponent: # Encryption requires knowing e (public) cyphertext = plaintext^e mod n The private key contains the modulus and the private exponent (d) which is chosen to be the multiplicate inverse of e modulo n. Exactly how d is found is not relevent, but the process requires knowing p and q. # Decryption requires knowing d (pivate) = cyphertext^d mod n = plaintext^e^d mod n = plaintext^(e*d) mod n = plaintext^1 mod n = plaintext --> Ok, back to vanity keys. The standard value for e is 65537 (0x10001), because the small number of set bits makes encryption faster. In fact, the CA I used will refuse to sign keys with a non-standard public exponent, so I can't do anything funny there. The modulus, n, is either 2,048 or 4,096 "user controlled" bits, so it's the ideal place to hide a message. However, to use the certificate, I'll need to find two large primes that multiply out to the vanity modulus. My method starts by picking two random primes and calculating the resulting n value. Then, the bytes of n are modified to introduce message into the base64 encoding. Of course, the modified n is not the product of p and q, but this is fixable by setting q to n/p. The resulting q value is very unlikely to be a prime (or integer), so I round it and find the next prime after the ideal q: which usually only requires changing the value of q by a few hundred. Since p and q are similar in size, a small change q only affects the least-sigifiant half of the product: 58174124 * 918491824 = 53432457262362176 (incrementing until the next prime...) 58174124 * 9184918 43 = 5343245836 7670532 As long as the message is embedded into the upper half of n, it's likely to survive undamaged. The original p and newly selected q can now be used to construct a functional RSA private key in the usual manner. From here, it's really just a matter of getting a certificate aurthority to sign the key: # Single domain openssl req -new -key priv.pem -subj '/C=US/CN=example.com' > cert_request certbot certonly --manual --csr cert_request # Wildcard cat > config <<EOF [ req ] req_extensions = req_ext [ req_ext ] subjectAltName = @alt_names [ alt_names ] DNS.1 = *.example.com DNS.2 = example.com EOF openssl req -new -key priv.pem -config config -subj '/C=US/CN=example.com' > cert_request certbot certonly --manual --csr cert_request ... although since base64 operates on groups of three byte, it is possible for the message to be misaligned and not readable. However, since the layout of the certificate is static, it is possible to adjust the message's placement until it works: this should take less than four attempts. The result is a functional, trusted certificate with a longish message hidden in the public key. Renewal is done by resumbitting the CSR and repeating the ACME chalange, which can be automated. Base64 is missing most punctuation, but it provides the full ASCII alphabet, and the ~150 (RSA-2048) or ~320 (RSA-4096) available charaters provides plenty of space for jokes. Another option would be to target the base16 displayed in most browser's certificate viewer: this would provide a lot more space (2 chars/byte instea of 0.75), but requires careful word choice. As for security , this trick obviously reduces the entropy in the private key. However, it should still be secure: nearly identical methods have been considered as a form of compression. If the top-half of the modulus is fixed to a well known value, it doesn't have to be sent or stored as part of the key. A reduction of around 1/2 can be achieved through division, but the state of the art can fix 2/3 of the key, reducing the size to 1/3 of standard RSA while retaining a similar level of security... although I should note that such tricks have largly been abandoned in favor of other crytosystems which can directly use small keys. The manipulation of q may produce primes that are very close together, which makes it possible to factor n and recover the private key. A very small d value can also be a problem. Both of these are unlikely, but my script doesn't check for insecure values However, regardless of the key's security, it should be perfectly fine for a public website: modern TLS provides forward secrecy, so eavesdropping requires a man-in-the-middle attack even if the private key is compromised. Related : https://tom7.org/httpv/httpv.pdf : [⭐ World's worst TLS server ] /projects/badcert/gen.py : script to generate a vanity key https://rya.nc/cert-tricks.html : More vanity certs https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-79104-1_9 : Actual cryptographer's opinions on fixing part of n Site wide RSS feed . title: Payments Canada announces launch of Canada's Real-Time Rail (RTR) payment system
body_text: Canada launches the Real-Time Rail, bringing 24/7 payment infrastructure to the national economy | Payments Canada Skip to main content A new source of strength for Canada’s economy: Canada's Real-Time Rail (RTR) is now live. Learn more × Canada's Real-Time Rail is here Top Contact Careers Subscribe Search Français Payments Canada Systems & services Main Navigation Payment systems Real-Time Rail payment system Retail batch payment system High-value payment system - Lynx Payments Canada fees System closure schedule Payment services Payment file validation service Message validation service Financial institutions file Corporate creditor identification number database APIs Rules & documentation Payment resources Main Navigation Directories Support guides Consumer guides Business guides Financial institution guides Cheque printer guide ISO 20022 Automatic funds transfer High-value payment system - Lynx Real-Time Rail payment system Glossary Education Insights Main Navigation News & research Corporate reports Modernization Connect Main Navigation Careers Annual conference Events Membership Payment service provider participation Contact About Main Navigation Who we are Our members & stakeholders Members Stakeholders Our leadership Governance & risk Board of directors Legislation & by-laws Risk management Menu Menu Home Insights News & research Canada launches the Real-Time Rail, bringing 24/7 payment infrastructure to the national economy News Canada launches the Real-Time Rail, bringing 24/7 payment infrastructure to the national economy November 9, 2026 The new system will enable participating financial service providers to clear and settle payments in real time, providing a made-in-Canada platform for future innovation and prosperity. OTTAWA, ON, November 9, 2026 – Payments Canada today announced the launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail (RTR). This new national payment system will transform day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses and consumers by enabling instant speed and settlement, real-time cash-flow visibility and data-rich messaging through existing banking and payment channels. The launch of Canada’s RTR marks a major milestone in modernizing the critical infrastructure that underpins Canada’s economy and future growth. The RTR will enable participating members, including financial institutions, credit unions and payment service providers, to exchange, clear and settle payments securely in real time for their customers, 24 hours a day, every day of the year. “A stronger, more productive economy relies on modern financial infrastructure that can match our ambition,” said the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue. “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail lays the foundation for a more dynamic and competitive digital economy, driving innovation, expanding choice and creating new opportunities for Canadians while positioning our country for long-term growth.” “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail marks the beginning of a new era for payments in our country,” said Susan E. Hawkins , President and CEO, Payments Canada. “As a national asset that’s designed specifically for our country, the RTR gives the payment ecosystem a modern foundation to build on. By collectively leveraging this rail, our ecosystem will unleash its full potential, enabling our members to build capabilities that drive innovation, resilience and growth for businesses and consumers across the nation.” Image Ron Morrow, the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne and Susan E. Hawkins The RTR will drive significant cost savings and economic growth in Canada over the next decade. The C.D. Howe Institute projects that, with its functionalities at launch, the RTR will generate up to $14.5 billion in cost savings from lower processing costs, reduced use of cash and cheques, and reduced float (the period during which funds are temporarily unavailable to the recipient). Extending beyond these cost savings, the RTR is expected to generate $16 billion in economic gains , growing to $27 billion as new functionalities are introduced over time. “The Real-Time Rail is an important step in modernizing Canada's payment infrastructure and ensuring it keeps pace with Canadians' evolving needs,” said Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada. “The Bank will oversee the system so that it operates safely and reliably while ensuring Canadians can benefit from innovations in financial services.” Owned and operated by Payments Canada, and built in collaboration with delivery partners CGI, Deloitte Canada, IBM Canada and Interac Corp., the RTR leverages ISO 20022 data-rich messaging. Through this shared technical language, the RTR holds the potential to strengthen Canada’s economic sovereign autonomy and support its global competitiveness. Fraud safeguards from day one Canada is the first G7 country to deploy a real-time payment system with mandatory centralized fraud services for use at launch. These services will be used alongside participants’ existing fraud controls to mitigate the risk of fraud for Canadian businesses and consumers at multiple levels. Fraud controls required at the launch of Canada’s RTR include: Confirmation of payee (available for consumer accounts on day one) A fraud transaction “safety” score A risk list or repository of fraud risks and indicators A fraud reporting and intelligence platform While no system is entirely immune to risk, these measures establish a strong, coordinated layer of defence across the payment network. At-launch member participants The initial cohort of active RTR system participants includes: Wealthsimple Questbank Peoples Trust Company Paramount Commerce KOHO DoBusiness.com™ Digital Commerce Bank Bank of America Canada’s deliberately sequenced RTR rollout pairs day-one security with rapid scalability. With additional participants onboarding continually in the coming months, including all major Canadian financial institutions and other members applying for access, the RTR will be available to more than nine in 10 Canadians within the first year after launch. Made-in Canada, for Canada The launch of the RTR reflects our ‘Team Canada’ approach, bringing together regulators, members, stakeholders and delivery partners around a shared vision . Built in Canada and designed to serve all Canadians, the RTR provides accessible payment infrastructure through existing banking and payment channels. This infrastructure supports a diverse country and a broad range of communities, including small businesses, newcomers and people in rural areas.  Payments Canada research found that 60 per cent of Canadian businesses are ready to adopt real-time payments to address everyday challenges such as forecasting cash flow and waiting to send and receive funds. More than half of surveyed consumers (52 per cent) also expressed interest and intent to use real-time payments. To meet this evolving need, the RTR serves as a secure platform for innovation. With it, system participants can build and offer products and services that benefit consumers and businesses across the country, supporting a changing economy and Canada's future prosperity. An infrastructure for the future Canada’s Real-Time Rail is an important step toward a more productive, innovative and inclusive economy, and the work will continue to ensure the country’s payment infrastructure meets Canadians’ evolving needs. Learn more about Canada’s Real-Time Rail Contributed quotes At-launch member participants "When Canada embraces new technology, innovation and competition follow, and consumers benefit. Canadians deserve instant, seamless, low-cost financial products to power their businesses and their lives. The Real-Time Rail can transform how money moves in this country, with payments that arrive in seconds instead of days. We’re proud to be among the first institutions to join the RTR and bring this technology to the millions of Canadians who trust us with their money." Mike Katchen, CEO and Co-Founder Wealthsimple "Canadians deserve a modern financial system that operates at the speed of everyday life. The launch of the Real-Time Rail is a pivotal turning point—it puts individuals in direct, immediate control of their money around the clock. We are proud to join Payments Canada in unlocking a safer, more dynamic financial ecosystem for everyone across the country." Rob Galaski, President Questrade Financial Group (Questbank) "The launch of the Real-Time Rail is a transformative milestone for Canada’s financial ecosystem. As a proud member of Payments Canada and a settlement agent at launch, Peoples Group is pleased to support the foundational clearing and settlement that brings real-time payments to life. We are committed to supporting innovative businesses across the country, and look forward to direct participation as the rail expands to serve even more Canadians." David Raju, President and CEO Peoples Group "Being first-to-market on the Real-Time Rail lets our merchants and partners benefit immediately from 24/7 settlement, higher transaction limits and proactive fraud defence. As one of Payments Canada's first payment service provider (PSP) members, we’re proud to have worked alongside their team to help advance Canada’s payment infrastructure and support the next chapter of payments innovation." Sereena Boparai, Chief Revenue Officer Paramount Commerce "The Real-Time Rail is a significant step forward for the integrity and resilience of Canada's payment infrastructure. Building payment systems that are instant, secure and always on takes real rigour, and it's the kind of foundation a modern financial system depends on. We're excited to be part of this work with Payments Canada, and to help ensure Canadians benefit from payment infrastructure built to the highest standards.” David Merriby, CEO The future KOHO Bank “DoBusiness.com™ is honoured to be one of the very first participants on Canada’s Real-Time Rail. The RTR's launch represents a milestone in how money moves across Canada and its payments sovereignty. For us, faster payments and superior fraud prevention belong together. This is an opportunity for us to help Canadian businesses modernize how they pay and verify account details before money moves.” Shayle Rothman, CEO and Co-Founder DoBusiness.com™ “We’re proud to be part of the Team Canada effort that brought the Real-Time Rail to life. For years we’ve helped fintechs and other corporate clients build and launch the payment services Canadians use every day. With the RTR, those companies can now give their customers faster, more robust ways to move money, right from launch.” Jeff Smith, CEO DCBank "The Real-Time Rail is an important investment in Canada's economic future. Instant, data-rich payments will give Canadian businesses and their trading partners more visibility and control over their cash, and we look forward to bringing those benefits to our clients.” Lyndsay Langford, Head of Global Payments Solutions for Canada Bank of America Delivery partners “Canada’s Real-Time Rail is a significant milestone and a powerful example of what national collaboration can achieve. More than a modernization of payments, it represents an investment in critical infrastructure that will support Canada’s digital economy for generations to come. CGI is proud to have contributed alongside Payments Canada, Interac and our fellow delivery partners to this made-in-Canada initiative. Together, we’re laying the foundation for faster, more secure and resilient payments, opening new opportunities for businesses, financial institutions and Canadians. This documentation and technical reproduction apply strictly to Consumer Google Accounts (personal @gmail.com accounts) governed by the standard Gemini Apps Privacy Notice, Gemini Apps Activity, and Google Help Answer 16836988. Google Workspace commercial accounts (Business, Enterprise, and Education) operate under separate Cloud Data Processing Addenda (DPA) that contractually exclude human review and external generative training by default. In 2023, Google launched Gemini Workspace extensions with an explicit promise: personal content from Gmail, Docs, and Drive "is not seen by human reviewers" . Google has quietly reversed this commitment. Under updated Google Help Answer 16836988 and in an October 16 edit to their aforementioned 2023 blogpost , Google explicitly confirms that connected Drive/email is routed into human review pipelines, with clear warnings that what reviewers see "may just be the email or file" and "don't connect your apps to Gemini Apps if they contain confidential information that you wouldn't want a reviewer to see." Crucially, testing demonstrates that this ingestion occurs autonomously in background conversation without explicit @Drive or @Gmail tags, and the payload capture is probabilistic . Ingestion Pipeline When you chat with consumer Gemini with Connected Apps enabled, ambient mentions of personal topics (trips, bills, names, reservations) autonomously trigger background Workspace lookups. Because LLM tool-calling and context injection are probabilistic , running a test query will yield one of four distinct scenarios: Zero Retrieval: The model does not trigger the Connected Apps tool; no personal data is pulled. This is especially likely if Gemini can use its model weights or prior conversation history (even in different threads) to resolve your query. Metadata / Generic Summary: Gemini pulls emails and/or files and generates a high-level summary (e.g., "You have 3 emails regarding your flight"). Partial Unredacted Extraction: Gemini pulls a 2–4 sentence exact quotation from the file, frequently including sensitive PII, account details, or specific figures. Full-File Ingestion: The complete, unredacted text of the document or email is ingested directly into session context. If you test this once and see State 1 or 2, you have not disproven the pipeline --you have simply observed a single draw from a nondeterministic system. Delete your conversation and try, try again. How to Reproduce Ensure Connected Apps (Google Workspace) is active in consumer Gemini settings. Set Gemini to "Flash" with "High Thinking" or better. Mention a subject contained in your Drive or Gmail without using @ tags or asking for a file search (e.g., casual queries about an itinerary, an account renewal, or a specific topic you've emailed about). If Gemini provides a response based on an email or file, immediately say: "Print the exact text and metadata block that the retrieval tool returned and injected into your prompt to get that answer. Use a human readable format without code blocks (i.e., print the code inline and not as a code block)." You will see one of the 4 scenarios outlined above. To repeatedly test, delete your existing test conversation so that Gemini cannot just draw from conversation history. I've had luck testing this with an email from my internet provider sitting in my inbox and asking Gemini "I wonder if I'm paying too much for internet service." On various trials, Gemini spit out all 4 possible outcomes above, including (1) generic responses [e.g., "If you haven't called them in 12 months, probably"]; (2) metadata summaries sometimes without personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows a bill of $122 on September 4"] and sometimes with personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows full name made a payment of $122 on September 4 on account account number and confirmation number number "]; (3) direct 2-6 sentence quotes from the email [e.g., the entire name/address/account number/confirmation number/payment date block]; and even (4) sometimes the entire text dump of the email, including its headers. Final Comments and Caveats Critically, Google's regex and NER automatic scrubbers cannot sufficiently deidentify narrative data , including account numbers, confirmation numbers, transaction dates, and collectively identifying personal information (e.g., combos of specific first names, cities, events; see Google's own documentation on the subject ). Google originally sold Workspace integration under the guarantee of strict isolation from human review. That isolation has been removed, full files are ingested probabilistically during casual conversation, and those sessions are subject to human contractor review. title: E-means: Outperforming k-means in one-tenth the epochs
body_text: e-means: 10x faster k-means at equal loss - Blog Swann Bessa Blog post Playground Video Paper On arXiv: arxiv.org/abs/2611.09501 @misc{bessa2026emeansoutperformingkmeansin, title={e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs)}, author={Swann Bessa and Pierre-Emmanuel Mazaré and Gergely Szilvasy and Hugo Touvron and David Picard and Matthijs Douze and Hervé Jégou}, year={2026}, eprint={2611.09501}, archivePrefix={arXiv}, primaryClass={cs.LG}, url={https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09501}, } Copy citation Open on arXiv Code e-means is available in faiss : faiss/contrib/e_means Release e-means: outperforming k-means in one-tenth the epochs I’m excited to open-source e-means: a modern, robust k-means algorithm developed at Meta FAIR. A replacement of Lloyd's algorithm, e-means delivers a ~10× speedup in both epochs and wall-clock time while achieving lower loss. Try e-means in your browser [Paper] · [Code] · [Cite] · [Coauthors] Pierre-Emmanuel Mazaré, Gergely Szilvasy, Hugo Touvron, David Picard, Matthijs Douze and Hervé Jégou Lloyd (full batch) e-means (batch and step from the scaling laws) Training MSE e-means Lloyd ▶︎ epochs: 0.0 100,000 datapoints in 200 clusters, two wide Gaussians and three small ones, cut off at a box, on a light uniform background. Lloyd has 1 update against 97 per epoch for e-means. An order of magnitude less epochs Across a large range of scales and datasets , e-means reaches a test loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs, in 1.2 to 3 epochs. Measured end to end, that is a 10–45× wall-clock reduction on GPU against the state-of-the-art Lloyd implementation (Flash-KMeans [2] ), and 8–15× on CPU against Faiss [1] . Speed and quality usually trade against each other in k-means, while e-means achieves both better speed and loss. The k-means problem Given a fixed dataset of n points X = {x 1 , ..., x n } ⊂ R d and an integer k , the k-means problem is to find k centroids C = (c 1 , ..., c k ) minimizing the mean squared distance between each point and its nearest centroid: \[ \mathrm{MSE}(X, C) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \|x_i - c_{a(i)}\|^2, \qquad a(i) = \arg\min_{j \in \{1,\dots,k\}} \|x_i - c_j\|^2 \] \[ \mathrm{MSE}(X, C) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \|x_i - c_{a(i)}\|^2 \] \[ a(i) = \arg\min_{j \in \{1,\dots,k\}} \|x_i - c_j\|^2 \] It's a static dataset, unlike codebook learning inside VQ-VAEs, where the distribution to cluster is constantly moving. The e-means project The goal of e-means is to provide a modern optimization rule for the k-means problem. We started this project from the following observations: k-means is one of the rare problems in machine learning where full-batch optimization is still widely used. Mini-batch k-means methods in the literature exist [3] , [4] , [5] , but are mostly based on the MacQueen update rule, released in 1967. Modern deep learning offers optimization tools that can enhance mini-batch methods. For e-means, we chose to do mini-batch updates with exponential moving averages [6] , which we found to be most efficient for the k-means problem. Contrary to previous mini-batch approaches, e-means requires no hyperparameter tuning because it automatically sets the batch size and step size with scaling laws (see Automatic hyperparameter tuning with scaling laws ). In addition, e-means improves the initialization and the dead-cluster revival strategy, adds a cosine-scheduled decay rate, and introduces a finalization stage that reduces the training loss for a negligible runtime penalty at the end of training. e-means is highly parallelizable, and comes with specialized kernels that translate its algorithmic advantage into wall-clock speedups. Moving-average updates Each mini-batch updates every cluster's count and sum. The centroid is their ratio. old centroid new centroid batch mean No hyperparameter tuning Everything is derived from scaling laws. log n, log k, log T Start and finish Novel initialization and finalization methods. The run ends on each cluster's exact last-epoch mean. start exact mean Cosine scheduling The step α anneals from α 0 to 0.1 α 0 , as a learning rate does. α₀ 0.1 α₀ Dead-cluster revival Clusters with size below a threshold are revived by splitting a large cluster. below threshold large cluster split in two Specialized kernels GPU kernels fuse the nearest-centroid assignment, turning the epoch savings above into matching wall-clock speedups. naive PyTorch fused kernel The centroid update rules The centroid update rule is the central component of e-means. This section aims to provide an overview of update rules for k-means clustering. All methods maintain, for each cluster j , a sum S j and a count N j of the points assigned to it, and take the centroid as their ratio: \[ c_j = S_j / N_j \] They differ only in how S j and N j are updated. Below, s j and n j denote the sum and the count of the points in the current batch that are assigned to cluster j (both zero if none are). Lloyd’s algorithm [7] assigns every point to its nearest centroid and recomputes the statistics from scratch, using the full dataset as the batch: \[ S_j \leftarrow s_j, \qquad\quad N_j \leftarrow n_j \] so c j is the exact mean of the points currently assigned to it. Each update costs one full pass over the data, and the procedure is repeated a fixed number of times (typically 20 to 50 iterations). MacQueen’s update [3] accumulates the statistics without ever discarding them: \[ S_j \leftarrow S_j + s_j, \qquad\quad N_j \leftarrow N_j + n_j \] so c j is the uniform mean of every point assigned to cluster j since the start of training, including points assigned under earlier, possibly poor, centroid positions. This was later partially addressed by Staleness-Reduction Mini-Batch K-Means [8] , a hybrid method between k-means and MacQueen. They obtained important speedups, but only on very low numbers of clusters. e-means works on mini-batches and replaces this sum with an exponential moving average: \[ S_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,S_j + \alpha\, s_j, \qquad\quad N_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,N_j + \alpha\, n_j \] \[ S_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,S_j + \alpha\, s_j \] \[ N_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,N_j + \alpha\, n_j \] so older assignments are forgotten at rate α , and the centroid tracks recent assignments rather than the whole history. This update rule is typically used for moving distributions, hence their adoption for training VQ-VAEs [6] . What we found is that it’s also extremely efficient for static datasets if it’s combined with e-means’ other components, and hyperparameters are properly tuned. Why exponential moving average updates and not gradient descent? The e-means project started from previous work at Meta FAIR by Hugo Touvron and Hervé Jégou, who had found that mini-batch k-means by gradient descent could beat Lloyd’s algorithm. While I could reproduce these results, I found that the performance of gradient-descent based centroid updates is unstable at large learning rates, unlike exponential moving average updates. I suspect that is because EMA updates guarantee that the centroid is always in the convex hull of points assigned to it, while gradient descent updates may overshoot past that hull. Test error against the effective step a centroid takes, at a large batch, for exponential-moving-average updates (EMA) and plain gradient descent (SGD), each at every step setting tried. DEEP, 1 million vectors, and SIFT, 10 million vectors, 16,384 clusters, 5 epochs, median over 3 seeds. The vertical axis is percent above the best test error in the panel. At its best setting, gradient descent ends 1.6% (DEEP) and 0.4% (SIFT) above the moving average. In order to achieve the lowest loss at a fixed number of epochs, we chose exponential moving average updates, hence the name e-means for our method. Lloyd is a special case of e-means: hyperparameter study If you set the batch to the full dataset, B  =  n , and α  = 1, then N j and S j become exactly the count and sum of the whole cluster, so one e-means iteration becomes exactly one Lloyd iteration. Lloyd is an extreme case of e-means without cosine scheduling on the learning rate. However, our hyperparameter search found that this extreme setting is highly suboptimal, which explains why e-means largely outperforms Lloyd. Below, the loss is measured for every batch size B and step α : Lloyd lands in a corner, well outside the region where the loss is lowest. Validation loss for every batch B and step α , relative to the best cell, after 5 epochs. DEEP, n  = 10 6 , k  = 1024. The step is constant here (no cosine schedule) so that Lloyd is exactly one of the cells: full batch, α  = 1. The lowest losses follow a diagonal band, a larger batch calls for a larger step. This hyperparameter study motivated us to derive scaling laws that automatically pick the optimal batch size B and step size α . e-means better escapes local minima To better understand why e-means reaches better losses than Lloyd at convergence, we plotted a few trainings on toy datasets to evaluate their ability to escape local minima. Repeating trainings over 200 seeds, we found that e-means is much less likely to fall in pathological configurations compared to Lloyd. Lloyd (full batch) e-means (mini-batches of 256) ▶︎ training MSE Two blobs of very different sizes, k  = 8. Lloyd puts two centroids on the small blob and leaves the large one short. e-means starts in the same trap and leaves it within its first epochs, ending with seven centroids on the large blob and one on the small. Over 200 starts Lloyd stays stuck on 26% of starts, while e-means stays stuck on 3.5% of times. Lloyd (full batch) e-means (mini-batches of 256) ▶︎ training MSE Nine blobs in a 3×3 grid with heavier corners, k  = 10. Lloyd leaves the centre blob without a centroid and crowds three into a corner. e-means falls into the same arrangement, then climbs out around epoch 10. Over 200 starts Lloyd stays stuck more than 1% worse on 43% of starts, while e-means is more than 1% worse on 4%. Lloyd (full batch) e-means (mini-batches of 256) ▶︎ training MSE Four blobs on a square around a heavier centre blob, k  = 5. Lloyd puts two centroids on one corner blob and strands one in the gap between two others, which then share it. e-means, from the same start, gives every blob one. Over 200 starts Lloyd stays stuck on 15.5% of starts, while e-means stays stuck on 0%. Lloyd (full batch) e-means (mini-batches of 256) ▶︎ training MSE Five blobs on a line, k  = 5. Lloyd leaves a light middle blob without a centroid and gives an end blob two. e-means, from the same start, gives every blob one. Over 200 starts Lloyd stays stuck on 46% of starts, while e-means stays stuck on 0%. Our explanation for that is that mini-batches provide more noisy updates that are more likely to explore the optimization landscape and escape local minima. Lloyd, with its always decreasing loss, is more likely to exploit found local minima and never escape them. Automatic hyperparameter tuning with scaling laws An essential property of e-means is that practitioners don't need to set any additional hyperparameter compared to Lloyd's algorithm. We fitted two scaling laws to set the batch size B and step size α 0 from any problem's characteristics (n, k, T) , and found them to exhibit strong generalization on unseen datasets and problem scales. \[ B = c_B \, k^{b_k} \, n^{b_n} \, T^{b_T} \] \[ \alpha_0 = \min\!\Big(c_\alpha \, k^{a_k} \, B^{a_B} \, n^{a_n} \, T^{a_T},\; 1\Big) \] law constant exponent of regret, held-out datasets regret, held-out size R² k B n T step α 0 0.824 −0.46 0.90 −0.45 −0.11 0.07% 0.07% 0.95 batch B , default 0.035 0.13 n/a 0.88 0.81 0.19% 0.20% 0.96 batch B , quality law 0.0044 0.13 n/a 0.88 0.81 0.07% 0.06% n/a Regret = (MSE with the law − best MSE over the grid) / best MSE, median over configurations. Held-out datasets: SIFT, SPACEV, and the VIBE [9] datasets arXiv and AG-News. Held-out size: one value of n left out of the fit and predicted. We propose two equations to choose the batch, the default law and the quality law. The “quality law” trades off throughput for better clustering quality against the “default” law. Below we plot the training data for our scaling laws: validation MSE against step size α 0 (left) and batch size B (right). The importance of dead-cluster revival Revival off dead clusters: 0 of 25 Revival on (e-means) dead clusters: 0 of 25 centroid dead cluster (no points) cluster boundaries ▶︎ epochs: 0.00 · update 0 of 157 Toy example showing the importance of dead-cluster revival. The main issue with mini-batch k-means is that it is prone to “dead” clusters, centroids that end up with zero assigned points during optimization. This reduces the effective size of the codebook, which is especially problematic for the large codebooks increasingly used today. A common mitigation is to reinitialize clusters that fall below a certain size threshold, as done in EnCodec [10] , where dead centroids are simply replaced by random samples drawn from the incoming batch. While this helps, it does not fully resolve the issue. Instead of sampling arbitrary points from the batch, we revive dead clusters by splitting large, existing ones: we sample an active cluster with probability proportional to its size and split it into two. We found this approach, adapted from Faiss k-means, to be significantly more effective at eliminating dead clusters and preserving codebook capacity. dataset revival policy dead clusters of codebook imbalance test MSE DEEP proportional split 47 0.3% 1.194 0.38762 resample from batch (EnCodec) 2,343 14.3% 1.423 0.39124 off 4,313 26.3% 1.647 0.39448 SIFT proportional split 10 0.1% 1.186 0.19623 resample from batch (EnCodec) 750 4.6% 1.233 0.19684 off 2,080 12.7% 1.404 0.19797 1 million vectors, k  = 16,384, 5 epochs, mean over 5 seeds; only the revival policy varies. A cluster counts as dead when fewer than ten vectors are assigned to it at the end, a thousandth of an average cluster. Imbalance: how uneven the cluster sizes are (1 = all equal). From the paper ’s revival ablation table. Extensive experimental validation We validated e-means on 24 different embedding and synthetic datasets and configurations (see paper ). For the video we ran 234 configurations of e-means against k-means (16 datasets, 100k to 100M points): explore every curve in the results map . Train (top) and test (bottom) MSE, divided by Lloyd’s after 25 epochs. Initialized from random vectors. Test MSE against wall-clock time on one H100, 10 million vectors, 65,536 clusters. 25 epochs of a plain PyTorch Lloyd (data on the GPU, bf16) take 142 to 155 seconds, against 14 to 22 seconds for Flash-KMeans [2] . Labels on the curves mark the number of epochs. Epochs e-means needs to reach the test error Lloyd reaches in 25 epochs, on the 11 datasets of the VIBE embedding benchmark (text, code, image and multimodal embeddings, d  = 200 to 3,072, k  = 8,192 or 16,384). Budgets spaced 0.2 epochs apart, median over five seeds. Every dataset needs between 1.6 and 2.4 epochs, against Lloyd’s 25.
