Probably the most interesting thing about it at the moment is the editor. The world, and most things in it, are represented as collections of SDFs. More accurately, they're density fields, but, potato-tomato. One neat thing about representing the world as SDFs is they've been thoroughly researched and documented by a guy named Inigo Quilez, and they have a lot of nice mathematical properties. For example, you can do a smooth union of arbitrary SDFs to get nice rounded contours where shapes join. The world generator and editor operate almost entirely on the GPU. The terrain and editor pipeline is a three stage process. The first stage is user-configurable; users write an arbitrary 'shaping' shader in GLSL. The second stage is a fused stage; it does a convolution on the output of the first stage to compute a normal, runs a second user-configurable 'decoration' function, and finally applies edits. Edits are collections of SDFs that are 'compiled' from a graph structure on the CPU into a bytecode, and interpreted in the shader. The last stage runs another convolution to compute the final normal, then packs an occupancy bit, color, and normal down into a 32-bit representation, suitable for transfer back to the CPU. I expect I will expand this to include additional user-level bits for encoding biome type and GPU-driven spawning. The entire shader pipeline is one fused 'ubershader' .. everything is bound at startup and the shader is dispatched three times, incrementing a 'Stage' uniform on each dispatch. This strategy conceptually makes the driver overhead nearly zero, and the profile agrees. The final step in the process is giving the CPU a chance to spawn additional entities and structures after generation. This is not completely fleshed out, but the bones are there. The idea is that the results of the GPU work are passed back to the CPU, which can run arbitrary callbacks to spawn additional edits and entities. Once spawning is complete, the result is meshed using a fast binary meshing algorithm and uploaded to the GPU. I keep 16 bits of data per voxel from the GPU work, 1 bit of occupancy, and 15 bits of normal for collision response, which works out to half a megabyte per chunk. At the moment I only keep chunks which contain a piece of the world surface, and discard the rest. Surface chunks are dense, and may be compressed in the future, but keeping this amount of data scales to world sizes greater than 1B voxels cubed, which seems good enough for now. In terms of raw performance, GPUs are ridiculous. My 3080ti mobile gets somewhere on the order of 500B-1T perlin samples per second with a naive perlin implementation. Compared to FastNoise2, that's about 1000x more, which sounds wrong since my GPU only has 35x more capacity, but, that's what my initial profiling said. That number is the marketing number; the real throughput is significantly less due to multi-stage nature of the system, but, there's a lot of headroom for improvement. For example, dropping the backing textures from 32bit to 16bit roughly quadruples performance. Since we only really care about the surface where values are near zero, I believe using 8 or 16 bit is a viable option, though this claim will require a fair amount of study to validate. All in all, I'm pleased with how this is all working out. My original goal was to write a highly flexible system giving users both easy-to-use tools and granular control over the final output. I think I've done a fairly good job at that, and the fact it's also super fast is the cherry on top. body_text: A Message to Our Company | NVIDIA Newsroom Artificial Intelligence Computing Leadership from NVIDIA --> PLATFORMS Autonomous Machines Cloud & Data Center Deep Learning & Ai Design & Pro Visualization Healthcare High Performance Computing Self-Driving Cars Gaming & Entertainment other links Developers Industries Shop Drivers Support About NVIDIA View All Products GPU TECHNOLOGY CONFERENCE NVIDIA Blog Community Careers TECHNOLOGIES Newsroom NVIDIA in Brief Exec Bios NVIDIA Blog Podcast Media Assets In the News Press Contacts Online Press Kits NVIDIA in Brief Exec Bios NVIDIA Blog Podcast Media Assets In the News Press Contacts Online Press Kits Press Release Share Tweet Twitter Share LinkedIn Share Facebook Email ic_arrow-back-to-top A Message to Our Company NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang sent the following email to NVIDIA employees earlier today. November 8, 2026 I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry. Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it. To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.  To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence. Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American. My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy. Technology Crypto foundation demanded employees endorse suicide pledge, then fired leaders who objected, Colorado lawsuit alleges Boulder woman is suing the Switzerland-based Ethereum Foundation for wrongful termination, discrimination Share this: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on Reddit (Opens in new window) Reddit Share on X (Opens in new window) X By Shelly Bradbury | sbradbury@denverpost.com | The Denver Post PUBLISHED: November 6, 2026 at 4:00 AM MST Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... On a Friday in March, employees at an international technology foundation received a 38-page document outlining leadership’s vision for the foundation for the next 1,000 years. The document went out to all employees of The Ethereum Foundation , a nonprofit organization registered in Switzerland that supports Ethereum , a popular cryptocurrency platform and the second-largest blockchain network in the world, valued at about $300 billion, according to a federal lawsuit filed by a Boulder resident Wednesday in U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado. Titled “The Ethereum Foundation Mandate,” the document featured ethereal illustrated scenes of glowing lights and anime-style characters voyaging through dark forests. The pages featured white text against a navy blue background and were adorned with cartoon flowers, rainbows and diamonds. And on page 11 — nestled between a winking anime woman and three yellow cats — was a suicide pledge. Authors, maintainers, editors and distributors of “this software” would pledge to ensure the software remained free and publicly accessible, and would also vow to “take his or her own life with a sword upon failure to uphold any of the pledges in this license,” the illustration read. It was labeled “Source Seppuku License,” an apparent reference to a traditional Japanese ritual suicide. When the document went out on that Friday in March, employees were told to commit to the principles in the mandate by Monday or quit their jobs, according to the lawsuit brought by Kayleen Fulton, a Boulder woman who was fired from the Ethereum Foundation after she led employee resistance to the suicide pledge. Employees were to return a form with one of two options checked, according to a copy of the document included in legal filings. Choice one: “I personally commit to the direction set out in the mandate, I commit to help translate it into thoroughly reasoned strategies for my domain, and I commit to an exclusive and energetic focus on the mission-critical tasks necessary for its implementation. From today and until my last day at the EF.” Or choice two: “I cannot confidently commit to the above and would like to request my extra months of compensation and leave the EF without undue delay.” An email to the foundation seeking comment on this story was not immediately returned Thursday, but a foundation leader at the time told employees the suicide pledge was not meant to be taken literally, according to the lawsuit. After employee pushback, managers updated the commitment form to clarify that the form had “nothing to do with literal seppuku,” according to the lawsuit. Resistance to the suicide pledge was swift and vocal, and began when the Ethereum Foundation’s board put out a draft of the mandate to staff in late February, Fulton alleged in the lawsuit. Employees soon asked whether they were pledging to die by suicide and wondered in workplace forums whether the pledge was a test of their loyalty to Ethereum’s core principles. One employee referenced a colleague’s recent death by suicide. “I have a new hire joining tomorrow,” another employee wrote in a discussion about the suicide pledge, according to the lawsuit. “The first thing he’s going to see… is a motion to drop a clause that mandates employees commit the ultimate sacrifice by falling on a sword.” Nearly 80 of the foundation’s 250 or so employees voted to nix the suicide pledge after the draft was released, according to the lawsuit, but leadership at the Ethereum Foundation ignored their objections and included the pledge word-for-word in the final version of the mandate. The final published version presented the suicide pledge in an illustration instead of including it in the main body of the mandate, as it had been in the draft version. This screenshot from a federal lawsuit shows a so-called 'suicide pledge' distributed to employees at The Ethereum Foundation as part of a document outlining the organization's vision for the future. (Screenshot via U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado) The mandate’s visual aesthetic — the anime and other illustrations — reflected imagery from a controversial online figure who was known to promote “white nationalist ideology and disturbing pro-anorexia content,” according to the lawsuit. When an Ethereum Foundation board member objected to the aesthetic, Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin responded that “the controversialness (sic) of those aesthetics is itself part of the point,” according to the lawsuit. After demanding that employees agree to the mandate, Bastian Aue, co-executive director of the Ethereum Foundation, defended the suicide pledge to employees as “part of the artwork of the mandate.” Suicide prevention resources Colorado Crisis Line : 1-844-493-8255, coloradocrisisservices.org . Chat online or text TALK to 38255. 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline Dial 988 for national hotline. Mental Health First Aid : mhfaco.org . Get trained to recognize the signs and how to respond. American Foundation for Suicide Prevention : afsp.org . Join one of their upcoming walks for awareness in Colorado. Crisis Text Line : crisistextline.org . Text 741741 from anywhere in the nation to reach a counselor. It was, he said, “a cultural reference like other elements in there. Chosen deliberately, but not meant to be taken literally.” In the days after the mandate was pushed out to employees, Fulton and a colleague organized and sent the foundation’s board a letter in which 53 employees endorsed the mandate’s general direction but declined to return the commitment form. The employees also declined to resign, according to the lawsuit. Aue ultimately allowed the letter-signers to keep their jobs. But he fired Fulton and her colleague who helped organize the letter. Buterin later told Fulton — who had just been diagnosed with cancer — that the firing was about company dynamics, according to the lawsuit. “If you reward making a stink with outcomes, then everyone will know that essentially making that kind of show both internally and externally is the way to cause outcomes inside of the EF,” he said, according to the lawsuit, which cited a recorded conversation between the pair. The mandate started an exodus at the Ethereum Foundation, according to the lawsuit. The board member who’d objected to the mandate’s visual aesthetics started a sabbatical the day Fulton was fired and resigned in June. By September, eight senior employees had left, according to the lawsuit, and most of the 53 people who signed the letter had resigned or been terminated. Related Articles Crypto wants its shine back The crypto world can’t wait for “the Merge” Crypto convention sues Denver company over “subpar” show Fulton, who had earned a salary of $195,000 in her role at the Ethereum Foundation, sued for disability discrimination, retaliation, interference with her rights under the Family and Medical Leave Act, unfair employment practices and related claims. Her lawsuit notes that the Ethereum Foundation “does not hire or pay its United States staff in its own name,” but instead uses employer-of-record service companies. One of her attorneys, James Bartolomei, declined to comment Thursday, saying the lawsuit spoke for itself. Get more Colorado news by signing up for our daily Your Morning Dozen email newsletter. title: What is malloc doing, anyway?
body_text: What is malloc doing, anyway? | Ben M. Andrew Skip to content Ben M. Andrew Blog Publications Projects Teaching Art Menu ; Safari, which supports neither, warms the HTTP cache with a low-priority fetch. A single shared listener collects the selectors from every include on the page; Chromium bails out early so it never double-fetches. The call below passes the selector through `json`, not wrapped in quotes of our own. Interpolated bare into a single-quoted literal, the header's `a[href^='/']` closed the string on its own apostrophe and the whole script was a SyntaxError — inert, and invisible, because the only browsers that reach this line are the ones with no native support to fall back from. --> What is malloc doing, anyway? Published Nov 8, 2026 malloc has a very nice and simple interface: you ask for a certain amount of memory, and you’re given a void pointer to your block of contiguous bytes that’s been magicked into existence. Once you’re done with it, you call free with the same pointer and the memory disappears into the ether. But what’s actually happening here? Obviously, as we’re running as a userspace program, malloc must be asking the kernel for the memory through syscalls . However, we may be allocating many small blocks, and syscalls are expensive (575 ns for an empty one, as measured below), so some bookkeeping is done in the background. We’ll demonstrate this on GNU libc ( glibc ) with the program snippet below, which calls malloc(16) a thousand times. static void * ptrs [ 1000 ] ; int main ( void ) { for ( int i = 0 ; i < 1000 ; i ++ ) ptrs [ i ] = malloc ( 16 ) ; } Using strace , we can see that the whole loop makes only two brk syscalls: the first asks where the program break is (the address where the process’s heap ends), and the second grows the heap by 132 KiB. These are both done in the first malloc call — the other 999 just take from that already allocated memory. $ strace -e trace = brk,mmap,munmap,write \ ./malloc1000 > /dev/null ... brk(NULL) = 0x59faca231000 brk(0x59faca252000) = 0x59faca252000 +++ exited with 0 +++ You may see both brk and sbrk mentioned in discussions. brk is a syscall that sets the program break to the address it is provided, and sbrk is a libc convenience wrapper that takes a delta , increasing the program break by that amount. The Address Space # A running process gets its own address space , split into a number of regions. These include text for executable code, data for initialised global variables, and bss for uninitialised global variables, among others. The following program prints one address from each region of the process. # define SHOW ( label , p ) \ printf ( "%-22s %p\n" , label , ( void * ) ( p ) ) SHOW ( "main (text)" , main ) ; SHOW ( "initialised (data)" , & initialised ) ; SHOW ( "uninitialised (bss)" , & uninitialised ) ; SHOW ( "malloc(16) (heap)" , malloc ( 16 ) ) ; SHOW ( "program break" , sbrk ( 0 ) ) ; SHOW ( "printf (libc)" , printf ) ; SHOW ( "local (stack)" , & local ) ; The addresses rise from the binary’s code up to its stack. $ ./layout main (text) 0x59c0791d7149 initialised (data) 0x59c0791da020 uninitialised (bss) 0x59c0791da028 malloc(16) (heap) 0x59c0903182b0 program break 0x59c090338000 printf (libc) 0x711dcf7c15b0 local (stack) 0x7ffff86c45ec Some of these regions can change as the program runs. For example, malloc(16) grows the heap and moves the break up. Note that in this run, the break and printf in libc are 23.4 TiB apart, about 1,530 times the machine’s 15.6 GiB of RAM. Nearly all of that range is unmapped, so it costs no physical memory. low high at start text data BSS gap break 23 TiB unmapped libc stack malloc(16) text data BSS gap heap break 23 TiB unmapped libc stack A Toy Allocator with sbrk # Because we can move the program break directly, we can write a little allocator of our own. This is called a bump allocator, because each call simply bumps up the amount of memory that we are allowed to use. void * my_malloc ( size_t size ) { void * p = sbrk ( align_up ( size ) ) ; return p == ( void * ) - 1 ? NULL : p ; } void my_free ( void * ptr ) { ( void ) ptr ; } This allocator is not very good! It moves the break on every single request, and each move is a syscall. We can time a syscall against malloc to see why malloc requests large blocks from the kernel and cuts them up itself. Each of the following three functions is timed over a million calls. static void * volatile sink ; static void call_getppid ( void ) { syscall ( SYS_getppid ) ; } static void call_sbrk ( void ) { sink = sbrk ( 16 ) ; } static void call_malloc ( void ) { sink = malloc ( 16 ) ; } sbrk(16) costs only 35 ns more than the empty syscall, whereas malloc(16) runs 22.7 times faster than sbrk(16) . $ ./syscall-cost syscall(SYS_getppid) 575.2 ns per call sbrk(16) 610.1 ns per call malloc(16) 26.9 ns per call sbrk(16) / malloc(16) 22.7x The bump allocator also has no way to reuse freed memory. Each request lands straight after the one before, so in the following example, d goes after c even though b has been freed. $ ./my-bump-1 a = my_malloc(16) start+0 b = my_malloc(1) start+16 c = my_malloc(100) start+32 my_free(b) d = my_malloc(1) start+144 break start+160 The rest of the post improves the allocator one stage at a time. Chunks and Headers # malloc actually allocates more memory than you request. This is because each allocation, or chunk , has a size header just before the returned pointer; this is how free works without passing an explicit size. Chunk sizes are always multiples of 16, so the low bits of the size are always zero, and glibc keeps three flags in them. header 24 bytes for the caller header p = malloc(24) next chunk chunk : 32 bytes size = 32 0 A 0 M 1 P one 8-byte word A : another arena M : own mapping P : chunk before in use size_t requests [ ] = { 1 , 24 , 25 , 1000 } ; size_t count = sizeof requests / sizeof requests [ 0 ] ; for ( size_t i = 0 ; i < count ; i ++ ) { char * p = malloc ( requests [ i ] ) ; size_t chunk = ( ( size_t * ) p ) [ - 1 ] & ~ ( size_t ) 7 ; printf ( "%8zu %8zu\n" , requests [ i ] , chunk ) ; } Each chunk is the request plus 8 bytes for the header, rounded up to a multiple of 16, with a minimum of 32. The rounding keeps every pointer that malloc returns 16-byte aligned, which is the alignment x86-64 gives max_align_t , so the memory suits any C type. The 32-byte minimum leaves room for the list pointers that a chunk stores once it is freed. $ ./chunk-header request chunk 1 32 24 32 25 48 1000 1008 When we free a chunk, it is put into what’s called a free list to allow reuse. When more data is requested, malloc looks through this free list and splits large chunks to fit small requests, and free merges free neighbours back together. Each chunk in the free list needs two pieces of information: its size (which we already have), and a pointer to the next chunk in the free list. glibc stores the pointer after the size, reusing the memory that the user stored their data in before it was freed! The toy allocator stores the same two fields in each chunk. typedef struct chunk { size_t size ; struct chunk * next ; } chunk_t ; Splitting and Coalescing # We can improve our my_malloc by rounding the request plus its header up to a multiple of 16 bytes, and taking the first chunk in the free list that is big enough. To keep things simple, the toy’s header is the whole chunk_t , so a chunk keeps room for next even while it is in use. That makes the header 16 bytes where glibc ’s is 8, and my_malloc(100) takes a 128-byte chunk where malloc(100) takes 112. void * my_malloc ( size_t size ) { size_t need = align_up ( size + HEADER_SIZE , ALIGN ) ; for ( chunk_t * * link = & free_list ; * link != NULL ; link = & ( * link ) -> next ) if ( ( * link ) -> size >= need ) return take ( link , need ) ; if ( grow_heap ( need ) != 0 ) return NULL ; return my_malloc ( size ) ; } We define take to split that chunk, leaving whatever the request does not need in the free list. static void * take ( chunk_t * * link , size_t need ) { chunk_t * c = * link ; if ( c -> size > need ) { chunk_t * rest = ( chunk_t * ) ( ( char * ) c + need ) ; rest -> size = c -> size - need ; rest -> next = c -> next ; c -> size = need ; * link = rest ; } else { * link = c -> next ; } return ( char * ) c + HEADER_SIZE ; } When no free chunk fits, grow_heap moves the program break up in 64 KiB steps using sbrk and puts the new space on the free list as one chunk. With headers, we can now actually implement a proper my_free function! It steps back from the pointer to the header and hands the chunk c to insert_free . That function walks the list to find the free chunks either side of c by address, prev and next , and links c in between them. Then, if c ends where next starts, or starts where prev ends, the two become one chunk. if ( next != NULL && ( char * ) c + c -> size == ( char * ) next ) { c -> size += next -> size ; c -> next = next -> next ; } if ( prev != NULL && ( char * ) prev + prev -> size == ( char * ) c ) { prev -> size += c -> size ; prev -> next = c -> next ; } A test program allocates a , b and c , frees a and b , allocates d , then frees the rest. a , b and c allocated a b c 65056 free_list my_free(a) 128 b c 65056 free_list my_free(b) merges a and b 352 c 65056 free_list d = my_malloc(50) splits the merged chunk d 272 c 65056 free_list my_free(c) merges both neighbours d 65456 free_list my_free(d) 65536 free_list Each line shows the chunk that the call allocated, if any, and then the free list. Every chunk is an [offset, size] pair counted from the start of the heap, and the offset is where its header starts, 16 bytes before the pointer that my_malloc returns. $ ./my-freelist-2 a = my_malloc(100) [0, 128] free: [128, 65408] b = my_malloc(200) [128, 224] free: [352, 65184] c = my_malloc(100) [352, 128] free: [480, 65056] my_free(a) free: [0, 128] [480, 65056] my_free(b) free: [0, 352] [480, 65056] d = my_malloc(50) [0, 80] free: [80, 272] [480, 65056] my_free(c) free: [80, 65456] my_free(d) free: [0, 65536] d gets the chunk at offset 0, split from the 352-byte chunk that a and b merged into. The bump allocator put its fourth request after everything else. Freeing c merges three chunks into one, and freeing d leaves the single 64 KiB chunk that grow_heap added. Demand Paging # my_free reuses memory, but it never returns any to the kernel. Whether a free chunk still costs RAM depends on when the kernel puts physical memory behind an address. Each process sees virtual memory , which the kernel maps onto physical RAM in 4 KiB pages . That separation allows the kernel to hand out address ranges with no physical RAM behind them — a virtual page only needs to be backed by physical memory on its first write . after sbrk : 8 pages added, none resident virtual physical after writing 3 pages : 3 faults, 3 resident virtual physical The following program moves the break up by 1 GiB, then writes one byte to every page and prints a row after each 256 MiB. char * p = sbrk ( SIZE ) ; print_row ( 0 ) ; for ( size_t offset = 0 ; offset < SIZE ; offset += PAGE_SIZE ) { p [ offset ] = 1 ; if ( ( offset + PAGE_SIZE ) % ( SIZE / 4 ) == 0 ) print_row ( ( long ) ( ( offset + PAGE_SIZE ) >> 20 ) ) ; } Virtual size counts the addresses the process has mapped, and resident set size (RSS) counts the pages that are in RAM. Straight after sbrk , virtual size is already just over 1 GiB, while RSS is 1308 KiB. Each 256 MiB written then costs 65,536 page faults, one per 4 KiB page, increasing the RSS. $ ./demand-paging written faults virtual resident 0 MiB 3 1050916 KiB 1308 KiB 256 MiB 65539 1050916 KiB 263536 KiB 512 MiB 131075 1050916 KiB 525680 KiB 768 MiB 196611 1050916 KiB 787824 KiB 1024 MiB 262147 1050916 KiB 1049968 KiB Once a chunk’s pages have been written, they stay resident after my_free , until the allocator gives them back to the kernel. Giving Memory Back # We give memory back to the kernel by lowering the break. We introduce a new function, trim , that lowers the break once the free chunk at the top of the heap reaches 128 KiB, keeping 64 KiB so that the next few requests don’t move the break straight back up. static void trim ( void ) { chunk_t * top = free_list ; if ( top == NULL ) return ; while ( top -> next != NULL ) top = top -> next ; char * end = ( char * ) top + top -> size ; if ( end != ( char * ) sbrk ( 0 ) || top -> size < TRIM_THRESHOLD ) return ; size_t release = ( top -> size - TOP_PAD ) / PAGE_SIZE * PAGE_SIZE ; top -> size -= release ; sbrk ( - ( intptr_t ) release ) ; } A test program allocates 1 MiB and then a 16-byte chunk above it, then writes to every page of the 1 MiB block. ( Anonymous RSS counts resident memory with no backing file, which keeps libc ’s code out of the numbers.) $ ./my-trim-3 break anonymous RSS my_malloc(1 MiB), my_malloc(16) start+1088 KiB 1124 KiB my_free(1 MiB) start+1088 KiB 1124 KiB my_free(16) start+64 KiB 160 KiB Freeing the 1 MiB block leaves the break at 1088 KiB and anonymous RSS at 1124 KiB, because the 16-byte chunk above it is still live. Once that chunk goes too, trim lowers the break to 64 KiB, dropping the anonymous RSS to 160 KiB. Only the top of the heap can be given back. A live chunk holds the break above it, so every free chunk below it stays resident, as the 1 MiB block did here. Over a long run, many allocations and deallocations leave free gaps between live chunks that later requests rarely fill, which is called fragmentation . These gaps stay resident, so in a long-running program, fragmentation can grow RSS until a memory limit kills the process. live chunk free chunk, or wholly free page page holding part of a live chunk all chunks freed … break all but the last freed … break every other chunk freed … break Large Blocks with mmap # The mmap syscall usually maps a file into the address space. With the MAP_ANONYMOUS flag there is no backing file, and the kernel creates a zero-filled, page-aligned mapping anywhere in the address space. Like the heap, its resident pages count towards the anonymous RSS. The munmap syscall returns a block with its own mapping to the kernel as soon as it is freed, whatever lies next to it. To integrate this into our own allocator, my_malloc chooses between sbrk and mmap by the size of the request. Any request of 128 KiB or more, header included, gets a mapping of its own from map_chunk , rounded up to whole pages; smaller requests take the existing sbrk free list path. static void * map_chunk ( size_t need ) { size_t len = align_up ( need , PAGE_SIZE ) ; chunk_t * c = mmap ( NULL , len , PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE , MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS , - 1 , 0 ) ; if ( c == MAP_FAILED ) return NULL ; c -> size = len | MMAPPED ; // chunk is mapped return ( char * ) c + HEADER_SIZE ; } For mmap ped chunks, we use one of the three flags in the size header (M) to record that this chunk has its own mapping. my_free checks this bit to know how to free it. It unmaps a mapped chunk with munmap , and puts any other chunk back on the free list, where trim can release it. void my_free ( void * ptr ) { if ( ptr == NULL ) return ; chunk_t * c = ( chunk_t * ) ( ( char * ) ptr - HEADER_SIZE ) ; if ( c -> size & MMAPPED ) { munmap ( c , c -> size & ~ ( size_t ) MMAPPED ) ; return ; } insert_free ( c ) ; trim ( ) ; } Running the previous demo again, we see that freeing the 1 MiB block drops the anonymous RSS while the 16-byte chunk is still live. $ ./my-mmap-4 break anonymous RSS my_malloc(1 MiB), my_malloc(16) start+64 KiB 1128 KiB my_free(1 MiB) start+64 KiB 100 KiB my_free(16) start+64 KiB 100 KiB The following diagram shows how this might look in the address space. low high before text data BSS gap heap break unmapped libc stack my_malloc(1 MiB) text data BSS gap heap break unmapped 1 MiB libc stack my_free(1 MiB) text data BSS gap heap break unmapped libc stack Why not mmap everything? Some allocators do! Even glibc creates extra heaps, called arenas , with mmap , and spreads threads across them so that they don’t all contend for the lock on the main heap. However, separate mappings have separate regions with no guarantee of contiguity, and chunks can’t be coalesced across these gaps. On the other hand, allocating with sbrk just bumps up the one contiguous region that you already have. A freed chunk that stays on the heap keeps its pages resident, so reusing it causes no page faults. Each new mapping starts with no physical memory behind it, and faults on every page it writes. Comparing Performance # We compare the performance of our allocators against glibc ’s malloc with a workload that repeatedly allocates and deallocates blocks of varying sizes 1 . To measure the speed, we find the average time of a step : free a random live block, allocate a replacement of random size, and write to each of its pages. At the end of the run, the live blocks hold 10.3 MiB. The last two columns give the anonymous RSS at that point, and again after every block is freed, which is the memory the allocator keeps. Allocator Average time per step (µs) Anonymous RSS, blocks live (MiB) Anonymous RSS, all freed (MiB) my-bump-1 1.72 1425 1425 my-freelist-2 5.12 17.8 17.8 my-trim-3 11.2 14.5 0.188 my-mmap-4 11.8 11.2 0.188 glibc 0.0789 19.0 19.0 my-bump-1 never frees or reuses memory, so its RSS is the 1425 MiB that the run allocates in total. Its 1.72 µs per step comes from an sbrk call for every request and page faults on new pages. my-freelist-2 reuses memory, so its RSS of 17.8 MiB is much closer to the 10.3 MiB of live data. However, each step walks the list twice: my_malloc walks it to find a fit, and insert_free walks it to find the chunk’s neighbours. my-trim-3 adds a third walk, because trim looks for the last free chunk on every my_free . my-freelist-2 and my-trim-3 run 65 and 142 times slower than glibc respectively. In return, my-trim-3 keeps only 0.188 MiB once every block is freed. my-mmap-4 calls mmap for large requests, which raises its time per step to 11.8 µs but gives it the lowest RSS with blocks live, at 11.2 MiB. Why is glibc so fast? The slowdowns in our allocators are due to having to walk a long free list of chunks multiple times. glibc instead keeps free chunks in bins , separate lists by size, so a request can walk a list of appropriately sized chunks directly. It also keeps up to seven freed chunks of each small size in a thread-local cache (tcache) and hands them straight back to the next request of that size. The tcache also explains the last column, where glibc keeps 19.0 MiB after every block is freed. The heap counts a cached chunk as in use, so one near the top stops glibc from lowering the break. The GLIBC_TUNABLES environment variable can turn the tcache off with GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.tcache_count=0 , or fix the mmap threshold at 128 KiB with GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.mmap_threshold=131072 . Allocator Average time per step (µs) Anonymous RSS, blocks live (MiB) Anonymous RSS, all freed (MiB) glibc 0.0789 19.0 19.0 glibc , tcache_count=0 0.121 17.4 0.250 glibc , mmap_threshold=131072 0.843 12.1 5.85 With the tcache off, freeing everything leaves 0.250 MiB, and each step takes 1.5 times as long as before. glibc makes 51 mmap calls in the whole run, against the 5040 that my-mmap-4 makes. Freeing a mapped chunk raises glibc ’s threshold to that chunk’s size, so later large requests come from the heap. With the threshold fixed at 128 KiB, every large request pays for its syscalls and page faults again, and glibc runs 10.7 times slower. malloc spends memory to stay away from the kernel, parcelling out large blocks in userspace so that most calls never make a syscall. Links # Reproducible snippets for each program ( link ). glibc ’s own description of its allocator’s internals, covering chunks, bins, arenas and the tcache ( link ). The man pages for brk(2) and sbrk(2) ( link ), mmap(2) ( link ), mallopt(3) ( link ) and malloc_trim(3) ( link ). The benchmark keeps 4000 blocks live, and each step frees a random block and allocates a replacement of a random size. Of the requests, 90% are 16 to 512 bytes, 9% are up to 16 KiB, and 1% are 128 KiB to 256 KiB. Each new block gets one write per page. An allocator runs 500,000 steps in a fresh process, built at -O2 . Run on an Intel Xeon E3-1230 v3. ↩︎ Liked this? I'm not convinced the AI bubble exists
body_text: Matteo's Website – I'm Not Convinced The AI Bubble Exists Github I'm Not Convinced The AI Bubble Exists Posted on Sun 08 November 2026 in AI The AI bubble is a speculative concept that the AI industry is extremely over-valued. If true, the value of most companies involved in AI (several of whom are worth well over a trillion dollars) will collapse, devastating the entire economy. If you check any online discussion about the financial situation of the AI industry, it's essentially taken for granted that the bubble exists and is going to pop any day now. I don't think that this is a reasonable assumption, though. Nobody can see the future, but I think that there's a pretty realistic chance that the meteoritic growth of AI companies in the past few years is justified, and that they have even more room for growth. Expenses Are Sky-High, But Constrained To say that AI companies are spending an absurd amount of money is an understatement. The debt and spending commitments for AI companies are handled through complex vehicles that make it difficult to tell exactly how much their expenses actually are (a serious problem, and one of the most salient points in favour of AI being a bubble), but they've committed to spending at least 3 trillion dollars so far . It's also been estimated that AI companies have already spent 1.9 trillion , bringing the overall expense of the AI industry to around 5 trillion dollars. This is unprecedented levels of investment, and AI just can't be profitable if this level of spending is maintained. However, there's no reason for why this level of spending has to be maintained in the first place. The reason why AI companies are spending so much money is to rollout data centres to run the AI in the first place. These expenses are one-off purchases, not regular operating expenses. Once all the data centres are built, AI spending is going to plummet. Outside of these expenses, AI doesn't cost that much to run. We don't have the full numbers for the entire industry here, but Anthropic's S-1 filing says that they make $2.08 for every $1 of compute. In other words, once you ignore the cost of building infrastructure, AI is very profitable. Crucially, the S-1 filing indicates that Anthropic has started to make more than their compute and infrastructure investments combined, which cuts against the idea that the cost of building data centres is inherently unsustainable. In a pinch, AI companies can also cut costs by no longer allowing people to use their products for free and temporarily suspending expensive AI research. This can be implemented instantly, whereas other kinds of expenses like leases and spending commitments are a lot harder to cut. The only serious long-term expenses to contend with here is the massive amount of debt that's been taken out to pay for these data centres in the first place. Like I said before, it's hard to really figure out these commitments because of the complex way that they're issued, but we can do some back of the envelope math. If the AI industry has to pay off 5 trillion dollars over the course of 20 years, that's 250 billion dollars a year. For context, Alphabet (parent company of Google and Youtube) reported earning almost 162 billion dollars of revenue just in 2019. Adjusted for inflation, that's an even more impressive 213 billion dollars. Because this is very rough math, the total needed revenue might come in to well over 250 billion dollars a year, but the point stands. Even though this is an enormous expense, paying it off isn't unthinkable with the data we have so far. Some of the debt is in convertible notes as well, which can be repaid through shares instead of cash. In the first 6 months of 2026, Anthropic has recorded 72 billion dollars of loss in the form of shares that are due to lenders. The cost is only so high because the valuation has skyrocketed to an estimated 1 trillion dollars, which means that Anthropic has more than enough equity to make lenders whole. Profits Can Grow, By A Lot In their S-1 filing, Anthropic records their revenue going from 41 million in 2023, 386 million in 2024, 4.585 billion in 2025, and 16.3 billion in the first 6 months of 2026. That's an insane increase in revenue, and it's safe to assume that other major AI companies like OpenAI are also seeing similar increases as well. At some point, the rate of increase has to level off, but that doesn't have to happen anytime soon. When I look at the current capacity of AI, it really feels like there's so much potential for frontier models to be used that just aren't being applied yet. Most (or maybe even all) programmers and mathematicians are worse at their respective field than an AI swarm equipped with a good harness, and a good deal more expensive as well. AI can't replace lawyers and doctors, but they can automate their paperwork and free up time for them to do other things. Outside of generative AI, self-driving cars are becoming a reality, with some evidence to suggest that they're even better than human drivers. AI adoption takes time, but there's no reason to think that AI usage isn't going to massively skyrocket, even if AI doesn't get any better than it is today (and it certainly will get better). In other words, there's massive unmet demand for AI companies to profit from. There's a weird contradiction you see from AI skeptics where they're afraid of how AI will change the world, but also seem convinced that AI will only ever produce slop that nobody would ever pay money for. You can't really have it both ways here. It's completely valid to be afraid of AI taking your job, but money is going to change hands when that happens. I don't know exactly what the future will look like or how long it'll take for mass AI adoption to really happen, but when I imagine how AI will change the world, it's hard for me to see AI consumption not being 10x what it is now. Google Has No Moat, But Neither Does McDonald's In 2023, a memo from Google called "We Have No Moat, And Neither Does OpenAI" was leaked, which outlined how the open source community was keeping pace with AI labs. More broadly, the memo rejected the idea that any company can really have a durable advantage when it comes to AI development. It would certainly be profitable if they could, but there's already so much information and research out there that nobody can ever hope for their frontier models to stay on the frontier for long. That means that there will never be a point where a company wins the AI wars, just nonstop fighting as each company in the industry tries to one-up the others. You know what other company didn't have a moat and found itself in a war to sell a product that its competitors could easily copy? Popeyes during the chicken sandwich war . I know that sounds goofy, but from a business perspective, it's remarkably similar. None of the restaurants involved in the chicken sandwich war had an enduring competitive advantage over any of the others, and all of them had to deal with potential customers choosing to just cook at home instead, but it was still highly profitable for everybody involved. Simply saying that a company doesn't have a moat isn't enough to say that the company can't make money. In theory, an AI company has to be worried about their users switching over to a competitor or using an open source model instead. In practice, this isn't a major concern. For starters, the average person isn't going to use a locally hosted model, ever. I know that it's a common hobby in tech circles, but normal users don't want to have to deal with the hassle or expense of setting up something that's going to perform at most the exact same as ChatGPT. That means that in principle, there's only going to be a few models that the vast majority of people will ever use. People can theoretically switch from model to model, but people tend to settle in with a product and develop brand loyalty. For example, I pretty much only use ChatGPT, not because I have any really reason to, but because it was the first LLM that I ever used. This partially offsets the risk of losing customers to a different product. Another way that companies can make money without having a moat is through institutional lock-in. Once a large corporation has integrated a particular AI into their day to day operation, transitioning away isn't costless. They may even have contracts agreeing to buy a certain amount of tokens, which binds them to keep using the AI instead of transitioning. There's Still Plenty Of Capital To Raise A potential way for a bubble to pop is for the companies involved to run out of capital to spend while they grow, causing them to fail. With the enormous amount of churn and debt that AI companies have, this is a serious risk to consider. Even so, I think that it's premature to worry about these companies failing to raise capital when most of them haven't even had an IPO yet. When SpaceX (which is partially an AI company, despite the name) went public, they raised more than 80 billion dollars . Besides that, many AI companies haven't issued public debt yet, which is a major way to get loans if private lenders decide that they don't want to put more of their capital into AI. The ones that have issued public debt, like Alphabet and Meta, have excellent bond ratings. If they need more capital, they won't struggle to find people to give them a loan. Of course, investors aren't the only way to get capital. Once AI companies become profitable (as they already seem to be), they can use those profits to fund growth and pay off debts. The idea that AI companies are forced to constantly look for new investors to keep their doors open is probably a few months antiquated. From how it looks from Anthropic's S-1, the AI world may be past the horizon when it came to taking risky bets and can now focus on reaping the rewards. The AI Industry Doesn't Look Like Any Bubble We've Seen Before When a bubble happens, it's usually preceded by the companies involved reaching obviously inflated evaluations, which makes the burst obvious in hindsight. With public AI companies, we don't see that happening. Alphabet, Meta, and NVIDIA are all AI companies that have seen their market capitalization explode over the past few years, but all of them have stable P/E ratios in their 20s. If the increase in their valuations were irrational (or even just in expectation of future growth as opposed to current earnings), you would expect the P/E ratios to go up. Instead, their valuations look exactly what we would expect from a healthy trillion dollar company. When the dot-com bubble happened, it was largely driven by companies that couldn't turn a profit or had P/E ratios in the hundreds. I'm not going to pretend that I'm an expert on financial bubbles, but I've never heard of a bubble where the companies involved had such a modest valuation based on their earnings, even if their earnings (and therefore their evaluations) are enormous. A potential way that this could be a bubble is if AI proves to be a fad. A lot of this rise in valuations has been because of increased demand for GPUs and data centre utilization, which is downstream of the demand for AI. We might imagine that the AI labs are propped up by an enormous amount of invested capital, and this capital ends up propping up the valuations for companies that make or rent out GPUs. However, this doesn't seem to be happening. Alphabet has a full-stack AI supply chain, where they create ASICs for AI, train their own AI, integrate AI into their products, and rent out compute to customers. Their prospectus helpfully divides their revenue streams into Google Cloud for their rented compute and Google Services, which makes it easy to tell if Alphabet's increased earnings are mostly because of their data centres. The answer is no. Google Cloud revenue is growing more in terms of percentage, but Google Services is growing far more in absolute terms. Specifically, Google Services revenue grew by 37.8 billion dollars for a 12% increase, while Google Cloud revenue grew by 15.5 billion dollars for a 36% increase. Alphabet is definitely benefiting from renting out their data centres, but it's not the main reason why their earnings have skyrocketed. Meta doesn't rent out their data centres at all, but their prospectus also records them having massive increases in their revenue, on the order of an extra 30 billion dollars from 2024 to 2025, and another extra 30 billion from 2023 to 2024. This isn't foolhardy investors throwing money at any company that makes AI, this is real profit from companies that have found ways to monetize AI. Anthropic also seems to be experiencing an exponential growth in their revenue as well, based on their S-1 filing. The only real unknown is OpenAI, which purchases an enormous amount of compute from other companies. It's possible that their finances are terrible, but even if they go under, I'm not convinced that this amounts to a bubble bursting. If anything, it seems more likely that their competitors will just consolidate and fight for more of a market share instead of the collapse triggering a chain reaction that takes the industry down with it. Conclusion I didn't write this article as some big takedown of the AI bubble theory. Even with this evidence, there are serious risks to the financial sustainability of the AI industry. Public backlash against data centres are going to make it harder for the infrastructure necessary for the AI revolution to continue, and regulatory barriers may make it harder to develop or deploy new models. Besides that, there's an enormous risk of an autonomous AI hacker causing serious damage, causing public demand for AI to plummet. Also, even after writing out it's possible for AI companies to pay off their debt, I'm still concerned by how much it actually is. It's not good that they're using increasingly complex ways to fund their infrastructure investments, and this gamble can backfire if revenue growth suddenly slows down, which it certainly might. Don't YOLO your life savings on the AI revolution, or at least don't blame me if you lose the shirt off of your back. The reason I wrote this article is because I felt that discussion about AI has become something of an echo chamber, which is never a good way to figure out what's right or wrong. Despite the echo chamber, people's stated beliefs and actual behaviour are wildly divergent. It's one thing to say that AI is a bubble that's going to burst, but where is this investor money coming from if we're all in agreement here? At the end of the day, when people have to put their money where their mouth is, they pull it out of their mouth and use it to buy NVIDIA. They might be wrong to do so, but maybe they're not. Time will tell. As one final note, I don't think the rhetoric about the AI bubble is really about finances. Conversation about the AI bubble is too widespread for it to be a contrarian position, and too gleeful to be driven by investors' fear. More than anything, I think the supposed AI bubble has become such a large talking point because it represents the hope that things can go back to how they used to be. People are afraid of what's going to happen with AI, and rightfully so. Beyond fear for the future, AI in the present has become uncomfortably common, with AI slop everywhere online and increasingly even IRL. This has all happened so fast, it's easy to forget that ChatGPT came out a little less than 4 years ago. Our world has changed in such a scary and odd way, and while I have a pretty optimistic view of AI overall, I get why people would want it all to go away. So, people wishcast. They tell themselves that this is all a giant bubble, and one day soon, everything will crash down and immediately go back to how it used to be. For better or worse, that's not going to happen. Even if AI turns out to be a bubble, it will be a bubble in the same way that the internet was a bubble, where the underlying technology remains useful. We're only ever going to live in the AI era from this point on, and whatever happens as a result of that, hopefully it will at least be good for the economy. Email address Subscribe All Articles Share: marketers-guide-to-open-claw Sponsored content Presented by â Image Credit: State of AI AI & Technology Goldman Sachs Is Pulling Claude Code From Its Bankers and Traders In July, Goldman's tech chief was praising the tools traders built with AI coding agents. New internal guidance hands those agents back to the engineers, weeks before Goldman takes Anthropic public. By State of AI Editorial Nov 2, 2026 Goldman Sachs has restricted Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub to its engineers, cutting off traders and bankers who used the tools to track client flows and build market models. The bank barred its Hong Kong bankers from Claude in April and is now a lead underwriter on Anthropic's IPO. Most traders and bankers at Goldman Sachs can no longer use AI coding tools at work. Internal guidance updated in October restricts Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub to the bank's engineers, Bloomberg News reported , following a review of productivity and risk concerns. Strats, who work across trading, quantitative research and software engineering, still have access, according to a second person familiar with the matter. The change has frustrated some traders, a person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg. They had been using the tools to monitor client trading flows, model market moves and positions, and put together written and graphic material. Goldman spokesperson Nick Carcaterra said the bank makes certain AI tools available to staff "to determine the best use cases" across the firm. Argenti was praising trader-built tools in July As recently as July, chief information officer Marco Argenti was talking up "vibe coding" by Goldman's non-technical employees. He told Bloomberg that traders and bankers had built tools with AI and passed them to the firm's engineers, of whom there are about 12,000, to be improved. That arrangement let the people closest to a problem build a first version without waiting for engineering time. It also meant thousands of employees without engineering training were running software that writes and executes code, on the same machines they use to handle client information. At a conference in Turin last month, Argenti described Goldman's AI adoption in waves and said developers, more than 12,000 of the bank's roughly 47,000 staff, had made up the first. The October guidance limits the coding agents to that group. Goldman restricted Claude in Hong Kong in April In April, Goldman removed Claude from its internal AI platform for bankers in Hong Kong. The Financial Times reported that the bank had read its contract with Anthropic strictly , and an Anthropic spokesperson said Claude had never been officially supported in Hong Kong. ChatGPT and Gemini remained available there. JPMorgan removed Claude from its Hong Kong approved list in June. The Hong Kong restriction was based on location and contract terms, and the new one is based on role. Goldman's in-house AI assistant, which uses models from several companies, is still available across the firm. The restriction applies to third-party agents that can write and run code by themselves. Goldman is still working closely with Anthropic Earlier this year, Goldman said Anthropic engineers had spent six months at the bank helping build Claude-based agents for trade accounting and client onboarding . Those agents sit in the back office and are run by Goldman's engineering teams. Goldman and Morgan Stanley are also the lead underwriters on Anthropic's IPO , according to the S-1 filed October 26. Anthropic is expected to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT before the end of November, as we reported last week . Over the next few weeks, Goldman's bankers will be marketing shares in a company whose coding agent most of them are no longer allowed to use. Why a coding agent is riskier on a trading desk Claude Code reads files, writes programs and runs them, typically with the same access as the person using it. Code an engineer writes with it usually goes through review, testing and deployment controls before it reaches anything important. A script a trader builds to watch client flows can end up in daily use without going through any of those. Banks are also required to keep information barriers between groups, for example between bankers working on deals and traders who could profit from knowing about them. Goldman built its internal AI platform around controls like these. A tool a trader puts together with an agent wasn't designed with them in mind, and engineers can only check it if someone sends it their way. There is also the matter of whether anyone understands the code. Last month a Meta engineer said he now ships code he can't fully account for , and writing software is his job. A trader using an agent to model positions is less likely to know how that code handles unusual cases, which on a trading desk can mean losses. Cost may also have played a part. Agent usage is billed by the token, and several companies that gave agents to everyone have seen spending climb. Amazon shut down an internal leaderboard after employees ran agents on pointless tasks to move up it, and Accenture now funds $29 a month of Claude per employee . Bloomberg's sources said productivity was part of Goldman's review. Barclays is moving in the other direction Barclays said in October that it expects half its developers to be using Claude Code by the end of the year, and three weeks later named developers among 5,000 job cuts . Like Goldman, it is giving coding agents to engineers. Unlike Goldman, it is also using them to reduce how many engineers it employs. Banks have tightened agent access in other places this fall. JPMorgan and Schwab are blocking outside agents from customer accounts , and Goldman has now set limits on which of its own employees can use them. Our take At State of AI, we think Goldman was right to restrict the tools and wrong in how it went about it. A trading floor is a bad place for unreviewed code written by people who can't read it, and the information barrier problem would be reason enough on its own. Requiring that agent-written code come from people trained to review it is a sensible rule for a regulated business. Goldman's own CIO was promoting traders' AI-built tools in July, though. Withdrawing access through a guideline update, with no replacement mentioned in Bloomberg's reporting, tells the traders who found good uses that they were the risk. Their complaints point to work the engineering team could take on, and Goldman would get more out of collecting them than out of waiting for them to fade. Leaders at other companies should settle who owns agent-built code before handing agents out. When someone outside engineering builds a tool with Claude Code or Copilot, a named engineer should take responsibility for it before it touches production data. Existing controls should cover code an agent writes. Information barriers, data entitlements and software approval rules still apply when the code came from a prompt. And when a tool is taken away, it's worth recording what people were using it for. Goldman's traders were watching client flows and modeling positions, and they will still need to do both. title: ChatGPT Desktop forwards your SSH agent to remote machines
body_text: ChatGPT Desktop forwards your SSH agent to remote machines | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login ChatGPT Desktop forwards your SSH agent to remote machines 215 points by DenGorbachev 1 day ago | hide | past | favorite | 77 comments The agent running on a remote machine can authenticate using your local SSH credentials. That means it can push to your private repos on GitHub, for example. Proof: https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/28131#discussion_r3410013180   help recsv-heredoc 1 day ago | next [–] It's amazing how often product decisions head this way for the purposes of 'removing friction'. In security, friction is a GOOD thing. You want to have some ceremony to do things. It's pretty much inevitable that people will give up control for convenience. Look at Artifacts for example. reply jasonjayr 1 day ago | parent | next [–] I think this is another oppertunity for folks to think of security, especially technical folks. (And maybe even another market pricing differentiator): User account management systems should more widely allow users to make permission-restricted 'subaccounts'. In this bold new era where folks are delegating their machines to take actions on their behalf, we need a new way that is far more fine grained than "all, ask every time, or nothing". Choosing how to sub-divide abilities, and allowing the user to manage that, will be an art unto itself, and depend largely on the system. Thinking a banking API with a rule like "Allow sub user to send payment to water utility once per month, not to exceed $200". The user only needs to intervene if something goes wrong and the amount goes over. reply saidnooneever 13 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] You are right. People should thing about it, and your comment is even very mild and polite. People give the keys to their kingdom to some program that will even hallucinate and do all sorts of stuff. WHY. it's stupid. that's not harsh, that's the truth. Before AI (LLMs), people were much more careful with this sort of stuff, but now they give their keys away to some program which has tons of agency and expect that program to somehow be responsible on their behalf. it's stupid. Be responsible. LLMs even if tailored truly correctly with all the safety guards can just hallucinate and do shit anyway, so if you don't lock them down, or if you give them your secrets, that _will_ end badly at some point. Even if hallucinations only happen 0.0001% of the time, that is 1 in 10000, and you do tons and tons of tool calls and model calls even if you only put in 1 prompt, so really, the probability is HIGH. Sure, the probability of that hallucination also involving a secret is much lower, but it is still HIGH if you consider using LLMs for months or years... reply novarii_ 5 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] check this out https://strandsagents.com/blog/strands-box-the-big-picture/ reply halJordan 22 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Not to naysay, but look no further than the people here to see why that wouldn't work. You think rbac or zero trust is gonna fly when half the people here decry it as a worthless checkbox when they see it on their mandated cybersecurity list? Come on man, be reasonable reply saidnooneever 13 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] rbac surely won't work if you chuck your keys into an LLM. People need to be responsible. They are all lazy. Happy to give away any agency and responsibility to a computer program and scream bloody murder when it goes awry. reply hgoel 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] I think it's always worth bringing up the risk of 'confirmation fatigue' in these kinds of discussions. Friction is not universally good for security. Too much friction and your users start blindly confirming everything instead of reading/thinking. This is already a problem with LLM tool calls (due to which, everyone seems to be pushing towards an 'allow all, with some exceptions' type model). reply 1broseidon 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] Friction is good when it serves a security purpose, not for its own sake. Too much of it and users either stop using the thing or find ways around it, which is arguably worse - as you pointed out! To have LESS friction you need MORE signals, ones that add up to "this action is low risk, proceed" as a cumulative risk score. Kind of like credit card transactions... most transactions go through silently because the issuer scores them on merchant, amount, device and history, and you only get the step-up prompt when the score is off. "Manual Approval" and "Bypass Everything" are both what you ship when you have no signals. reply cyanydeez 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] it took NIST a decade to realize that constantly making users change passwords for no other reason but the wall clock changed increased the use of insecure password practices. It is indeed a world of reality vs what sounds good on paper. reply arghwhat 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] Which is in turn why for convenience, security is a bad thing, making people who do not think about threat models in their sleep opt out. Problem is striking the right balance, and auto-forwarding your agent to foreign machines is not the right balance. At least not without being able to filter and approve individual signing requests. reply api 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] It's an inherent tension, and is also why so many things are insecure. People hate friction, and so they don't use secure stuff and turn security features off. Security abominations like "curl | bash" and package managers that traverse trees and download stuff and run scripts are popular for a reason. It's true in the real world too which is why even in secure buildings a person can often slip in by coat-tailing someone. Stopping every single person to check ID is cumbersome and slows everyone down. People have stuff to do. Truly high security environments are zero-tolerance, which makes them annoying and expensive to work in. I've talked to people who have worked in US military and CIA/NSA places and a very meaningful amount of time is spent complying with security and jumping through hoops. Even with all that, stuff gets leaked and stolen. reply xg15 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] > Security abominations like "curl | bash" Just to be clear: As a user, I would love to get rid of curl | bash and use the OS package manager instead. This would actually be more convenient to me: I wouldn't have to hunt through the documentation to find out what was installed, where it was installed, how I can update it (or does it run its own auto-updater?) and how - or if - I can uninstall it again. Unfortunately, I can't, if this is pushed as a software's primary - or only - installation method on Linux. This seems more like a "convenience" for certain software projects that can't be bothered to interact with distro maintainers and instead want to circumvent the distro system entirely. reply api 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] The problem is there’s no other way. Linux is 20 OSes in a trenchcoat. There is no standard way to do what you ask. reply xg15 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] No, but there is a handful of widely used distributions, which could us already get 80% of the way done. Why not at least provide a Debian/Ubuntu and Red Hat package? reply 10111001 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] > It's an inherent tension, and is also why so many things are insecure. People hate friction... It's not just in computer security, it's in almost everything. People hate friction, but they need it make good decisions. What we really need is smart people creating well-designed eusocial frictions, rather than trying to mindlessly eliminate friction from all areas. But guess which thing leads to products that can be sold more successfully on the market? reply siva7 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] > In security, friction is a GOOD thing. Oh boy, it isn't. Friction leads to frustration and therefore more likelihood to ignore the importance altogether. reply mjr00 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] This is a great point. If something is overly complex and arduous often times people will find a way to go "under the table" and do something in a way that accomplishes the goal but undermines the process. The classic example is password rotation. It used to be standard to force users to rotate their passwords every 30/90 days, but that led to users having a sticky note on their monitor with their password on it, so security authorities no longer recommend this practice. reply rolosa 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] My work still forces password rotations. Everyone I know jokes about just changing the last character of their password each time, eg horse-staple-battery-1 to -2 to -3 etc. reply aleksskoz 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] It's about balance between security and getting things done. When I give an AI a task, I say: do this and this, but your boundaries are here and here. It should only do what it's allowed to. Even in simple cases, like running separate sessions on different tasks, they shouldn't be able to touch each other's work. One more thing on balancing security and speed: I run regular audits and vulnerability checks, so I know the gaps are actually closed. reply scotty79 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] > In security, friction is a GOOD thing. Sure, but in work, friction is not a good thing. So maybe security, if it involves friction, is not a good thing in work? Popularity of npm might be and evidence of that. Distribution system (along in its integration in a myriad of pojects) that's pretty insane from the security stanpoint contributed to so much great stuff and cooperation. reply NoPicklez 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] What about Artifacts for example? reply littlecranky67 1 day ago | prev | next [–] I'd suggest to use ssh keys inside the secure enclave on macOS that require your fingerprint for every new session [0]. That way agents cannot initiate anything, and you will always be aware when a new ssh connection is being made. [0]: https://gist.github.com/arianvp/5f59f1783e3eaf1a2d4cd8e952bb... reply bradfa 1 day ago | parent | next [–] Or in a Yubikey and set the touch-required mechanism (light in the key will blink when it needs a touch to continue the auth). reply itissid 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] I've been using secretive on the mac for exactly this. reply lucasoshiro 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] Secretive is amazing! I know that it's not its purpose, but it would be great if it could store more than ssh keys, like providing a safe place for my .envs reply vulture916 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] I know it's not open-source, but this is how I use 1Password with FIFO .envs. I'm unsure if 1P stores its SSH in the enclave, but it works the same way - whenever SSH key is accessed, it prompts for TouchID or password. Besides the open source, any reason why I should use secretive over 1P? - someone trying to be better about security no matter how annoyed. reply lucasoshiro 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] > know it's not open-source, but this is how I use 1Password with FIFO .envs I tried it some months ago, but it didn't work so well... The FIFO approach looks elegant, but in practice it doesn't work so well (maybe because the application was trying to read it twice?). The best I could do with 1P was to store the env var as a password and retrieve through the CLI... reply petesergeant 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] > I'm unsure if 1P stores its SSH in the enclave I am reasonably sure the answer is no, as evidenced by it being exportable reply littlecranky67 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] macOS secure enclave supports exportable keys (see the link I posted). Still think 1P is not using it, though. reply petesergeant 20 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Your link is describing keys that are encrypted using a key in the secure enclave, not keys exportable from the secure enclave; the latter would defeat the whole purpose of a secure enclave. reply vulture916 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Good point, that makes sense. reply causal 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] 1Password also supports this BUT that does not prevent your agent from being forwarded and you still have to inspect each command being used if you don't trust your agent. Halfway better would be a separate key for each concern, then check that the key you expect to be used is being used before authorizing. reply Lukas_Skywalker 1 day ago | prev | next [–] The Bitwarden desktop app has a built in SSH agent [1], which lets you store SSH keys inside Bitwarden. I have set the app to always ask me for confirmation when the key is requested. [1] https://bitwarden.com/help/ssh-agent/ reply InsidiousWombat 1 day ago | parent | next [–] you can make your SSH agent do that, no need to use bitwarden. If you're using say yubikey for hardware ssh key (via gpg ssh agent/smartcard interface) you can also make it require physical touch of the key to confirm every operation reply hgoel 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] Plus, if you're using the Yubikey for hardware SSH, you can't use the Bitwarden SSH agent anyway. It just isn't compatible. It's one of my bigger frustrations with its SSH agent feature, as I prefer to have my GitHub SSH key on Bitwarden. reply alsdkgjhgd 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] the biggest issue with the yubikey touch verification is that you have no way of telling what you're verifying, especially if some tool helpfully forwarded your agent, or is trying to maintain ssh connections in the background first time you see the light blinking without doing anything intentional is a bit of a sinking feeling reply tylergetsay 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] If your machine has a TPM chip you can also use that and require a PIN to unlock it, with a mandatory lock out period enforced by the chip reply rolosa 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] How do I do it with touchid and a MacBook Air? reply MSP_Logic 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] Secretive should do this. It generates a key inside the secure enclave, and you can set it to require TouchID, so you know whenever it's used. Keys can't be exported either. reply concretebush 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] you can generate a key in the secure enclave then use that with touchid every time to authenticate - see eg. https://nmattia.com/posts/2026-10-19-setting-up-ssh-keys-tou... reply WhyNotHugo 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] Himitsu's ssh-agent does the same, and if you use some agent that uses a secret-service backend, you'd get the same result. It's mostly the default ssh-agent that has a different security model. reply petesergeant 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] 1Password too, FWIW reply wolttam 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] As well as KeepassXC reply yfontana 1 day ago | prev | next [–] I don't understand what the linked pull request is supposed to prove, considering it was closed and not merged. reply paxy 1 day ago | parent | next [–] You’re supposed to look at the title and get outraged. reply m000 1 day ago | prev | next [–] At this point, should cases like this even be news? Isn't that a fundamental security design issue? Local agent security guardrails appear to always be built around blacklists, which will always be unreliable and leaky. It is left as an exercise to the user to properly sandbox them. There may be some limited form of whitelisting, but often it is just a facade, as it is very coarse-grained. So, with tools with very broad capabilities (ssh, kubectl, gcloud, etc) you end up with the agent performing unwanted actions. reply wizardashwin 3 hours ago | prev | next [–] I wonder if they skip running security reviews before every release. The latest models catch these while building and its surprising to see that end products are shipped with vulnerabilities reply carterschonwald 1 day ago | prev | next [–] this is a normal ssh feature meant to allow keys to be used while keeping keys local … its actually a keystone of secure infrastructure setups, aka jump hosts. granted its meant for human or scripted uses, as is everything else reply minitech 1 day ago | parent | next [–] You don’t need to (and should not) forward your SSH agent just to set up a tunnel, especially with the default OpenSSH ssh-agent. It allows the intermediate host to decide what operations to do with your key(s). `ProxyJump` is a way safer default. reply hamburglar 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] A normal ssh feature that a lot of people consider a really clever maneuver, but many highly locked down environments expressly forbid because it’s a liability. reply krunck 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] > keystone of secure infrastructure But only when YOU choose where your SSH agent is accessible. reply carterschonwald 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] very true :) reply otterley 1 day ago | prev | next [–] If this bothers you, it can be guarded against in your ssh config file: Host trusted-server HostName server.example.com ForwardAgent yes Host another-trusted-server HostName another.example.com ForwardAgent yes Host * ForwardAgent no reply mbreese 1 day ago | parent | next [–] Isn’t that the default setting for `Host *`? That’s why you have explicitly turn it on for other hosts, right? reply eosis 1 day ago | prev | next [–] Things are awful for this at the moment. [Was the same for docker desktop at some point.]( https://rupertrutledge.com/posts/docker-sbx-s-ssh-security-i... ) Same for [devpod]( https://devpod.sh/ ) for sshing to devcontainers. They are particularly annoying because they just dump it into your config. Use an include statement to your own file for goodness sake. It was often not ideal in the old world. Now agents are doing everything in those boxes, it is kind of mad. I have my own utilities now for managing these sockets and files now to deal with this stuff. reply cyberpunk 1 day ago | prev | next [–] This is why your ssh key should be on a yubi and you should have to touch it (confirm presence) to use it. you dont even need anything special anymore to do this just ssh-keygen -t whatever-sk and the magic happens. same key can sign commits... reply mbreese 1 day ago | prev | next [–] I’m not sure this is quite the smoking gun. This PR was closed as not merged and the entire process is described as opt-in. Is there other evidence of Codex abusing or surreptitiously extending an ssh agent? reply UndividedDev 1 day ago | prev | next [–] Setting up fingerprint / password authentication via secretive for ssh key access made me realize how often these tools try to do something without explicitly asking reply stemc43 1 day ago | prev | next [–] Opencode open chamber and just using openrouter models. Nobody needs codex or Claude these days. Deepseek 4.1 is just as good. reply VCFundedGenYer 1 day ago | prev | next [–] Regular reminder to never download/install AI chatbot apps - they all work in a browser where they can be isolated. Do not let these things loose on your computer. reply mrweasel 1 day ago | parent | next [–] At work we have rather strict rules for how to run AI agents, and for good reasons apparently. The problem is that once these rules are in place and enforced, using an agent is just more hassle that I feel it's worth. The agents work in complete isolation in a VM with access to pretty much nothing. Some colleagues are making good use of them, but just looking at the policies and tooling we have put in place makes me give up in advance. reply causal 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] I find a lot of people take a very backward approach to agents: They adopt desktop versions with full access first, and only later discover sandboxes and cloud environments. Claude and ChatGPT both come with free cloud sandboxes that work great! If they are just writing code there's little reason to hand over your laptop. reply stephbook 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] Not everyone programs nuclear reactors. If you have a business account where client requests come in over GMail/Slack and you just do web design/payment integration or some such, go wild. If you have a corporate codebase and access to prod, as well as family photos, well — different beast. reply afzalive 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] For e2e testing? reply viccis 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] >free cloud sandboxes Can't speak to Claude, but the OpenAI cloud environments cost you something like 3x token usage last I looked into it. reply TacticalCoder 1 day ago | prev | next [–] > The agent running on a remote machine can authenticate using your local SSH credentials. No it doesn't. I'm using and enforcing SSH U2F keys. You physically press on a Yubikey (or similar) or you don't authenticate. As for my own Git server, it's of course over SSH and it requires pressing the Yubikey too. As a sidenote as I do it from Magit I modified Magit to add a small but obvious message stating that the Yubikey probably awaits touching (otherwise it's easy to miss / not realize). The great thing with all these hacks and bad practices is that I believe, eventually, people are going to learn better security hygiene. reply viccis 1 day ago | prev | next [–] Back in my pen testing days, agent forwarding was a gift from heaven when I was on a Linux machine. reply simoncion 1 day ago | prev | next [–] This sucks, a lot, but you've gotta never run these tools as your ordinary daily-driver account. These tools are rather unpredictable and -because of the nature of the incredibly reckless development methodology- it's nearly impossible to understand every behavioral change in new versions of the ones that are largely or entirely vibecoded.
